nodes.name: Cardholder
nodes.description: The person a payment card is issued to, who pays with it and can challenge charges through the card issuer.
nodes.markdown:
A cardholder is the person a payment card is issued to. In the [four-party model](node:Four-party%20model), the cardholder pays a [merchant](node:Merchant), and their [issuer](node:Issuer) decides whether to approve the payment and then bills them or debits their account.

The cardholder is not always the party that owns the account or the person who placed the order. Those differences explain many payment support cases.

| Role                | Who it is                         | Example                            |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Cardholder          | Person issued the card            | Employee with a company card       |
| Account holder      | Party responsible for the account | The company paying the card bill   |
| Merchant's customer | Person who placed the order       | A teenager using a parent's card   |

The last row causes a common failure. A parent sees an unfamiliar line on a statement, does not connect it with a purchase made by someone in the household, and reports it to the bank. The merchant then receives a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) for an order that was delivered correctly. This is one route to [friendly fraud](node:Friendly%20fraud), and a clear [statement descriptor](node:Statement%20descriptor) makes it less likely.

Cardholder protection depends on region and product. In the EU, [PSD2](node:PSD2) gives payers [refund](node:Refund) rights for unauthorised transactions and limits their liability. In the US, Regulation Z covers credit cards and Regulation E covers debit cards, with different limits. Network dispute rights sit alongside these laws, and the cardholder uses them by contacting the issuer rather than the [card network](node:Card%20network).

Merchants should keep only the cardholder data they need. The card number, or [PAN](node:PAN), and the [CVV](node:CVV) are covered by [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS), so most systems hold a [token](node:Tokenization) in their place.
quotes: This customer says they never bought from us, but the order shipped to their home address.
Someone else in the household may have used the card. Send the cardholder the order details before the dispute goes further.

nodes.name: Merchant
nodes.description: A business or person that accepts card payments for goods or services, directly or through a facilitator.
nodes.markdown:
A merchant is a business or person that accepts a card as payment for goods or services. Visa's rules separate a merchant with its own agreement with an [acquirer](node:Acquirer) from a sponsored merchant that contracts through a [payment facilitator](node:Payment%20facilitator). Mastercard uses similar categories, and treats the facilitator as acting for the acquirer.

A business selling online is not automatically the merchant on the card transaction. The contract decides that.

| Setup                                                | Contract is with                      | Seller shown on the transaction |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Direct merchant                                      | Acquirer                              | The business                    |
| Sponsored merchant                                   | Payment facilitator                   | The business                    |
| Retailer on a marketplace                            | Marketplace                           | Usually the marketplace         |
| Product sold through a [merchant of record](node:Merchant%20of%20record) | Reseller acting as merchant of record | The reseller                    |

The merchant agrees to follow [card network](node:Card%20network) rules through its contract. In practice this means describing the business accurately, showing a recognisable [statement descriptor](node:Statement%20descriptor), protecting card data under [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS), issuing a [refund](node:Refund) when owed, and answering each [chargeback](node:Chargeback). For most online payments the merchant also carries the loss from fraud unless a [liability shift](node:Liability%20shift) applies.

Each merchant is identified by a merchant ID assigned by its acquirer and classified with a [merchant category code](node:Merchant%20category%20code). This classification is a frequent source of trouble. A business approved to sell software that starts selling supplements or gift cards no longer matches what it declared. The acquirer may notice through monitoring, then pause its [payout](node:Payout) or close the [merchant account](node:Merchant%20account) while it reviews the activity.

To avoid that, tell the acquirer or [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) before adding a product line, changing ownership, or selling in a new country.
quotes: Why did our payouts stop after we launched the gift card range?
We were onboarded as a software merchant. Risk flagged the new product, so we need to update our business profile with the acquirer.

nodes.name: Issuer
nodes.description: The bank or licensed institution that provides a card, approves or declines its payments and handles cardholder disputes.
nodes.markdown:
An issuer is the bank or licensed financial institution that provides a payment card to a [cardholder](node:Cardholder) and holds the account behind it. When a card is used, the issuer makes the final decision on the [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization).

| Stage         | What the issuer does                                                    |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Card issue    | Checks the customer, opens the account, sets limits, provides the card  |
| Authorization | Checks funds, card status and fraud risk, then approves or declines     |
| [Clearing](node:Clearing)      | Receives the final transaction record and posts it to the account       |
| [Settlement](node:Settlement)    | Pays the amount owed through the [card network](node:Card%20network)                              |
| Dispute       | Takes the cardholder's claim and may raise a [chargeback](node:Chargeback)                    |

The issuer is often confused with the network. A customer may say "Visa declined my card", but Visa and Mastercard do not usually make the credit or balance decision. The issuer does, and a [merchant](node:Merchant) or [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) cannot override it. When a payment fails at checkout with a generic [decline code](node:Decline%20code), the person who can explain it is usually the issuer's support team. The merchant often sees only the code.

The issuer is also a different party from the [acquirer](node:Acquirer), which works for the merchant. One bank can play both roles in different transactions.

Consumer fintech cards add a layer. The app's brand may appear on the card while a licensed bank or e-money institution is the actual issuer, often with a program manager running the product. A [sponsor bank](node:Sponsor%20bank) arrangement of this kind is common in the US.

In the EU, [PSD2](node:PSD2) treats issuing payment instruments as a regulated payment service, and the issuer is responsible for applying [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication) unless an exemption applies.
quotes: The customer says their card works everywhere except on our site.
Our logs show a do-not-honor from the issuer. We can't see why, so they need to call the number on the back of the card.

nodes.name: Acquirer
nodes.description: The licensed institution that signs merchants, submits their card transactions and answers to the network for them.
nodes.markdown:
An acquirer is the bank or licensed institution that contracts with a [merchant](node:Merchant) to accept card payments, enters those transactions into the [card network](node:Card%20network), and arranges for the merchant to be paid. Visa's rules define it as a member that signs a merchant or [payment facilitator](node:Payment%20facilitator) and enters transactions into interchange, the exchange of transactions between members. In the EU, [PSD2](node:PSD2) treats acquiring as a regulated payment service.

The acquirer is the merchant-side counterpart of the [issuer](node:Issuer).

| Party                                         | Works for    | Main job                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Issuer                                        | [Cardholder](node:Cardholder)   | Approves payments and bills the card account             |
| Acquirer                                      | Merchant     | Sponsors the merchant on the network and funds it        |
| [Payment processor](node:Payment%20processor) | Either party | Runs the transaction systems, often for an acquirer      |
| [Payment gateway](node:Payment%20gateway)     | Merchant     | Connects the checkout to the processing systems          |

The acquirer carries financial responsibility to the network for the merchants it signs. If a merchant closes while [chargebacks](node:Chargeback) are still arriving, and cannot repay them, the acquirer can be left covering the loss. Mastercard's rules also make an acquirer responsible for the acts and omissions of its payment facilitators and their sponsored merchants.

An acquirer therefore reviews a business before onboarding, using [KYB](node:KYB) checks, and keeps monitoring it afterwards. A sudden jump in sales, a rising [chargeback ratio](node:Chargeback%20ratio), or a move into a higher-risk product can lead it to delay a [payout](node:Payout), impose a [rolling reserve](node:Rolling%20reserve), or end the relationship.

Many businesses never deal with an acquirer directly. A [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) may hold the acquiring relationship, or partner with one or more acquirers, and present a single contract. If support asks "who is your acquirer?", check the provider's terms or [settlement](node:Settlement) reports rather than assuming the provider is the acquirer.
quotes: Why are they holding back part of our payouts all of a sudden?
Our volume tripled in a month. The acquirer is on the hook if those orders turn into chargebacks, so it added a reserve.

nodes.name: Card network
nodes.description: The organisation that runs a card brand's rules and message rails between issuers and acquirers, such as Visa or Mastercard.
nodes.markdown:
A card network, also called a card scheme, is the organisation that operates a card brand. It connects [issuers](node:Issuer) and [acquirers](node:Acquirer), carries their messages, calculates what they owe each other, and publishes the rules they must follow. Visa and Mastercard operate globally. Others include American Express, Discover, JCB and UnionPay, along with domestic schemes such as Cartes Bancaires in France and girocard in Germany.

| Function | What the network does                                                                 |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Routing  | Passes each [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) from acquirer to issuer and back       |
| [Clearing](node:Clearing) | Exchanges final transaction records between members                                   |
| [Settlement](node:Settlement) | Calculates net positions so members can pay each other                                |
| Rules    | Sets acceptance, data, dispute and monitoring requirements                            |
| Fees     | Charges [scheme fees](node:Scheme%20fee) and administers [interchange](node:Interchange%20fee) where applicable |

In the [four-party model](node:Four-party%20model), the network does not hold the [cardholder's](node:Cardholder) account or lend money. This is why "Visa declined the payment" is usually inaccurate: the issuer declined it, and the network delivered the answer. The network can still affect the result in narrower cases, such as stand-in processing when an issuer is unavailable, or fraud services an issuer chooses to use.

Network rules are private contracts that bind members, which then pass them on to [merchants](node:Merchant) through their agreements. They are not law, and they vary by network and region. A rule that applies to Visa in Europe may not apply to Visa in the US or to Mastercard anywhere. Networks also revise their rules regularly.

For engineers, this means a behaviour observed on one brand should not be assumed for another. If code branches on `network`, check the current rulebook or your provider's documentation for each brand, and record which edition the logic was based on.
quotes: Mastercard let us capture this after a week, so Visa should too, right?
Not necessarily. The networks have different authorization rules, so check each one before we hard-code the window.

nodes.name: Four-party model
nodes.description: The card payment structure linking cardholder, merchant, issuer and acquirer through a card network.
nodes.markdown:
The four-party model is the standard structure of a card payment. The four parties are the [cardholder](node:Cardholder), the [merchant](node:Merchant), the cardholder's [issuer](node:Issuer) and the merchant's [acquirer](node:Acquirer). A [card network](node:Card%20network) sits between the two institutions and is not counted as one of the four.

| Party      | Relationship                          | Role in a payment                       |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Cardholder | Customer of the issuer                | Presents the card                       |
| Merchant   | Customer of the acquirer              | Sells goods and requests payment        |
| Issuer     | Member of the network                 | Approves and pays on the cardholder's behalf |
| Acquirer   | Member of the network                 | Submits transactions and funds the merchant |
| Network    | Connects issuer and acquirer          | Routes messages and applies rules       |

The structure explains why a merchant cannot ask "the bank" what happened to a payment. The merchant has a relationship only with its acquirer or [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider), and the cardholder has one only with the issuer. A decline reason, a missing [refund](node:Refund) or a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) has to pass through that chain, so each side sees only part of the picture. Shared references such as the [acquirer reference number](node:Acquirer%20reference%20number) exist to connect the two views.

The alternative is a three-party scheme, in which the scheme itself acts as both issuer and acquirer. EU [Interchange](node:Interchange%20fee) Fee Regulation 2015/751 defines both structures, and treats a three-party scheme as four-party when it licenses other providers to issue or acquire, or issues cards with a co-branding partner or through an agent. American Express and Discover are commonly described as three-party networks, but both also work with partner institutions in some markets, so the label depends on the product and country.

Money flows between issuer and acquirer through [settlement](node:Settlement).
quotes: Can't we just ask the customer's bank why it failed?
They won't talk to us. We're on the acquirer side of the four-party model, so the customer has to contact their issuer.

nodes.name: Payment service provider
nodes.description: A company that lets merchants accept payments, or in EU law, an institution authorised to provide payment services.
nodes.markdown:
A payment service provider (PSP) is a company that gives [merchants](node:Merchant) the means to accept payments, usually through one contract and one API. The term has two meanings, and they do not always describe the same company.

| Sense      | Meaning                                                                                                     |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Commercial | A vendor that bundles checkout, processing, reporting and payouts                                           |
| EU legal   | Under [PSD2](node:PSD2), a defined category such as a credit institution, e-money institution or payment institution |

A company can be a PSP commercially while relying on a licensed partner for the regulated activity. Check the contract to see which entity holds the funds and which is the [acquirer](node:Acquirer).

The roles around a PSP are often blurred because one vendor may perform several of them.

| Role                                              | What it does                                   | Holds merchant funds? |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| [Payment gateway](node:Payment%20gateway)         | Passes payment data to processing systems      | Usually not           |
| [Payment processor](node:Payment%20processor)     | Runs authorization and [clearing](node:Clearing) messages       | Usually not           |
| Acquirer                                          | Signs the merchant and answers to the network  | Yes, or via a partner |
| [Payment facilitator](node:Payment%20facilitator) | Onboards sub-merchants under an acquirer       | Often                 |
| [Merchant of record](node:Merchant%20of%20record) | Is the legal seller of the goods to the buyer  | Yes                   |
| PSP                                               | Packages some or all of the above              | Depends on the model  |

A PSP may be a payment facilitator for small accounts and offer a direct acquiring contract to large ones, so the same vendor name can imply different responsibilities.

The cost of this bundling appears when a merchant tries to leave. Saved cards are often held as PSP-specific [tokens](node:Tokenization) in the provider's [card vault](node:Card%20vault), so they do not work elsewhere until the card data is migrated. Ask about export terms before integrating, and store your own record of each payment rather than treating the PSP's dashboard as your only source of truth.
quotes: We can switch PSPs over the weekend, right?
Not with saved cards. Our tokens only work with the current provider, so we need a vault migration first.

nodes.name: Payment gateway
nodes.description: The technical service that carries payment details from a checkout to processing systems and returns the result.
nodes.markdown:
A payment gateway is the technical service that takes payment details from a [merchant's](node:Merchant) checkout, sends them securely toward the [payment processor](node:Payment%20processor) or [acquirer](node:Acquirer), and returns the response. It is the connection between the merchant's system and the card payment infrastructure. In a physical shop, the terminal and its software do a similar job.

| Role                                                  | Main question it answers                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Gateway                                               | How does this request reach the card rails?  |
| Payment processor                                     | How is the transaction message handled?      |
| Acquirer                                              | Which licensed institution takes on this merchant? |
| [Payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) | Who sells the merchant the packaged service? |

A standalone gateway usually does not hold the merchant's money. Under [PSD2](node:PSD2), technical service providers that support payments without ever possessing the funds are excluded from the directive, which is one reason a pure gateway may not need a payment licence in the EU. Whether a specific business qualifies depends on what it actually does. Many modern providers combine gateway, processing and acquiring, so "gateway" often describes one layer of a larger product.

Because it handles card data, a gateway falls under [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) as a service provider. It commonly also offers [tokenization](node:Tokenization), [hosted payment fields](node:Hosted%20payment%20fields), and [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) integration.

The failure engineers meet most often here is a timeout. The merchant sends a charge to the gateway, the connection drops, and nobody on the merchant's side knows whether the [issuer](node:Issuer) approved it. This is an [unknown payment outcome](node:Unknown%20payment%20outcome). Retrying blindly can produce a [double charge](node:Double%20charge). Instead, send a stable idempotency key (a client-generated value that makes retries safe) if the gateway supports one, then query the transaction status before attempting the payment again.
quotes: The gateway timed out on that order. Should the worker just retry the charge?
Not yet. Look up the payment by its reference first. It may have been approved even though we never got the response.

nodes.name: Payment processor
nodes.description: The company whose systems handle card transaction messages and records for an acquirer or issuer.
nodes.markdown:
A payment processor is a company that runs the systems handling card transactions on behalf of an [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or [issuer](node:Issuer). It formats and routes messages, tracks transaction state, and produces the files used for [clearing](node:Clearing) and [settlement](node:Settlement). The licensed institution remains accountable to the [card network](node:Card%20network) even when a processor does the technical work.

Processors are usually divided by side and by stage.

| Type                | Works for | Handles                                                         |
| ------------------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Acquirer processor  | Acquirer  | Card acceptance, batches and reporting              |
| Issuer processor    | Issuer    | Card accounts, authorization decisions under issuer rules, posting |
| Front-end processor | Either    | Real-time [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) messages                    |
| Back-end processor  | Either    | Clearing files, settlement data and dispute records             |

The distinction from nearby terms is about responsibility. A [payment gateway](node:Payment%20gateway) connects a [merchant's](node:Merchant) checkout to processing. A processor runs the transaction work behind that connection. An acquirer holds the licence or network membership and takes on the merchant's risk. A [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) may package all three. Merchants often say "our processor" when they mean whichever vendor they pay, so confirm the actual role before relying on the word.

Processor problems tend to appear as gaps between systems. A batch that was not submitted on time means authorized sales do not reach clearing, so funds arrive late and the hold stays on the customer's card. A partial outage may produce approvals in one system with no matching record in another. These cases surface during [payment reconciliation](node:Payment%20reconciliation), when expected sales are missing from a [settlement file](node:Settlement%20file).

When investigating, compare identifiers across stages: the authorization code, the [network transaction ID](node:Network%20transaction%20ID) and, once cleared, the [acquirer reference number](node:Acquirer%20reference%20number). The stage where the identifier disappears shows where the transaction stopped.
quotes: Tuesday's sales were authorized, but they're missing from the settlement report.
Looks like the processor never submitted that batch. Ask them to confirm it and resubmit before the authorizations go stale.

nodes.name: Payment facilitator
nodes.description: A company registered through an acquirer to onboard and process payments for smaller sponsored merchants.
nodes.markdown:
A payment facilitator, or PayFac, is a company registered through an [acquirer](node:Acquirer) to accept card payments on behalf of smaller businesses, called sponsored [merchants](node:Merchant) or sub-merchants. Instead of each business getting its own [merchant account](node:Merchant%20account), the facilitator onboards them under its own acquiring relationship, often quickly.

Network definitions differ. Visa classes a facilitator as a third-party agent and treats an entity as one if it deposits transactions, receives [settlement](node:Settlement), or contracts with an acquirer on behalf of a sponsored merchant. Mastercard defines it as a service provider registered by an acquirer to facilitate transactions for submerchants, and its rules make the acquirer responsible for the facilitator and those submerchants.

| Party                                        | Responsibility                                        |
| -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Acquirer                                     | Registers the facilitator, answers to the network     |
| Payment facilitator                          | Onboards, monitors and usually pays sub-merchants     |
| Sponsored merchant                           | Sells goods and remains the seller to the [cardholder](node:Cardholder)  |
| [Card network](node:Card%20network)          | Sets the facilitator program rules                    |

The term is often confused with two others. A [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) is a broader commercial label, and many PSPs operate as facilitators for small accounts. A [merchant of record](node:Merchant%20of%20record) is itself the seller, whereas a sponsored merchant stays the seller and the facilitator provides the acceptance. Visa also treats a marketplace as a separate category.

Fast onboarding has a visible cost. The facilitator may let a business start charging after light checks, then complete fuller [KYB](node:KYB) review once volume grows. A seller can therefore process payments for weeks and then find its [payout](node:Payout) paused until it supplies ownership documents. Facilitators do this because they carry risk for [chargebacks](node:Chargeback) from sub-merchants that disappear.
quotes: Our new seller processed fine for a month, and now their payout is frozen.
They hit the review threshold on our PayFac. Ask them for the ownership documents so compliance can release it.

nodes.name: Merchant of record
nodes.description: The legal entity that sells to the buyer in a card payment and takes responsibility for that sale and its disputes.
nodes.markdown:
A merchant of record (MoR) is the legal entity that sells goods or services to the buyer in a transaction. Its name appears on the [cardholder's](node:Cardholder) statement, it takes the payment, and it handles [refunds](node:Refund) and [chargebacks](node:Chargeback) for that sale. A software company may sell through an MoR, which buys or licenses the product and resells it to the end customer.

The term is widely used but is not defined identically everywhere. Visa's risk guidance uses it for a marketplace that contracts with the [acquirer](node:Acquirer), rather than the underlying retailers. Visa's rules also look at who sells to the cardholder, whose name identifies the outlet, and who gives the cardholder recourse.

| Model                                             | Legal seller to the buyer | Who handles disputes              |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Direct merchant                                   | The business              | The business                      |
| [Payment facilitator](node:Payment%20facilitator) | The sponsored merchant    | Sponsored merchant, via facilitator |
| Marketplace                                       | Usually the marketplace   | Marketplace, under its terms      |
| Merchant of record                                | The MoR                   | The MoR                           |

A facilitator helps a business accept cards while that business stays the seller. An MoR takes the seller's position, so it commonly also handles customer invoices and sales tax or VAT collection. The business then receives a net [payout](node:Payout) from the MoR after its fee, taxes and refunds. Which obligations move, and in which countries, depends on the contract and local tax law.

The symptom customers notice is an unfamiliar name. Someone buys a tool from a small software company and sees the MoR's name on their statement, assumes it is fraud, and calls their bank. A clear [statement descriptor](node:Statement%20descriptor) and a receipt naming both companies reduce these disputes.
quotes: Customers keep asking why their receipt shows a company they've never heard of.
That's our merchant of record. Let's put our product name in the descriptor and explain the reseller on the receipt.

nodes.name: Merchant account
nodes.description: The acquiring relationship that lets a business accept cards, identified by a merchant ID. It is not a normal bank account.
nodes.markdown:
A merchant account is the arrangement between a business and an [acquirer](node:Acquirer) that allows the business to accept card payments. It is identified by a merchant ID and carries the terms agreed at onboarding, including what the business sells, its [merchant category code](node:Merchant%20category%20code), currencies and risk limits.

Despite the name, it is usually not an account the business can spend from. Card proceeds are tracked against it, then paid to a separate bank account.

| Item                     | What it is                                      | Can the business spend from it? |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Merchant account         | Acquiring contract and transaction record       | No                              |
| PSP balance              | Amount a provider currently owes the business   | Only by [payout](node:Payout), in most setups |
| Business bank account    | Ordinary account that receives the payout       | Yes                             |

This explains a common question from finance teams: the dashboard shows sales as successful, but the bank balance has not moved. The funds are still between [settlement](node:Settlement) and payout, or they have been reduced by [refunds](node:Refund), fees, [chargebacks](node:Chargeback) or a [rolling reserve](node:Rolling%20reserve).

There are two common setups. With a dedicated merchant account, the business has a direct contract with an acquirer, which usually involves more underwriting and more control over pricing and data. With an aggregated setup, a [payment facilitator](node:Payment%20facilitator) holds the acquiring relationship and the business is a sponsored merchant beneath it, which is quicker to start but gives the provider more control over funds and account status.

If an acquirer closes a merchant account for rule violations, the closure can be recorded in network-run lists of terminated merchants, such as Mastercard's MATCH, which can make it harder to open a new one.
quotes: The dashboard says we took 40k this week, so why isn't it in the bank?
That's the merchant account view. The payout goes out after settlement, minus refunds and the reserve.

nodes.name: Sponsor bank
nodes.description: A licensed bank or network member that gives a non-member company access to card networks under its membership.
nodes.markdown:
A sponsor bank is a licensed bank, and member of a [card network](node:Card%20network), that lets a company without its own membership take part in card payments. A fintech issuing cards, a non-bank [payment processor](node:Payment%20processor) or a [payment facilitator](node:Payment%20facilitator) can operate under the sponsor's membership, while the sponsor remains answerable to the network and its regulators.

Sponsorship can sit on either side of a transaction.

| Side      | Sponsored company                         | What the sponsor provides                                     |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Issuing   | Fintech card program or program manager   | The [issuer](node:Issuer) role, [BIN](node:BIN) access, regulated accounts |
| Acquiring | Independent sales organisation, PayFac    | [Acquirer](node:Acquirer) membership and access to [settlement](node:Settlement)   |

A sponsor bank differs from a partner bank that only holds deposits. The sponsor's network membership is what gives the company access to the card rails. It also differs from a processor, which runs technology but does not itself provide the membership.

The model is common in the US, where non-bank companies frequently reach Visa and Mastercard through a sponsoring bank. It is not universal. The Bank of England's guide for FCA-authorised non-bank providers says it is possible to be a direct participant in Visa and Mastercard in most respects while settling through another organisation. In the EU, [PSD2](node:PSD2) generally requires payment system access rules to be objective, non-discriminatory and proportionate. Each network sets its own eligibility criteria.

Because the sponsor carries the regulatory exposure, it sets conditions on the program. It may review marketing, require [KYC](node:KYC) and [AML](node:AML) controls, and audit the company's operations. If a sponsor exits a program or a regulator restricts it, the company can lose card access or need to migrate customers to a new BIN, which means new card numbers for customers. Check what the contract says about termination and transition.
quotes: Why does compliance need to approve the copy for our card launch?
We issue under our sponsor bank's membership. If our marketing breaks its rules, it's their licence at risk.

nodes.name: Card authorization
nodes.description: A real-time request asking the card issuer to approve a payment and usually reserve funds, without moving money yet.
nodes.markdown:
A card authorization is a real-time request asking the [issuer](node:Issuer) whether a card payment can go ahead. If approved, the issuer usually reserves the amount with an [authorization hold](node:Authorization%20hold). In the usual dual-message card flow, no money moves at this step.

| Step | Who                                 | What happens                                         |
| ---- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | [Merchant](node:Merchant)           | Sends amount and card details through its provider   |
| 2    | [Acquirer](node:Acquirer)           | Formats the request and forwards it to the network   |
| 3    | [Card network](node:Card%20network) | Routes the request to the issuer                     |
| 4    | Issuer                              | Checks status, funds and risk, then responds         |
| 5    | Merchant                            | Receives an approval or a [decline code](node:Decline%20code) |

Authorization is the first of four stages that people often merge into "the payment".

| Stage            | Question it answers                     | Money moves?             |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Authorization    | Will the issuer approve this?           | No, funds are reserved   |
| [Capture](node:Capture)    | Does the merchant want to take payment? | No                       |
| [Clearing](node:Clearing)   | What is the final transaction record?   | No, amounts are calculated |
| [Settlement](node:Settlement) | Who pays whom?                          | Yes, between institutions |

Treating an approval as completed payment causes a familiar bug. An order system marks a sale "paid" after authorization, the capture job later fails, and the goods ship with no money collected. The approval eventually expires and the hold disappears. Record authorized and captured as separate states in the [payment state machine](node:Payment%20state%20machine).

Some transactions combine stages. A "sale" API call authorizes and captures together. In a single-message system, common for PIN debit, one message carries both the authorization and the financial transaction.

How long an approval stays valid varies by network, region and transaction type. Mastercard, for example, distinguishes preauthorizations, final and undefined authorizations. A valid approval also does not prove that the real [cardholder](node:Cardholder) made the purchase, so it does not protect the merchant from a later fraud [chargeback](node:Chargeback).
quotes: The order says paid, but finance can't find the money.
It was only authorized. The capture job failed, so nothing ever went to clearing.

nodes.name: Authorization hold
nodes.description: A temporary reduction in a cardholder's available funds after an approved authorization, before any money is taken.
nodes.markdown:
An authorization hold is a temporary reduction in a [cardholder's](node:Cardholder) available balance or credit after an [issuer](node:Issuer) approves a [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization). The money stays in the account but cannot be spent. Banking apps usually show it as "pending", which is why customers often read a hold as a completed charge.

This is the source of a frequent support ticket. A customer's first checkout attempt appears to fail, they try again, and now see two pending amounts. Only one order exists, but both approvals are holding funds. The customer reports being charged twice, even though neither hold has been captured. On a debit card with a low balance, the extra hold can also cause an unrelated payment or rent debit to fail.

| Event                                          | Effect on the hold                         |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| [Capture](node:Capture) and [clearing](node:Clearing)                         | Replaced by the posted transaction         |
| [Partial capture](node:Partial%20capture)      | Unused part should be released             |
| [Incremental authorization](node:Incremental%20authorization) | Held amount increases                      |
| [Authorization reversal](node:Authorization%20reversal) | Issuer releases the funds                  |
| No further action                              | Issuer drops it after its own time limit   |

A [merchant](node:Merchant) controls whether a hold is captured or released, but the issuer controls how quickly the customer sees the change. A released hold can continue to display for some time in a banking app. How long an unused hold lasts depends on the issuer, the network and the transaction type, so avoid promising customers a specific number of days.

The fix for abandoned or duplicate approvals is to send a reversal as soon as you know the funds are not needed. Visa's rules require a reversal in specified cases, including when a transaction is cancelled or finishes below the authorized amount, and Visa can assess a fee on approvals that are neither cleared nor reversed. Mastercard has its own requirements.
quotes: A customer says we charged her twice for one order.
One is a stale hold from the failed attempt. Send the reversal and tell her it should drop off once her bank processes it.

nodes.name: Capture
nodes.description: The merchant's instruction to collect an authorized card payment, which sends the transaction toward clearing.
nodes.markdown:
Capture is the [merchant's](node:Merchant) instruction to collect funds that were approved in a [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization). It converts "the [issuer](node:Issuer) said yes" into "take this amount". Capture is a provider and API term. At network level, the equivalent step is the submission of a [clearing](node:Clearing) record, which Mastercard calls first presentment.

| Stage                         | Who acts                   | Result                                 |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Authorization                 | Issuer                     | Approval and [authorization hold](node:Authorization%20hold)   |
| Capture                       | Merchant or its system     | Final amount is confirmed              |
| Clearing                      | [Acquirer](node:Acquirer), network, issuer | Transaction record is exchanged        |
| [Settlement](node:Settlement) | Institutions               | Funds move between them                |

A provider may capture individually or collect captures into a daily batch, so a successful capture response does not mean the money has arrived.

Merchants choose between two flows. With automatic capture, authorization and capture happen together, which suits digital goods delivered immediately. With manual capture, the merchant authorizes at checkout and captures later, which suits physical goods that ship after stock is confirmed. Card rules or local law may also restrict charging before goods are shipped, so check what applies in each market.

The main failure with manual capture is forgetting to do it. A background job crashes, the approval expires, and a shipped order has no payment behind it. Capturing late carries a second risk. Visa has a dispute condition for no authorization or late presentment, and Mastercard has an authorization-related [chargeback](node:Chargeback) with a defined protection period, so a late capture can be charged back even if the goods were delivered. Time limits differ by network and transaction type.

Alert on authorized payments approaching their capture window, and make the capture call safe to retry so a repeated job cannot create a [double charge](node:Double%20charge). If you need less than the approved amount, use a [partial capture](node:Partial%20capture).
quotes: Why did we get a chargeback on an order that definitely arrived?
We captured it three weeks after authorizing. The approval had expired, so proof of delivery doesn't help.

nodes.name: Partial capture
nodes.description: Collecting less than the authorized card amount, for example when only part of an order ships.
nodes.markdown:
A partial capture collects less than the amount approved in a [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization). A customer orders three items for 90, the [merchant](node:Merchant) authorizes 90, one item is out of stock, and the merchant captures 60.

The step people miss is what happens to the remaining 30. Capturing 60 does not guarantee that the rest of the [authorization hold](node:Authorization%20hold) is released promptly. The customer can see a 60 charge and a 90 pending amount at the same time and believe they were overcharged.

| Situation                 | Correct handling                                                     |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Final amount is lower     | Capture the lower amount, release the difference     |
| Order cancelled entirely  | Send a full [authorization reversal](node:Authorization%20reversal)  |
| Final amount is higher    | Use [incremental authorization](node:Incremental%20authorization) if eligible |
| Already settled, too high | Issue a [refund](node:Refund) for the difference                     |

Network rules address the unused amount. Visa requires a merchant to submit an authorization reversal for the difference when a completed transaction's final amount is less than the amount authorized. Mastercard's rules for Europe require a reversal when a transaction is finalised at a lower amount, and its other regions have their own wording. Many [payment service providers](node:Payment%20service%20provider) send this automatically, but confirm it rather than assume.

Partial capture is different from multiple capture, which takes several amounts against one authorization, usually for split shipments. Multiple capture is more restricted. Visa permits a single authorization with multiple [clearing](node:Clearing) records only in listed cases, including airlines, cruise lines, US railways, and card-absent merchants shipping goods in parts, with conditions such as telling the [cardholder](node:Cardholder).

Engineers should store authorized, captured and refunded amounts as separate fields in [minor units](node:Minor%20unit). A single `amount` column cannot represent a partly captured payment, and support then cannot tell what the customer actually paid.
quotes: She was charged 60 but her bank still shows 90 pending.
We did a partial capture and never released the other 30. Check whether the provider sent the reversal.

nodes.name: Incremental authorization
nodes.description: An added authorization that raises the approved amount on an existing card transaction when the final cost grows.
nodes.markdown:
An incremental authorization is an extra request that increases the amount approved on an existing card transaction. It is used when the cost grows after the first approval: a hotel guest extends a stay, a rental car is kept longer, or a bar tab increases.

Visa defines it as a request that follows an approved estimated [authorization](node:Card%20authorization) and covers an additional amount the [cardholder](node:Cardholder) is expected to spend or has incurred in that same transaction. Mastercard handles the same need through preauthorizations, with additional requests referencing the original by its trace identifier. Eligibility varies by network, region, [merchant category](node:Merchant%20category%20code) and [acquirer](node:Acquirer), so a flow that works for one brand may not work for another.

| Option                    | Links to original? | Effect on the customer                  |
| ------------------------- | ------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Incremental authorization | Yes                | One growing [authorization hold](node:Authorization%20hold) |
| New separate authorization | No                 | Two holds, which can look like two charges |
| Reauthorization           | Yes, by rule       | Refreshes an approval that is expiring  |
| [Partial capture](node:Partial%20capture) | Yes                | Takes less than was approved            |

The link matters because the [issuer](node:Issuer) needs to know this is the same purchase. Without it, a [merchant](node:Merchant) that sends a fresh approval for the extra amount creates a second hold and a second record. The customer sees two pending entries, and [clearing](node:Clearing) may no longer match cleanly to one authorization.

An incremental request is a new decision and can be declined. A guest with a nearly full credit limit may be approved at check-in and declined when the stay is extended. The merchant is then exposed for the extra amount unless it collects another payment method, so request the increase before providing the additional service.

Pass the [network transaction ID](node:Network%20transaction%20ID) from the original approval on each increment and release any unused amount at the end.
quotes: The guest added two nights and now has two pending hotel charges.
We sent a new auth. It should have been an incremental on the original transaction.

nodes.name: Void
nodes.description: Cancelling a card payment before it is submitted for clearing, so that no money is collected from the customer.
nodes.markdown:
A void cancels a card payment before it has been submitted for [clearing](node:Clearing). Because the transaction has not been finalised, no money is taken and no [refund](node:Refund) is needed. A shop assistant who rings up the wrong amount and cancels it immediately is performing a void.

"Void" is mainly a term used by [payment service providers](node:Payment%20service%20provider), terminals and processors, and its exact behaviour depends on the provider. What happens underneath depends on how far the payment has gone.

| Term                                                 | When it applies                   | What happens                                  | Customer sees                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Void                                                 | Before clearing submission        | Provider cancels the pending transaction      | Pending entry, then nothing   |
| [Authorization reversal](node:Authorization%20reversal) | After approval, before [capture](node:Capture) | Message tells the [issuer](node:Issuer) to release funds | Hold disappears               |
| Refund                                               | After clearing or [settlement](node:Settlement) | New credit transaction returns the money      | Charge, then a separate credit |

A void and a reversal are often the same event seen at two levels. The [merchant](node:Merchant) calls "void" in an API, and the provider sends an authorization reversal to the issuer. A void can, however, fail to release the customer's money if the provider only removes the transaction from its own batch and sends no reversal. The sale is cancelled, but the [authorization hold](node:Authorization%20hold) stays on the card until the issuer's time limit passes. Check which behaviour your provider documents.

Timing is the common source of errors. Providers usually close batches on a schedule, and after the cutoff a void call is rejected with an error such as "already settled". Support tools should try a void first when the payment is eligible and otherwise issue a refund. Doing both can credit a customer for money never taken, so code the choice from the payment's current state in the [payment state machine](node:Payment%20state%20machine).
quotes: Support tried to void yesterday's order and got an error.
The batch already closed, so it can't be voided. Issue a refund instead.

nodes.name: Authorization reversal
nodes.description: A message telling the issuer to cancel all or part of an approved authorization so the held funds are released.
nodes.markdown:
An authorization reversal is a message that cancels all or part of an approved [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization), telling the [issuer](node:Issuer) to release the funds it was holding. Visa's rules describe it as a system message that cancels an approval response. It applies before the transaction has been cleared.

| Term                  | Stage                          | Mechanism                         | Money already moved? |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| Authorization reversal | After approval, before [clearing](node:Clearing) | Network message to the issuer     | No                   |
| [Void](node:Void)     | Before clearing submission     | Provider action, often sends a reversal | No                   |
| [Refund](node:Refund) | After clearing                 | New credit transaction            | Yes                  |

A [merchant](node:Merchant) needs a reversal in four common situations: the customer cancels, stock runs out, the final amount is lower than approved, or a timeout leaves an approval the merchant cannot use. The issuer approves, the response is lost, and the merchant records a failure. The customer's funds stay on hold for an order that does not exist. Visa's rules require a reversal when a point-of-sale merchant receives an approval after timing out.

Requirements are network-specific. Visa requires merchants to submit reversals in listed cases and can charge a misuse-of-authorization fee on approvals matched to neither a clearing record nor a reversal. Mastercard's Transaction Processing Rules set separate requirements, including a timed rule in the Europe region for cancelled or reduced transactions.

Reversals can be full or partial. A partial reversal reduces the held amount and is the usual companion to a [partial capture](node:Partial%20capture). The message must reference the original authorization, normally through the [network transaction ID](node:Network%20transaction%20ID) or matching data, or the issuer may not connect the two.

Visa also uses "Reversal" for a separate correction of a transaction sent through clearing in error. When reading a rulebook or provider log, check which of the two is meant.
quotes: The auth call timed out, so we marked the order failed. Are we done?
No. It may have been approved. Send a reversal, or the customer's money stays on hold.

nodes.name: Refund
nodes.description: A new credit transaction returning money to a card after the original payment has been captured and cleared.
nodes.markdown:
A refund returns money to a customer's card after the original payment has been [captured](node:Capture) and [cleared](node:Clearing). It is a new transaction in the opposite direction. The original charge stays on the statement, and a separate credit appears later.

| Action                                                  | Timing                      | Result on the statement          |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| [Void](node:Void)                                       | Before clearing submission  | Usually no posted entry          |
| [Authorization reversal](node:Authorization%20reversal) | Before clearing             | Pending hold disappears          |
| Refund                                                  | After clearing              | Charge plus separate credit      |
| [Chargeback](node:Chargeback)                           | After a dispute with the [issuer](node:Issuer) | Credit forced through the network |

A refund is initiated by the [merchant](node:Merchant), which distinguishes it from a chargeback, initiated by the issuer. The money is deducted from the merchant's balance or a future [payout](node:Payout). If the balance is too low, the provider may delay the refund or debit the merchant's bank account.

A common complaint is "you said you refunded me, but I don't have it". The merchant's system shows success because the provider accepted the instruction, but the credit still has to pass through clearing and be posted by the issuer. That can take days, and the exact time varies. Give the customer the [acquirer reference number](node:Acquirer%20reference%20number) when your provider exposes one, since their bank can use it to trace the credit.

Refunds interact badly with disputes. If a customer has already opened a chargeback and the merchant also issues a refund, the customer can receive the money twice. Check for an open dispute first. If a refund was issued before the dispute, submit that as evidence through [representment](node:Representment).

Visa's rules require a refund to the same payment credential where possible, with listed exceptions. Refunds to a different card are a known fraud pattern. Whether the merchant recovers its processing fees depends on its contract.
quotes: The customer says the refund never arrived, but our dashboard shows it succeeded.
Send them the ARN. Their bank can use it to find the credit.

nodes.name: Clearing
nodes.description: The exchange of final card transaction records between acquirer and issuer, which sets what each institution owes.
nodes.markdown:
Clearing is the exchange of final transaction records between an [acquirer](node:Acquirer) and an [issuer](node:Issuer) through a [card network](node:Card%20network). It tells the issuer the final amount to post to the customer's account and calculates what the institutions owe each other. Visa's rules describe it as the validation and valuation of records exchanged between Visa and its members. Mastercard calls the record a first presentment.

Clearing sits between the [merchant's](node:Merchant) instruction and the actual movement of money.

| Stage                                     | What it does                          | Output                           |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| [Card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) | Issuer approves the payment           | Approval and hold                |
| [Capture](node:Capture)                   | Merchant confirms the amount          | Instruction to acquirer or batch |
| Clearing                                  | Records are exchanged and valued      | Final amounts, fees, positions   |
| [Settlement](node:Settlement)             | Institutions pay net amounts          | Funds transferred                |
| [Payout](node:Payout)                     | Provider pays the merchant            | Bank deposit                     |

Clearing is where the actual transaction amount becomes final, and it can differ from the authorized amount. A restaurant authorizes the bill and clears it with a tip. A clearing record is also where [interchange](node:Interchange%20fee) and [scheme fees](node:Scheme%20fee) are typically determined, so data quality at this stage affects cost. Incorrect [merchant category codes](node:Merchant%20category%20code) or missing fields can lead to a higher fee category.

Most card transactions use a dual-message flow, with one message for authorization and another for clearing. Some debit systems use a single message for both.

A common engineering problem is treating the authorization as the final record. If the clearing amount differs, or clears on a different date or in a different currency, a ledger built from authorization data will not match the [settlement file](node:Settlement%20file). Build [payment reconciliation](node:Payment%20reconciliation) from cleared records. Visa also assesses fees on clearing records with no matching approval, so clearing transactions must keep the references from the original authorization.
quotes: Why does the charge in our ledger differ from the settlement report by the tip amount?
The ledger used the auth. Clearing carried the final amount, so reconcile against that.

nodes.name: Settlement
nodes.description: The transfer of net funds between issuers, acquirers and the card network after clearing has set the amounts owed.
nodes.markdown:
Settlement is the movement of money between financial institutions after [clearing](node:Clearing) has established what each one owes. In a card payment, the [issuer](node:Issuer) pays, usually on a net basis, through the [card network's](node:Card%20network) settlement arrangements, and the [acquirer](node:Acquirer) receives funds. Visa's rules define settlement as the reporting and funds transfer of amounts owed by one member to another, or to Visa, as a result of clearing.

Networks usually settle net positions rather than each individual card payment. An acquirer may be owed for millions of purchases and owe for [refunds](node:Refund) and [chargebacks](node:Chargeback), so one net amount moves in a settlement currency.

| Stage                         | Parties                        | What moves                     |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| [Card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) | [Merchant](node:Merchant) to issuer | A message and a hold           |
| Clearing                      | Acquirer, network, issuer      | Transaction records            |
| Settlement                    | Issuer, network, acquirer      | Net funds between institutions |
| [Payout](node:Payout)         | Acquirer or provider to merchant | Funds to a business bank account |

The word causes a specific misunderstanding. A provider dashboard may show a payment as "settled" while the merchant's bank has received nothing. That status can mean the transaction was submitted, that the provider has received funds, or that the payment is in the next payout. Each provider defines it differently, so read the documentation rather than assuming that settled means deposited.

Settlement timing depends on the network, currency, business days and bank holidays. A [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) may add its own payout delay.

Engineers usually meet settlement through a [settlement file](node:Settlement%20file) or report. It often lists amounts grouped by batch and net of fees, in the settlement currency, which may differ from the customer's currency. Matching those records to orders requires shared identifiers, and it is the purpose of [payment reconciliation](node:Payment%20reconciliation). Track settlement in your [ledger](node:Ledger) as a separate event from [capture](node:Capture) so finance can see money in transit.
quotes: The dashboard says Friday's sales settled. Why isn't the money in the bank?
Settled just means the acquirer has it. The payout runs on Tuesday.

nodes.name: Payout
nodes.description: The transfer of a merchant's available funds from its acquirer or payment provider to its bank account.
nodes.markdown:
A payout is the transfer of funds from an [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) to a [merchant's](node:Merchant) bank account. It is the last step of the card flow and the first point at which the business can spend the money. Some providers call it a deposit, remittance or funding.

A payout differs from [settlement](node:Settlement), which moves money between institutions. Settlement can complete while the merchant still has not been paid.

A payout is rarely the sum of the day's sales. It is a net amount.

| Line item                                         | Effect on payout |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| Captured sales                                    | Adds             |
| [Refunds](node:Refund)                            | Subtracts        |
| [Chargebacks](node:Chargeback) and dispute fees   | Subtracts        |
| Processing fees                                   | Subtracts        |
| Newly withheld [rolling reserve](node:Rolling%20reserve) | Subtracts        |
| Released reserve                                  | Adds             |
| Reversed chargebacks                              | Adds             |

This is why finance teams often find a deposit that matches no order total. Reconcile by obtaining the provider's list of transactions included in each payout, using its payout ID, rather than comparing bank deposits with daily sales. This is a main task of [payment reconciliation](node:Payment%20reconciliation).

A balance can also go negative. If refunds and chargebacks exceed new sales, there is nothing to pay out, and the provider may debit the merchant's bank account or recover the shortfall from future sales. A payout can fail when bank details are wrong or an account is closed, and the funds then return to the provider's balance.

Providers may pause payouts during a risk or compliance review, for example when [KYB](node:KYB) details are missing, sales patterns change sharply, or a [sanctions screening](node:Sanctions%20screening) alert is unresolved.

On a platform, the term also covers payments to sellers, which may use a [split payment](node:Split%20payment). Model each payout in your [ledger](node:Ledger) as a separate record linked to the transactions it contains, and treat a provider's "paid" status as provisional until the bank confirms receipt.
quotes: Today's deposit is 3,100 but we sold 4,000 yesterday.
Pull the payout breakdown. It nets out refunds, fees and that chargeback from last week.

nodes.name: PAN
nodes.description: The primary account number on a payment card, which identifies the issuer and card account under ISO/IEC 7812.
nodes.markdown:
A PAN, or primary account number, is the long number that identifies a payment card account. Its format comes from ISO/IEC 7812, which allows up to 19 digits. Sixteen is common, but not universal, so a form or database column that assumes 16 digits will reject or corrupt valid cards.

| Part                 | Position         | Purpose                                         |
| -------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| [Issuer](node:Issuer) identifier | Leading digits   | The [BIN](node:BIN), identifying the issuer or program |
| Account identifier   | Middle digits    | The individual account within that issuer       |
| Check digit          | Final digit      | Catches typing errors using the Luhn formula    |

The Luhn check only detects mistyped numbers. A number that passes is well formed, and that says nothing about whether the account exists, is open, or belongs to the person typing it. Only a [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) can check that.

[PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) treats the PAN as the defining element of cardholder data: if a system stores, processes or transmits it, that system is in scope. Masking and truncation are different. Masking hides digits on a screen while the full value may still exist underneath. Truncation permanently removes digits from the stored value. PCI SSC publishes the formats it accepts for truncation, and these changed with the move to longer BINs.

The usual incident is accidental storage. A debug log captures a full request body, a support agent pastes a card number into a ticket, or an analytics script reads a checkout field. This widens compliance scope and requires clean-up across logs and backups.

Most [merchants](node:Merchant) avoid handling the PAN by using [hosted payment fields](node:Hosted%20payment%20fields) and keeping a [PSP token](node:Tokenization) or [network token](node:Network%20token). A network token is itself a different number in PAN format, so code should not assume that every card-shaped value is the underlying card number.
quotes: Why is compliance asking us to purge three months of application logs?
The request logger captured full PANs from the checkout endpoint. Those logs are now in PCI scope.

nodes.name: BIN
nodes.description: The leading digits of a card number, identifying the issuer or program. ISO calls it the issuer identification number.
nodes.markdown:
A BIN, or bank identification number, is the leading part of a [PAN](node:PAN) that identifies the [issuer](node:Issuer) or card program. ISO/IEC 7812 calls it the issuer identification number, or IIN.

The BIN was historically six digits. ISO revised the standard to make it eight, converting each six-digit range into a block of one hundred eight-digit ranges. Visa set April 2022 as the date for its clients to support eight-digit BINs and stopped assigning new six-digit issuing BINs after that.

Systems use BIN data to answer questions about a card before or during payment.

| Question                      | Used for                                                 |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Which network?                | Showing the logo, [payment routing](node:Payment%20routing) |
| Credit, debit or prepaid?     | Pricing, eligibility, blocking card types                |
| Issuing country?              | Fraud rules, [cross-border fee](node:Cross-border%20fee) estimates |
| Consumer or commercial?       | Fee estimates, invoicing flows                           |

The move to eight digits created a quiet failure. Code that takes `pan.slice(0, 6)` and looks it up in a local table still runs, but two different programs can now share the same first six digits. A fraud rule or a block aimed at one program can then hit another, and a credit card can be classified as debit. Use the longest available prefix, and refresh BIN tables from your provider or network, because ranges are reassigned.

BIN data is an attribute of the card, so it is not proof of anything about the person using it. Issuing country in particular says where the card was issued, which may differ from where the customer lives. A [network token](node:Network%20token) can carry its own token range rather than the underlying card's BIN.

A sudden run of declines on sequential cards from the same BIN at one [merchant](node:Merchant) is a warning sign of [card testing](node:Card%20testing).
quotes: Our prepaid block started rejecting normal credit cards from this bank.
The rule matches on six digits. That range is now split across products, so move the lookup to eight-digit BINs.

nodes.name: CVV
nodes.description: The short card security code checked by the issuer on remote payments. PCI DSS forbids storing it after authorization.
nodes.markdown:
A CVV, or card verification value, is the short security code on a payment card that an [issuer](node:Issuer) can check during a [card-not-present transaction](node:Card-not-present%20transaction). It is meant to show that the person paying has access to the card rather than only the [PAN](node:PAN). The name varies by network.

| Network          | Common name | Usual length and location     |
| ---------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------- |
| Visa             | CVV2        | Three digits, back of card    |
| Mastercard       | CVC2        | Three digits, back of card    |
| American Express | CID         | Four digits, front of card    |

The printed code differs from the value encoded on the magnetic stripe, and chip transactions use separate cryptographic values.

[PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) classes the card verification code as sensitive authentication data. Requirement 3.3.1 forbids storing such data after [authorization](node:Card%20authorization), even if encrypted. Issuers and companies supporting issuing services have a narrow exception. Teams building subscriptions sometimes save the CVV for later charges. That breaches the standard and is unnecessary: a later [merchant-initiated transaction](node:Merchant-initiated%20transaction) relies on the [stored credential](node:Stored%20credential) framework and does not need the code. Keep it out of logs and queues too.

A CVV check is a signal and does not prove identity. The result comes back with the authorization, and a mismatch does not always cause a decline, because some issuers approve anyway and leave the decision to the [merchant](node:Merchant). Decide in your [risk scoring](node:Risk%20scoring) rules whether to reverse an approved payment with a failed check. If you do, send an [authorization reversal](node:Authorization%20reversal) so the funds are released.

Stolen card data often includes the code, so a correct CVV does not rule out fraud. Unlike [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure), a passing CVV check does not by itself give the merchant a [liability shift](node:Liability%20shift). Repeated CVV failures across attempts on one card are a sign of [card testing](node:Card%20testing).
quotes: Can we store the CVV encrypted so renewals don't need the customer?
No, PCI DSS bans storing it after authorization, even encrypted. Renewals should use the stored credential flow.

nodes.name: EMV
nodes.description: Technical specifications managed by EMVCo for chip and contactless card payments, and for related payment technologies.
nodes.markdown:
EMV is a family of technical specifications for secure card payments, best known for chip cards and contactless payments. The name comes from Europay, Mastercard and Visa. The specifications are managed by EMVCo, a technical body collectively owned by American Express, Discover, JCB, Mastercard, UnionPay and Visa.

A chip card differs from a magnetic stripe in how it proves itself. A stripe holds static data that can be copied. A chip holds secret keys and generates a cryptogram, a one-time code computed over the transaction's details, which the [issuer](node:Issuer) can verify.

| Step | Who      | What happens                                                    |
| ---- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Terminal | Reads the card and sends transaction details to the chip        |
| 2    | Card     | Generates a cryptogram for this transaction                     |
| 3    | Terminal | Sends it in the [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) request            |
| 4    | Issuer   | Recalculates the cryptogram and approves or declines            |
| 5    | Card     | Can verify the issuer's response and complete the transaction   |

Because each cryptogram is tied to one transaction, data captured from a chip payment cannot be replayed to make a counterfeit card work. This is the protection chip adds in a [card-present transaction](node:Card-present%20transaction).

EMV does not protect a [card-not-present transaction](node:Card-not-present%20transaction), because no chip takes part. For that channel, EMVCo publishes separate specifications for [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) and for payment tokens, which are used in [network tokens](node:Network%20token). The shared name causes confusion: "EMV 3DS" is an online authentication protocol and has no chip involved.

EMVCo does not set network rules or enforce adoption. Each [card network](node:Card%20network) decides those separately, including the chip [liability shift](node:Liability%20shift). Where it applies, a [merchant](node:Merchant) that swipes a chip card on a terminal that cannot read chips can be liable for resulting counterfeit fraud.
quotes: The new terminal keeps failing on chip, so staff are just swiping.
Stop that. If those turn out to be counterfeit, the liability can land on us. Get the reader replaced.

nodes.name: ISO 8583
nodes.description: The international standard for card transaction messages exchanged between acquirers and issuers.
nodes.markdown:
ISO 8583 is the international standard for the messages that card systems exchange, such as authorization requests and responses. It defines a common interface between [acquirers](node:Acquirer) and [issuers](node:Issuer), usually through a [card network](node:Card%20network). The current edition is ISO 8583:2023. Older editions remain in production.

An ISO 8583 message has three main parts.

| Part                  | Purpose                                       | Example                     |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Message type indicator | Says what the message is                     | `0100` authorization request |
| Bitmap                | Marks which data fields are present           | Bits for fields 2, 3, 4     |
| Data elements         | Carry the values                              | [PAN](node:PAN), amount, response code |

Mastercard's rules show how these labels appear in practice.

| Message | Meaning                         |
| ------- | ------------------------------- |
| `0100`  | Authorization request           |
| `0110`  | Authorization response          |
| `0400`  | Reversal request                |
| `0420`  | Acquirer reversal advice        |
| `1240`  | First presentment, for [clearing](node:Clearing) |

The standard is a framework, and each network implements its own variant. Field usage, private data elements and code values differ between Visa, Mastercard and domestic switches. A parser built from the ISO document alone will not correctly handle a real network feed, so work from the network or processor's interface specification.

Most application developers never see ISO 8583 because a [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) wraps it in a JSON API. It still shapes what they receive. A [decline code](node:Decline%20code) such as `51` comes from a response code field, and a truncated [statement descriptor](node:Statement%20descriptor) reflects a fixed-length name field.

Engineers working closer to the rails meet different failures: a bitmap that does not match the fields sent, an amount in the wrong [minor unit](node:Minor%20unit), or a reversal that omits the original transaction's reference data. Log parsed messages with the PAN and other sensitive fields masked, since raw dumps bring logs into [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) scope.

ISO 8583 is separate from [ISO 20022](node:ISO%2020022), the data standard widely used for bank payments.
quotes: The processor rejected our message but the JSON looks fine.
Check the ISO 8583 output. The bitmap flags field 43, but our mapper never set the merchant name.

nodes.name: Decline code
nodes.description: The response code returned when a card authorization is refused, indicating the reason and whether a retry makes sense.
nodes.markdown:
A decline code is the value returned when a [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) is refused. It usually originates from the [issuer](node:Issuer) in the response code field of an [ISO 8583](node:ISO%208583) message, though a network, [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or fraud tool can also generate one. Examples include `51` for insufficient funds and `05` for "do not honor".

Meanings are not identical across networks, and [payment service providers](node:Payment%20service%20provider) often translate raw codes into their own labels. Keep the original code as well.

Visa's rules group decline codes into four categories that control retry behaviour.

| Visa category                | Example codes                            | [Merchant](node:Merchant) response                      |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| 1. Issuer will never approve | `04`, `41` lost, `43` stolen, `46` closed | Do not retry this card                 |
| 2. Cannot approve at this time | `51` funds, `61` limit, `91` issuer down | Retry within Visa's limits             |
| 3. Data quality              | `54` expired, `82` failed card check     | Correct the data, then retry           |
| 4. Generic                   | All other codes                          | Retry within limits, or ask for another card |

These categories are Visa's. Mastercard signals retry guidance differently, including through merchant advice codes in its responses. Reattempt limits are set by each network and can change, so take them from current rules or your provider.

The practical distinction is between a [soft decline](node:Soft%20decline), which may succeed after a change, and a [hard decline](node:Hard%20decline), which will not. A retry job that treats all failures the same will keep charging lost or closed cards, adding cost and possibly breaching network limits. This is a common defect in [recurring billing](node:Recurring%20billing) and [dunning](node:Dunning).

Be careful with customer messages. Showing "suspected fraud" or "stolen card" can alert a criminal and embarrass a real customer. Say the payment was declined and suggest another method. A jump in one code can indicate an integration problem or [card testing](node:Card%20testing).
quotes: The billing job retried this card eleven times last week.
It's a code 46, closed account. That's category 1 for Visa, so we should never have retried it.

nodes.name: Soft decline
