nodes.description: A card decline that may succeed after a change, most specifically when the issuer requires stronger authentication.
nodes.markdown:
A soft decline is a card refusal that may succeed if something changes. The term has two uses, and teams often mix them up.

| Use    | Meaning                                                    | Correct response                  |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Narrow | [Issuer](node:Issuer) requires [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication) | Authenticate, then send a new request |
| Broad  | Any temporary condition, such as insufficient funds or an issuer outage | Retry later, within network limits |

The narrow sense comes from European regulation. Under [PSD2](node:PSD2), when a payment needs authentication and arrives without it, the issuer can decline with a specific code asking for it. Mastercard's Transaction Processing Rules require issuers in its listed SCA countries to use a "soft decline" response in this case, and require the [merchant](node:Merchant) to attempt [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) with a mandated challenge or use another SCA method. Visa's rules list code `1A`, "additional customer authentication required", for its Europe and CEMEA regions.

The typical symptom appears after a merchant requests an [SCA exemption](node:SCA%20exemption). The issuer does not accept it and returns a soft decline. If the checkout shows a generic "card declined" message, the customer leaves even though one authentication step would probably have completed the sale.

The handling should be explicit in the [payment state machine](node:Payment%20state%20machine):

| Step | Who      | What happens                                                |
| ---- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Merchant | Sends the [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization)   |
| 2    | Issuer   | Returns the authentication-required code                    |
| 3    | Merchant | Starts 3-D Secure with the customer present                 |
| 4    | Merchant | Sends a new authorization with the authentication data      |

If the customer is absent, as in a [merchant-initiated transaction](node:Merchant-initiated%20transaction), step 3 cannot happen immediately. Ask them to return and authenticate through an email or in-app prompt.

The broad usage needs a [payment retry](node:Payment%20retry) policy with limits and spacing. Contrast both uses with a [hard decline](node:Hard%20decline), where retrying the same card will not help.
quotes: Conversion in Germany dropped after we turned on the low-value exemption.
Those are soft declines. We're showing an error instead of falling back to 3DS.

nodes.name: Hard decline
nodes.description: A card refusal that retrying will not fix, such as a closed account or a card reported lost or stolen.
nodes.markdown:
A hard decline is a card refusal that will not be resolved by trying the same card again. The account may be closed, the card may be reported lost or stolen, or the transaction type may not be allowed. The next step is to get a different payment method.

"Hard decline" is industry shorthand and has no single definition across networks. Visa's rules contain the closest formal version: Category 1 [decline codes](node:Decline%20code), labelled "[issuer](node:Issuer) will never approve", which a [merchant](node:Merchant) must never reattempt.

| Visa Category 1 code | Meaning                              |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `04`                 | Pick up card, no fraud               |
| `07`                 | Pick up card, special condition      |
| `41`                 | Lost card                            |
| `43`                 | Stolen card                          |
| `46`                 | Closed account                       |
| `57`                 | Transaction not permitted to [cardholder](node:Cardholder) |
| `R0`, `R1`, `R3`     | Stop-payment instructions            |

Other networks classify codes differently. Mastercard, for example, uses merchant advice codes to tell merchants how to respond, so a mapping built only from Visa's table is incomplete. Generic codes such as `05` "do not honor" should not automatically count as hard or soft. A [soft decline](node:Soft%20decline), by contrast, may succeed after a change.

The common failure occurs in [recurring billing](node:Recurring%20billing). A subscription job retries a closed card on every [dunning](node:Dunning) cycle. Each attempt fails, adds authorization cost, and lowers the merchant's [authorization rate](node:Authorization%20rate), and it can also breach network retry rules.

The correct handling is to stop retries, mark the stored card unusable, and ask the customer to update it. An [account updater](node:Account%20updater) or [network token](node:Network%20token) can sometimes supply new details after a reissue, but do not use these to continue charging a card reported stolen or an account the customer closed deliberately. Tell the customer only that the payment was declined.
quotes: This subscription has failed six months in a row. Should dunning keep going?
Check the code. If it's a 46, that's a hard decline, so stop retrying and email them for a new card.

nodes.name: Merchant category code
nodes.description: A four-digit code classifying a merchant's type of business, used for fees, card restrictions and risk rules.
nodes.markdown:
A merchant category code (MCC) is a four-digit number that classifies a merchant's type of business, such as a grocery store, airline or software seller. ISO 18245 defines a set of these codes, and [card networks](node:Card%20network) publish their own lists and assignment rules. Visa's Merchant Data Standards Manual says the MCC describes a merchant's primary business, based on annual sales volume.

The [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) normally assigns the code at onboarding. It then travels in each [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) and [clearing](node:Clearing) record, where several parties use it.

| Party       | How it uses the MCC                                                 |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Issuer](node:Issuer) | Applies rewards, spending controls and block rules         |
| Network     | Applies category-specific rules and [interchange](node:Interchange%20fee) programs |
| Acquirer    | Assesses merchant risk and pricing                                  |
| [Cardholder](node:Cardholder) | Sees spending categories in a banking app                 |

An incorrect code can cause failures that look unrelated. A company card program may block some categories, so a business coded as gambling or money transfer can see declines from customers whose cards work elsewhere. A wrong MCC can also change the fees the merchant pays, or remove eligibility for a feature such as [incremental authorization](node:Incremental%20authorization), which networks often limit by category.

MCC is different from a product category in your own catalogue. It describes the business as a whole, so one transaction for a single item does not get its own code. A merchant with distinct lines of business may need separate merchant IDs with separate MCCs, depending on network rules.

Deliberately using a misleading code to obtain lower fees or avoid a restricted category is a rule violation, and it can lead to network penalties passed on by the acquirer or to closure of the [merchant account](node:Merchant%20account). If the business changes, ask the acquirer to review the code.
quotes: Corporate cards keep getting declined on our site, but only corporate cards.
We're coded under a restricted MCC. Ask the acquirer to review our classification.

nodes.name: Acquirer reference number
nodes.description: A reference created for a cleared card transaction, used to trace refunds and disputes between acquirer and issuer.
nodes.markdown:
An acquirer reference number (ARN) is an identifier attached to a card transaction when it enters [clearing](node:Clearing). Both the acquirer and the [issuer](node:Issuer) can use it to find the same transaction, so it is the reference most often used to trace a [refund](node:Refund) or a dispute. Visa's rules refer to the acquirer reference number, and Mastercard's rules call the equivalent value acquirer reference data (ARD).

The ARN is one of several identifiers that appear at different stages, and they are easy to confuse.

| Identifier                                             | Created at          | Main use                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Authorization code                                     | Approval            | Short code from the issuer for that approval |
| [Network transaction ID](node:Network%20transaction%20ID) | Authorization       | Links related network messages           |
| ARN                                                    | Clearing            | Tracing between acquirer and issuer      |
| Provider payment ID                                    | Provider API        | Finding the payment in your provider     |
| [Merchant's](node:Merchant) order ID                   | Checkout            | Finding the order in your own system     |

Because the ARN comes from clearing, it does not exist at authorization. A payment that has been authorized but not [captured](node:Capture) has none, and one that has just been refunded may not have one until the refund is submitted. Model it as optional and populate it from a later event or report.

A typical use is a refund complaint. A customer says the money never arrived, and the [cardholder's](node:Cardholder) bank says it has no record. The merchant asks its [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) for the refund's ARN and gives it to the customer, who gives it to the bank. The bank can then search its records for that exact credit. The refund has its own reference, so make sure you send that one and not the ARN of the original purchase.

In a [chargeback](node:Chargeback), the ARN ties the dispute back to the original sale. Store it against the payment record.
quotes: Her bank says they can't see the refund we sent.
Get the ARN for the refund from the provider. The bank can trace the credit with that.

nodes.name: Network transaction ID
nodes.description: A card network's identifier for a transaction, used to link later messages and stored-card payments to the original.
nodes.markdown:
A network transaction ID is the identifier a [card network](node:Card%20network) assigns to a transaction, returned with the [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) response. Later messages for the same payment, and later payments that depend on it, carry this value so that the network and [issuer](node:Issuer) can connect them. The generic term covers different network-specific fields.

| Network    | Name in the rules      | Notes                                                             |
| ---------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Visa       | Transaction Identifier | Assigned per transaction, used as an audit trail through the life cycle |
| Mastercard | Trace ID               | Built from network reference data and settlement date             |

It is different from the [acquirer reference number](node:Acquirer%20reference%20number), which appears at [clearing](node:Clearing) and is the usual reference for tracing a [refund](node:Refund) with a bank. The network transaction ID exists from authorization onward and is primarily for system-to-system linking.

The ID matters most for [stored credentials](node:Stored%20credential). When a customer saves a card, the first [customer-initiated transaction](node:Customer-initiated%20transaction) establishes consent. Each later [merchant-initiated transaction](node:Merchant-initiated%20transaction) references that original ID, showing the issuer that this charge belongs to an agreed series. Under [PSD2](node:PSD2), this link also helps show why a later charge, made without the customer present, was sent without [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication).

The failure usually appears during a migration. A company moves to a new [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider), imports card numbers or tokens, but leaves the original network IDs behind. Renewals now look like unlinked payments with no customer present, and issuers decline more of them, often with an authentication-required [soft decline](node:Soft%20decline). Ask for the network transaction IDs in the export, and confirm the new provider can accept them.

Store the ID with the payment method and with each payment, and pass through the value from the correct original transaction. Fabricating or reusing an unrelated ID misrepresents the transaction.
quotes: Renewal declines jumped right after the PSP migration.
We imported the tokens but not the network transaction IDs, so the issuers can't link those charges to the original consent.

nodes.name: Statement descriptor
nodes.description: The merchant name and details a cardholder sees for a payment on a bank or card statement.
nodes.markdown:
A statement descriptor is the text identifying a [merchant](node:Merchant) on a [cardholder's](node:Cardholder) bank or card statement. It is built from the merchant name and location data carried in the [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) and [clearing](node:Clearing) messages, such as the card acceptor name field in [ISO 8583](node:ISO%208583). The [issuer](node:Issuer) decides how to display it, so the same payment can look different across banking apps.

An unclear descriptor directly causes disputes. A customer buys from a shop called Northwind but the statement reads `NWD HOLDINGS LTD`. Weeks later they do not recognise it and report it to their bank as fraud, producing a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) on a legitimate order. This is a common form of [friendly fraud](node:Friendly%20fraud).

Visa's Merchant Data Standards Manual calls the merchant name the most important factor in cardholder recognition, and requires it to be the name most prominently displayed by the merchant and recognised by cardholders. Visa's rules also require [acquirers](node:Acquirer) to correct names that are non-compliant or that confuse cardholders.

| Descriptor                 | Result                                         |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Legal company name only    | Often unrecognised                             |
| Trading or brand name      | Usually recognised                             |
| Brand and order reference  | Easier to match to a receipt                   |
| Platform name only         | Customer may not recognise the actual seller   |

Length limits are tight and vary by network and provider, so test the shortened version. A [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) may let you set a static descriptor for the account and a dynamic suffix per payment. Platforms often use a prefix and seller name. If a [merchant of record](node:Merchant%20of%20record) is involved, its name normally appears, so mention it at checkout and on the receipt.

To reduce disputes, use the name customers see on your website, send a receipt that shows the exact descriptor, and include a support contact where the format allows.
quotes: Half of this month's fraud disputes are from customers who did get their orders.
Our descriptor still shows the holding company. Change it to the store name.

nodes.name: Address verification
nodes.description: A check comparing a customer's billing postcode and street address with the card issuer's records for online payments.
nodes.markdown:
Address verification, often called AVS after the Address Verification Service, is a check that compares the billing address a customer enters with the address held by their [issuer](node:Issuer). It runs during a [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) for a [card-not-present transaction](node:Card-not-present%20transaction). The issuer returns a result code, and the [merchant](node:Merchant) decides what to do with it.

| Result                  | What it suggests                    | Common handling                          |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Full match              | Address details agree               | Treat as a positive signal               |
| Postcode only           | Street differs or was not checked   | Weigh with other signals                 |
| Street only             | Postcode differs                    | Weigh with other signals                 |
| No match                | Neither agrees                      | Review or request more authentication    |
| Unavailable             | Issuer or region does not support it | Do not treat as a failure                |

Exact result codes vary by network and provider.

AVS is regional. Visa's rules require issuers to participate in listed regions and countries, including the US, Canada, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and Singapore, and added several Latin American countries effective October 2026. Those rules focus on postal code verification, with street address checked when present. Coverage elsewhere is limited, so a global rule that blocks every non-match will reject many valid international customers.

An AVS mismatch usually does not stop an approval on its own. An issuer can approve a payment with a failed address check, so the merchant holds an approved transaction and has to choose. If it rejects the order, it should send an [authorization reversal](node:Authorization%20reversal). Otherwise the customer sees a pending [authorization hold](node:Authorization%20hold) for an order that was refused.

False mismatches are common, because customers move house or abbreviate street names.

Treat AVS as one input to [risk scoring](node:Risk%20scoring). It does not authenticate the [cardholder](node:Cardholder), and a match does not provide the [liability shift](node:Liability%20shift) that [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) can.
quotes: We're rejecting a lot of UK orders on address mismatch.
Stop hard-blocking on AVS. Use it as one risk signal and send a reversal when we do refuse.

nodes.name: PCI DSS
nodes.description: The security standard for organisations that store, process or transmit payment card account data.
nodes.markdown:
PCI DSS, the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, is the security standard for organisations that store, process or transmit payment card account data, or that can affect its security. It is published by the PCI Security Standards Council (PCI SSC), founded by the major [card networks](node:Card%20network). The current series is v4.x, and the Council's document library holds the latest revision.

Account data has two parts, and the rules treat them differently.

| Data type                     | Examples                                  | Storage after authorization        |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Cardholder data               | [PAN](node:PAN), name, expiry, service code | Allowed if protected and justified |
| Sensitive authentication data | Full track, [CVV](node:CVV), PIN          | Not allowed, even if encrypted     |

A narrow exception exists for [issuers](node:Issuer) and companies supporting issuing services.

The Council writes the standard, but it does not enforce it. Whether an organisation must comply or validate is decided by those running compliance programs.

| Party                      | Role                                                  |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| PCI SSC                    | Publishes the standard and trains assessors           |
| Payment brands             | Set compliance programs and any penalties             |
| [Acquirers](node:Acquirer) | Require their [merchants](node:Merchant) to validate  |
| Qualified Security Assessor | Independently assesses an organisation               |
| Merchants and providers    | Implement and maintain the controls                   |

PCI DSS is a contractual industry standard and not, in general, a law, although some jurisdictions refer to it. A merchant usually encounters it through an acquirer's request for a [self-assessment questionnaire](node:Self-assessment%20questionnaire) or a formal assessment report.

The practical work is reducing scope, meaning the set of systems the standard covers. Teams do this by not handling card data at all, using [hosted payment fields](node:Hosted%20payment%20fields), [tokenization](node:Tokenization) or [point-to-point encryption](node:Point-to-point%20encryption).

Scope often grows by accident. A log line captures a card number, or a marketing script is added to the payment page. Requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 address that second risk by requiring control and monitoring of payment page scripts.
quotes: We use a PSP, so PCI doesn't apply to us, right?
It still applies. The PSP shrinks our scope, but we still validate with the right SAQ.

nodes.name: Self-assessment questionnaire
nodes.description: A PCI DSS validation form for eligible organisations, with the version chosen by how they handle card data.
nodes.markdown:
A self-assessment questionnaire (SAQ) is a form that eligible organisations use to validate their [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) compliance without a full on-site assessment. The right version depends on how the business accepts cards.

| SAQ    | Typical [merchant](node:Merchant)                                     |
| ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A      | Card-not-present, with all account data functions fully outsourced    |
| A-EP   | E-commerce where the merchant's site can affect payment page security |
| B      | Imprint machines or standalone dial-out terminals                     |
| B-IP   | Standalone approved terminals with an IP connection                   |
| C      | Payment application connected to the internet, no electronic storage  |
| C-VT   | Manual entry into a third-party virtual terminal on an isolated device |
| P2PE   | Only a validated, PCI-listed [point-to-point encryption](node:Point-to-point%20encryption) solution |
| SPoC   | Listed software-based PIN entry solution on a commercial mobile device |
| D      | All other eligible merchants, and all eligible service providers      |

An [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or payment brand decides whether a merchant may self-assess or needs an assessor's report.

A common mistake is assuming any hosted checkout qualifies for SAQ A. The v4.0.1 revision of SAQ A removed requirements 6.4.3, 11.6.1 and 12.3.1 from that form and added an eligibility criterion: an e-commerce merchant must confirm its site is not susceptible to attacks from scripts that could affect its systems.

PCI SSC's FAQ 1588 explains that this criterion applies to pages that embed a provider's form, such as through an iframe with [hosted payment fields](node:Hosted%20payment%20fields). It does not apply to a full redirect to the provider or a fully outsourced flow such as an emailed payment link. A merchant can meet it with protective techniques or a compliant provider's confirmation.

If a developer later adds a custom card form or stores card numbers, the business may no longer qualify, so review eligibility whenever checkout changes.
quotes: We embed the PSP's iframe, so we just tick SAQ A?
Only if we meet the script-attack criterion. Get the provider's confirmation or put the controls on our page.

nodes.name: Tokenization
nodes.description: Replacing a card number with a substitute value, so most systems never hold the real account data.
nodes.markdown:
Tokenization replaces a sensitive value, such as a card's [PAN](node:PAN), with a substitute called a token. The token can be stored and passed around in place of the card number, and only a controlled system can map it back or use it to make a payment. It is the usual way a [merchant](node:Merchant) keeps a customer's card on file without holding the card number.

Tokenization differs from encryption. Encrypted data can be recovered by anyone holding the key, while a token normally has no mathematical relationship to the original and is resolved by lookup in a [card vault](node:Card%20vault) or by a token service.

"Token" covers several things in payments, and the differences matter.

| Type                               | Created by                       | Usable where                     |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| PSP token                          | [Payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) | Usually that provider only |
| [Network token](node:Network%20token) | Network token service         | Across the network, within its domain limits |
| Device wallet token                | Network token service, for a wallet | That device or wallet          |
| Merchant-internal token            | Merchant's own vault             | That merchant's systems          |

The first two are often confused. A team switching providers can discover that its saved PSP tokens do not work elsewhere, and that a card data migration is needed before renewals can continue.

Tokenization reduces [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) scope but does not remove it. PCI SSC's tokenization guidance says the tokenization system itself remains part of the cardholder data environment. Systems holding only tokens may fall out of scope if they have no route back to the PAN. A token that can itself initiate a transaction may still need protection because it can be used to spend money.

For that reason, restrict which API keys can charge a token, and treat token stores as sensitive even when they contain no card numbers.
quotes: We tokenized everything, so a leak of this table is harmless, right?
Not quite. Those tokens can charge customers through our API key, so they still need protecting.

nodes.name: Network token
nodes.description: A card-network-level substitute for a card number, limited to a merchant, device or payment scenario.
nodes.markdown:
A network token is a substitute for a card's [PAN](node:PAN), issued through a [card network's](node:Card%20network) token service and recognised from the point of purchase through the [acquirer](node:Acquirer) and network to the [issuer](node:Issuer). It follows EMVCo's Payment Tokenisation Specification, where it is called an [EMV](node:EMV) Payment Token. Visa Token Service and Mastercard Digital Enablement Service are two network implementations.

| Role                  | Who                                    | What it does                                   |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Token Requestor       | [Merchant](node:Merchant), wallet or provider | Registers and requests tokens                  |
| Token Service Provider | Usually the network                   | Creates tokens and maps them to the PAN        |
| Issuer                | [Cardholder](node:Cardholder)'s institution               | Approves token creation and the payments       |
| Token User            | Merchant or wallet                     | Presents the token for payment                 |

A token is limited in use, for example to one merchant, one device, or a specific payment scenario, so a stolen token is worth far less than a card number. Depending on the use case, a one-time token cryptogram accompanies the payment to prove it is genuine. EMVCo also defines a Payment Account Reference, which lets systems link different tokens for the same underlying account without exposing the PAN.

The term is most often confused with a PSP [token](node:Tokenization).

| Property            | Network token                    | PSP token                     |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Issued by           | Token service, usually network   | Payment provider              |
| Seen by issuer      | Yes                              | No, the issuer sees the PAN   |
| Works across providers | Possible, if set up for it    | Generally no                  |
| Follows card changes | Can be updated by the issuer    | Depends on the provider       |

Because a network token can stay valid when the physical card is reissued, it can reduce failures on [recurring billing](node:Recurring%20billing) after a card expires. A payment sent without a required cryptogram can still be declined. Code that reads a token's first digits as the card's [BIN](node:BIN) may also misclassify the card, so ask your provider for the underlying card attributes.
quotes: Renewals keep failing whenever banks reissue cards.
Turn on network tokens for stored cards. The issuer updates them when the card changes.

nodes.name: Card vault
nodes.description: A secured system that stores card numbers and returns tokens so other systems never need to hold the real data.
nodes.markdown:
A card vault is a secured system that stores card numbers and gives other systems a [token](node:Tokenization) to use in their place. When a payment is needed, an authorised service sends the token, and the vault supplies the [PAN](node:PAN) to the payment connection without exposing it to the rest of the application.

| Step | Who                  | What happens                                     |
| ---- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| 1    | Checkout             | Sends card details directly to the vault         |
| 2    | Vault                | Encrypts and stores the PAN, returns a token     |
| 3    | Application          | Stores only the token and display details        |
| 4    | Payment service      | Requests a charge using the token                |
| 5    | Vault                | Forwards the PAN to the [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or processor    |

A vault holds the data that attackers want, so it is firmly in [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) scope. It can store the PAN and expiry date, but it must not keep the [CVV](node:CVV) after [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization).

| Option                                                        | Benefit                   | Cost                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| [Payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) vault | Least effort and scope    | Tied to that provider                |
| Independent third-party vault                                 | Can route to several PSPs | Another vendor, some integration work |
| Self-hosted vault                                             | Full control of the data  | Full PCI burden and security operations |

The choice usually becomes visible when a business wants to change provider or add a second one for [payment routing](node:Payment%20routing). With a provider vault, stored cards cannot be moved by the [merchant](node:Merchant). The old provider must export the data securely to a PCI-compliant recipient, which can take weeks and depends on the contract. Read the export terms before committing.

Migrations carry their own failure risk. Token mappings can be incomplete, and renewals can start declining if [network transaction IDs](node:Network%20transaction%20ID) were not transferred with the cards. Run a test batch and compare [authorization rates](node:Authorization%20rate) before and after.
quotes: Can we export our saved cards ourselves and upload them to the new provider?
No. The old vault has to transfer them directly to the new one under PCI controls.

nodes.name: Point-to-point encryption
nodes.description: Encrypting card data at the payment terminal so it stays unreadable until it reaches a secure decryption environment.
nodes.markdown:
Point-to-point encryption (P2PE) encrypts card data inside a secure payment terminal at the moment the card is read, and keeps it encrypted until it reaches a protected decryption environment away from the [merchant](node:Merchant). The shop's network, tills and back-office systems carry only ciphertext they cannot read. It is used with payment terminals, not online checkout.

The term has a general meaning and a specific one under [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS). Any vendor can describe its terminal as "encrypted". PCI P2PE is a separate PCI SSC standard, and only solutions validated against it and listed by the Council carry its compliance benefits.

| Feature                  | Encrypted terminal (generic)     | Validated PCI P2PE solution              |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Independently assessed   | Not necessarily                  | Yes, against the P2PE standard           |
| Listed by PCI SSC        | No                               | Yes                                      |
| Eligible for SAQ P2PE    | No                               | Yes, if the merchant meets the criteria  |

A retailer buys terminals advertised as end-to-end encrypted and assumes it qualifies for the shorter [self-assessment questionnaire](node:Self-assessment%20questionnaire). An assessor then finds the solution is not on the PCI list, so the shop's network remains in scope. Check the PCI SSC listing before buying and again at renewal, because a solution whose listing has expired is no longer treated as validated, and the merchant should then ask its [acquirer](node:Acquirer) what applies.

SAQ P2PE covers merchants that take account data only through a validated solution's terminals and have no clear-text account data on their computer systems. It does not apply to e-commerce. The merchant must also follow the solution's instruction manual.

P2PE is different from TLS, the encryption used for web traffic, which protects data between two connected systems. P2PE protects the card data from the terminal itself.
quotes: The vendor says the terminals are encrypted, so our network is out of scope.
Only if it's a validated P2PE solution. Check that it's listed by PCI SSC.

nodes.name: Hosted payment fields
nodes.description: Card inputs served by a payment provider inside a merchant's page, so card data bypasses the merchant's servers.
nodes.markdown:
Hosted payment fields are card input boxes served by a [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) and embedded in a [merchant's](node:Merchant) checkout, usually as iframes. An iframe is a small page from another domain displayed inside the main page. The customer appears to type on the merchant's site, but the [PAN](node:PAN) and [CVV](node:CVV) go directly from the browser to the provider, which returns a [token](node:Tokenization).

| Step | Who      | What happens                                          |
| ---- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Browser  | Loads the merchant page and the provider's iframes    |
| 2    | Customer | Types card details into the iframes                   |
| 3    | Provider | Receives the card data and returns a token            |
| 4    | Merchant | Sends the token from its server to create the payment |

The approach sits between two other integration styles.

| Integration            | Who controls the page | Card data reaches merchant servers? | Common SAQ        |
| ---------------------- | --------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| Full redirect          | Provider              | No                                  | SAQ A             |
| Hosted payment fields  | Merchant, with provider inputs | No                         | SAQ A, if eligible |
| Merchant script-built form | Merchant          | No, but its page handles the data | SAQ A-EP          |
| Direct API             | Merchant              | Yes                                 | SAQ D             |

Embedded fields do not make the page safe by default. A malicious script on the surrounding page cannot normally read an iframe from another origin, but it could draw a fake form over it or send the customer elsewhere. For this reason, the [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) v4.0.1 version of the [self-assessment questionnaire](node:Self-assessment%20questionnaire) SAQ A requires merchants embedding a provider's form to confirm their site is not susceptible to script attacks.

Engineers usually encounter a different failure. A tightened Content Security Policy, the browser rule listing allowed content sources, blocks the provider's domain. The card fields then render blank or the Pay button does nothing, often in production only. Allow the provider's documented domains and test checkout after changing security headers.
quotes: The card fields are blank in production, but they work locally.
The new CSP is blocking the provider's iframe. Add their domains to frame-src.

nodes.name: 3-D Secure
nodes.description: A protocol that lets a card issuer authenticate the customer during an online payment, with or without a challenge.
nodes.markdown:
3-D Secure (3DS) is a messaging protocol that lets a card [issuer](node:Issuer) authenticate a customer during an online payment. [EMVCo](node:EMV) publishes the current specification as EMV 3-D Secure, and networks brand their programs, for example Visa Secure and Mastercard Identity Check. The "three domains" are the [acquirer](node:Acquirer) side, the issuer side and the interoperability layer connecting them.

| Step | Who                 | What happens                                                |
| ---- | ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | [Merchant's](node:Merchant) 3DS Server | Sends transaction and device data                          |
| 2    | Directory Server    | Run by the network, routes the request to the issuer        |
| 3    | Access Control Server | Issuer's system assesses risk                              |
| 4a   | Issuer              | Frictionless: authenticates without involving the customer  |
| 4b   | Customer            | Challenge: completes an app approval, passcode or biometric |
| 5    | Merchant | Includes the authentication result in the [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) |

Authentication and authorization are separate. 3DS asks "is this the real [cardholder](node:Cardholder)?". The authorization that follows asks "will the issuer approve this payment?". A customer can pass a challenge and still be declined for insufficient funds.

3DS is often confused with [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication). SCA is a legal requirement under [PSD2](node:PSD2) in the EEA. 3DS is a technical protocol and a common way of meeting that requirement for cards. A frictionless 3DS result is not necessarily SCA, and 3DS is also used in regions with no SCA rule.

3DS also supports a [liability shift](node:Liability%20shift) for fraud, under network rules. Visa's rules, for example, make certain fraud disputes invalid for a transaction authenticated through Visa Secure when the authorization carried the required authentication value and indicator.

A frequent bug is losing that value. The challenge succeeds, but the integration does not pass the authentication data into the authorization, so the issuer sees an unauthenticated payment. It can then return a [soft decline](node:Soft%20decline), and the merchant loses any fraud protection.
quotes: The customer passed the 3DS challenge, but we still got a fraud chargeback.
Check the auth request. We dropped the CAVV, so the issuer never saw the authentication.

nodes.name: Strong customer authentication
nodes.description: The EU requirement under PSD2 to authenticate payers with two independent factors, for many electronic payments.
nodes.markdown:
Strong customer authentication (SCA) is a legal requirement in the European Economic Area, set by [PSD2](node:PSD2), that a payer be authenticated using at least two independent factors from different categories. Article 4(30) defines the categories, and independence means that compromising one factor does not compromise the others.

| Category   | Meaning                        | Examples                     |
| ---------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
| Knowledge  | Something only the user knows  | PIN, password                |
| Possession | Something only the user has    | Registered phone, chip card  |
| Inherence  | Something the user is          | Fingerprint, face            |

Article 97 requires a [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) to apply SCA when a payer accesses a payment account online, initiates an electronic payment, or takes a remote action that could carry fraud risk. For remote payments, the authentication must also be dynamically linked to the specific amount and payee. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 holds the detail, and the UK maintains its own version through the FCA.

SCA is an outcome and [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) is a method. For online card payments, 3DS with a challenge is the usual way to meet it.

The obligation falls on the payer's provider, usually the [issuer](node:Issuer), and the [merchant](node:Merchant) must support the flow. Under Article 74(2), if the payer's provider does not require SCA, the payer does not bear financial losses unless they acted fraudulently, and a payee or payee's provider that fails to accept SCA must [refund](node:Refund) the damage caused to the payer's provider.

An [SCA exemption](node:SCA%20exemption) can remove the step, and purely [merchant-initiated transactions](node:Merchant-initiated%20transaction) and mail or telephone orders are outside the requirement.

The symptom for a merchant is a rise in [soft declines](node:Soft%20decline) from European cards when checkout does not support authentication. Saved-card flows often fail the same way if SCA was not performed when the card was first stored.
quotes: Why are EU cards failing when our US cards are fine?
Issuers are asking for SCA and our checkout has no 3DS step. We need to add it.

nodes.name: SCA exemption
nodes.description: A condition in EU rules that allows a payment provider not to apply strong customer authentication to a payment.
nodes.markdown:
An SCA exemption is a condition in EU rules that allows a [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) not to apply [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication) to a payment. The exemptions are in Chapter III of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 under [PSD2](node:PSD2). A provider is "allowed not to apply" SCA and is never obliged to skip it. The table lists the main payment exemptions.

| Article | Exemption                  | Applies to                                                  |
| ------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| 11      | Contactless at point of sale | Small in-person payments, within cumulative limits        |
| 12      | Unattended terminals       | Transport fares and parking fees                            |
| 13      | Trusted beneficiaries      | Payees the payer listed with their provider                 |
| 14      | Recurring transactions     | Later payments in a series with the same amount and payee   |
| 16      | Low-value transactions     | Small remote payments, within cumulative limits             |
| 17      | Secure corporate payments  | Dedicated non-consumer processes accepted by the regulator  |
| 18      | Transaction risk analysis  | Low-risk remote payments, tied to the provider's fraud rate |

Amount limits are in the regulation and may change.

An exempt payment is covered by SCA rules but relieved of the step, while out-of-scope payments are not covered at all. The EBA and ECB list purely [merchant-initiated transactions](node:Merchant-initiated%20transaction), mail and telephone orders, and many "one-leg" payments where one provider is outside the EEA as outside SCA.

The [merchant](node:Merchant) or [acquirer](node:Acquirer) can request an exemption, but the [issuer](node:Issuer) has the final say. An EBA Q&A confirms the issuer can accept an acquirer's risk-analysis exemption, or refuse it and apply SCA. Cumulative counters are invisible to the merchant, so a small payment can still receive a [soft decline](node:Soft%20decline). Checkout must be able to fall back to [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure).

An exempted payment also generally does not get the fraud [liability shift](node:Liability%20shift) that an authenticated one can, although network rules vary.
quotes: We flagged this as low value, so why did the issuer decline it?
The issuer tracks the cumulative limit and can refuse the exemption. Fall back to 3DS on that code.

nodes.name: Liability shift
nodes.description: A network rule moving the cost of certain card fraud from one party to another, usually after chip or 3-D Secure use.
nodes.markdown:
A liability shift is a [card network](node:Card%20network) rule that moves the cost of certain fraud from one party to another when a security measure was or was not used. It determines whether the [merchant's](node:Merchant) side or the [issuer](node:Issuer) absorbs the loss on a fraudulent transaction. The two common forms cover chip payments and online authentication.

| Type                    | Where                               | Who usually bears the fraud                                       |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Chip                    | [Card-present](node:Card-present%20transaction), participating regions | The party that did not support [EMV](node:EMV) chip                |
| [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) | [Card-not-present](node:Card-not-present%20transaction) | Issuer, where the payment was properly authenticated  |
| No shift                | Other online payments               | Usually the merchant                                              |

The details are network- and region-specific.

| Network    | Chip rule                                   | Authentication rule                                          |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Visa       | Dispute Conditions 10.1 and 10.2, with listed regions | Condition 10.4 invalid for qualifying Visa Secure payments |
| Mastercard | Reason code 4870, chip liability shift      | Reason code 4837 excludes properly authenticated payments    |

A common misunderstanding is believing that 3-D Secure stops all [chargebacks](node:Chargeback). The shift applies to fraud claims. A customer who says goods never arrived or were defective can still dispute an authenticated payment, because that is a consumer dispute.

A shift can also fail for technical reasons. If an integration drops the authentication value from the [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization), or sends the wrong electronic commerce indicator, the network treats the payment as unauthenticated even though the customer completed a challenge. Network rules also contain exclusions, and an [SCA exemption](node:SCA%20exemption) generally leaves liability where it was.

This contractual shift is different from the legal allocation under [PSD2](node:PSD2). Article 74(2) says that a payee or payee's provider that fails to accept [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication) must [refund](node:Refund) the financial damage caused to the payer's provider.

Store the authentication result on each payment so it can be used as evidence in [representment](node:Representment).
quotes: We used 3DS on that order, so why are we losing this chargeback?
It's a not-received dispute. The liability shift only covers fraud claims.

nodes.name: PSD2
nodes.description: The EU Payment Services Directive (EU) 2015/2366, which regulates payment providers and requires strong authentication.
nodes.markdown:
PSD2 is the EU's second Payment Services Directive, formally Directive (EU) 2015/2366. It sets the rules for who may provide payment services in the EU and European Economic Area, what those providers owe their customers, and how payments must be secured. It takes effect through each member state's national law, so details differ by country.

| Area              | What PSD2 does                                                          |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Licensing         | Defines payment services and who must be authorised to provide them     |
| Security          | Requires [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication) (SCA) in Article 97 |
| Customer rights   | Sets [refund](node:Refund) and liability rules for unauthorised payments               |
| Third-party access | Creates regulated access to accounts, the basis of EU [open banking](node:Open%20banking) |

Detailed security rules are in a separate, directly applicable law, Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389. SCA is one part of PSD2, and [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) is a technical protocol the directive does not name.

When both the payer's and payee's providers are in the EEA, SCA generally applies. When only one is, the payment is a "one-leg" transaction. A Commission answer published by the European Banking Authority says that an [acquirer](node:Acquirer) outside the EU is not subject to PSD2, and the EU [issuer](node:Issuer) must decide whether to block such a payment or carry the liability. A non-EU [merchant](node:Merchant) selling to Europeans may therefore see [soft declines](node:Soft%20decline) despite having no direct PSD2 obligations.

The UK implemented PSD2 before leaving the EU and now maintains its own rules through the FCA.

A replacement is in progress. The EU reached a provisional agreement in November 2025 on a Payment Services Regulation and a third directive, PSD3. As of November 2026, Parliament's procedure files list both as awaiting a second-reading vote, with no Official Journal publication. Until the new laws apply, PSD2 remains in force.
quotes: We're a US company. Why does PSD2 affect our checkout?
Our customers' banks are in the EU, so they may still ask for SCA. Add 3DS for those cards.

nodes.name: KYC
nodes.description: Know Your Customer, the checks regulated firms use to identify and verify the people they do business with.
nodes.markdown:
KYC, or Know Your Customer, is the process a regulated firm uses to identify a customer, verify that identity, and understand the purpose of the relationship. It is part of [AML](node:AML) compliance. In a payments company, KYC normally applies when opening an account, and again when something about the customer or their activity changes.

International standards come from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), whose Recommendation 10 sets out customer due diligence. Actual obligations come from national or regional law, so they depend on the firm's licence and location.

| Region | Main source                                                                                   |
| ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| EU     | National laws implementing the AML directives. Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 applies generally from 10 July 2027 |
| US     | Bank Secrecy Act rules, including customer identification programs for banks                  |
| UK     | Money Laundering Regulations                                                                  |

A typical KYC flow has several steps.

| Step      | What happens                                                            |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Collect   | Name, date of birth, address, identity document                         |
| Verify    | Check the document or data against reliable sources                     |
| Screen    | Run [sanctions screening](node:Sanctions%20screening) and politically-exposed-person checks |
| Assess    | Assign a risk level                                                     |
| Monitor   | Review activity and refresh information over time                       |

KYC concerns individuals, while [KYB](node:KYB) applies similar checks to businesses and their owners. It is also separate from authentication: KYC establishes who a customer is at onboarding, whereas [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication) checks that the person making a payment is that customer.

Users experience KYC as friction. A wallet asks for a passport before raising a limit, a selfie check rejects a valid document, or an account is restricted because details need renewing. Engineers should model verification as a set of states, such as pending, verified, rejected and needs refresh. A single boolean cannot represent an expired document or a re-review.

Treat identity documents as highly sensitive personal data, and keep them out of support tools and logs.
quotes: Why can't this user withdraw? Their balance is fine.
Their KYC expired when the ID document lapsed. They need to re-verify before we can release payouts.

nodes.name: KYB
nodes.description: Know Your Business, the checks used to verify a company, its ownership and the people who control it.
nodes.markdown:
KYB, or Know Your Business, is the process of verifying a business customer: that it legally exists, what it does, who owns it and who controls it. Banks, [acquirers](node:Acquirer) and [payment facilitators](node:Payment%20facilitator) run KYB before letting a company accept or move money, as part of their [AML](node:AML) and risk controls.

The difficult part is identifying beneficial owners, the natural persons who ultimately own or control a company. FATF standards and Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 both require firms to identify beneficial owners and understand the ownership and control structure. In the US, FinCEN's customer due diligence rule sets beneficial ownership requirements for covered financial institutions, and FinCEN proposed changes to it in November 2026. Ownership thresholds and methods differ by jurisdiction.

| Check          | Question                               | Typical evidence                     |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Legal entity   | Does the company exist?                | Registry extract, tax number         |
| Business model | What does it actually sell?            | Website, invoices, description       |
| Ownership      | Who ultimately owns it?                | Shareholder register, group chart    |
| Control        | Who runs it?                           | Director list, officer details       |
| Individuals    | Are those people who they say?         | [KYC](node:KYC) on owners and directors |
| Screening      | Is anyone restricted?                  | [Sanctions screening](node:Sanctions%20screening) |

For a [merchant](node:Merchant), KYB also covers commercial risk: [refund](node:Refund) policy, delivery times and whether the product fits its [merchant category code](node:Merchant%20category%20code).

The failure businesses feel is a hold on funds. Many platforms allow a new seller to begin processing after basic checks, then request full documents once volume grows. If the seller does not respond, or a new investor changes the ownership, the [payout](node:Payout) can be paused until the review is complete.

Ownership and directors change, so records need periodic and event-driven review. Engineers should store ownership as a graph or linked records, since a flat field for "owner" cannot represent a chain of holding companies.
quotes: This seller's payout has been on hold since their funding round.
The cap table changed. We need updated beneficial owner details before KYB can clear.

nodes.name: AML
nodes.description: Anti-money laundering, the laws and controls for detecting and reporting attempts to disguise the origin of criminal funds.
nodes.markdown:
AML, or anti-money laundering, is the set of laws and internal controls that regulated firms use to detect, prevent and report attempts to pass off criminal money as legitimate. The FATF Recommendations set the international standard, and each country turns them into binding law.

A program usually has these parts.

| Control                 | What it does                                                         |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Risk assessment         | Identifies which products, customers and countries carry most risk   |
| Customer due diligence  | [KYC](node:KYC) for people and [KYB](node:KYB) for businesses        |
| Transaction monitoring  | Flags activity that does not fit the customer's profile              |
| Investigation           | Analysts review alerts and record decisions                          |
| Reporting               | Files suspicious activity reports with the national authority        |
| Record keeping          | Retains evidence for a legally required period                       |

AML differs from fraud prevention, though the tools overlap. Fraud controls protect the firm and its customers from being robbed. AML looks for customers who may be successfully moving their own illicit funds, where nobody complains. [Sanctions screening](node:Sanctions%20screening) is also distinct: it checks whether dealing with a party is prohibited at all.

Warning patterns include activity far above a customer's stated business, funds moving in and immediately back out, and payments split to stay under reporting limits. A [merchant](node:Merchant) account processing payments unrelated to its declared business can indicate transaction laundering, where one business runs card payments for another, undisclosed one.

The symptom for customers is an unexplained restriction. Support cannot say why, and this is often deliberate. Laws in many jurisdictions prohibit "tipping off", meaning telling someone that a suspicious activity report has been filed or is being considered. Engineers should therefore keep case details out of customer-facing logs and support tools, and give agents an approved neutral script.

Record each alert, the analyst's decision and the reasoning, since regulators may ask to see that trail.
quotes: A customer is demanding to know why their account is restricted. What can I say?
Use the standard compliance script. Don't speculate, and don't mention any AML review.

nodes.name: Sanctions screening
nodes.description: Checking customers and payments against government sanctions lists to stop prohibited dealings.
nodes.markdown:
Sanctions screening is the process of checking customers, counterparties and payments against government sanctions lists to avoid prohibited dealings. Common sources include the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the EU consolidated list, the UK's sanctions list and United Nations lists. Which regimes bind a firm depends on its location, nationality and partners.

Screening usually happens at several points.

| Point       | What is checked                                         | Example result                     |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Onboarding  | Customer, directors and beneficial owners | Account opening is paused          |
| Ongoing     | Existing customers against updated lists                | Account is restricted              |
| Transaction | Payer, payee, banks, countries and payment text         | Payment is held for review         |

[AML](node:AML) is largely risk-based and focuses on suspicious behaviour. A sanctions prohibition can apply regardless of behaviour, and OFAC can impose civil penalties on a strict liability basis, meaning a firm can be liable even if it did not know a transaction was prohibited. Some regimes extend to entities owned or controlled by a listed person, so combine screening with [KYB](node:KYB) ownership data.

Under US rules, some property must be blocked, meaning frozen and reported, while other prohibited transactions are rejected and returned. Returning funds that should have been blocked can itself be a violation. Compliance teams, and not application code, should decide which outcome applies.

The main operational problem is false positives. Names are transliterated in different ways and many people share them, so screening uses fuzzy matching. A customer named similarly to a listed person may find a [payout](node:Payout) or payment held until an analyst clears the alert.

Engineers should rescreen when lists change, version the list used for each decision, and fail closed if the screening service is unavailable on flows that require it. Record who cleared each alert and why.
quotes: Why is this payout stuck in review? The seller's been with us for years.
Their name partly matched a new sanctions listing. Compliance has to clear the alert before it can go out.

nodes.name: Card-present transaction
nodes.description: A card payment where the card and cardholder are physically at the terminal, typically by chip or contactless.
nodes.markdown:
A card-present transaction is a payment in which the card and [cardholder](node:Cardholder) are physically at the point of sale. Visa's rules call this a Card-Present Environment, and define it by both being present at the [merchant's](node:Merchant) premises or a similar acceptance point.

| Entry method           | How data is captured              | Fraud protection                       |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Chip                   | Card generates a cryptogram       | Strong against counterfeit cards       |
| Contactless card       | Card generates a cryptogram       | Strong against counterfeit cards       |
| Mobile wallet tap      | Device presents a [network token](node:Network%20token) | Token and device authentication |
| Magnetic stripe        | Static data read from the stripe  | Weak, data can be copied               |
| Key-entered at terminal | Staff type the number            | Weak, may lose card-present treatment  |

The contrast is with a [card-not-present transaction](node:Card-not-present%20transaction), where no terminal reads the card. Because an [EMV](node:EMV) chip proves the card is genuine, card-present payments generally carry lower fraud risk, and pricing often reflects that.

The classification comes from data in the [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) message, such as point-of-sale entry mode. It is not inferred from where the merchant is. A card number keyed in after a chip failure may cost more and give the merchant weaker evidence in a dispute. If a chip card is swiped or keyed where the [liability shift](node:Liability%20shift) applies, the merchant can be liable for counterfeit fraud.

Physical presence does not rule out all fraud. A lost or stolen card can be used in person, particularly for low-value contactless payments that do not ask for a PIN. Under EU rules, the contactless [SCA exemption](node:SCA%20exemption) has cumulative limits, so a terminal may occasionally ask a customer to insert the card and enter a PIN.
quotes: The terminal asked her for a PIN on a tiny coffee payment. Is it broken?
No. She hit the contactless limit on that card, so the issuer wants a chip and PIN.

nodes.name: Card-not-present transaction
nodes.description: A card payment made without the physical card at a terminal, such as online, in an app or by phone.
nodes.markdown:
A card-not-present (CNP) transaction is a payment made without the card being read by a terminal, typically online, in an app, by phone or by mail order. Visa's rules call this a Card-Absent Environment. Because no chip takes part, the [merchant](node:Merchant) has to rely on other signals that the person paying is the real [cardholder](node:Cardholder).

| Property          | [Card-present](node:Card-present%20transaction) | Card-not-present                        |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Card verification | [EMV](node:EMV) chip cryptogram                 | [CVV](node:CVV), [network token](node:Network%20token) |
| Customer check    | PIN or device, where required                   | [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure), account signals |
| Address check     | Not usually relevant                            | [Address verification](node:Address%20verification), where supported |
| Fraud liability   | Depends on chip support                         | Often the merchant, unless authenticated |

The main risk is stolen card details. Data taken in a breach, by phishing or by skimming code on a checkout page can be used remotely without the physical card. For this reason, fraud [chargebacks](node:Chargeback) concentrate in this channel, and network monitoring focuses on it. Visa's [chargeback ratio](node:Chargeback%20ratio) under its Acquirer Monitoring Program, for example, is based on card-not-present activity.

Controls work best in layers, combining authentication, [velocity checks](node:Velocity%20check), device data and [risk scoring](node:Risk%20scoring). Applying 3-D Secure can provide a [liability shift](node:Liability%20shift) on qualifying fraud claims.

Regulation differs by channel. Under [PSD2](node:PSD2), remote electronic payments generally need [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication), with dynamic linking to the amount and payee. Mail and telephone orders are treated as outside that requirement, so correctly flagging them matters. Marking ordinary web payments as telephone orders to avoid authentication misrepresents the transaction and can breach network rules.

CNP data handling also has consequences for compliance. Card entry through [hosted payment fields](node:Hosted%20payment%20fields) can reduce [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) scope. Phone payments can bring call recordings into scope.
quotes: Fraud is only showing up on the website, never in our stores.
That's expected. Online is card-not-present, so there's no chip. Turn on 3DS for the risky orders.

nodes.name: Card testing
nodes.description: Automated use of a merchant's checkout to find which stolen card details work, seen as bursts of small failed payments.
nodes.markdown:
Card testing is a fraud attack in which criminals use a [merchant's](node:Merchant) payment flow to find out which stolen or generated card details are valid. Visa calls the wider activity account enumeration. The checkout is used as a validity check, and working cards are used or sold elsewhere.

The usual sign is a sudden burst of [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) attempts, many of them declined, often for small amounts and often outside business hours.

| Signal                                       | Where to look                     |
| -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Spike in authorization attempts              | Provider dashboard, API metrics   |
| Sharp fall in [authorization rate](node:Authorization%20rate) | Payment monitoring |
| Many different cards from one device, IP or session | Checkout and fraud logs    |
| Many cards sharing a [BIN](node:BIN)         | [Decline code](node:Decline%20code) reports |
| Repeated [CVV](node:CVV) or expiry failures  | Authorization responses           |
| Unusual activity on add-card or donation pages | Endpoint metrics                |

The cost falls on the merchant in several ways: authorization fees, a damaged reputation with [issuers](node:Issuer), later [chargebacks](node:Chargeback) on successful attempts, and holds on real customers' cards. Visa's monitoring program, VAMP, includes a separate enumeration measure, so sustained attacks can bring network attention to the merchant and its [acquirer](node:Acquirer).

Visa's guidance for merchants recommends layered controls.

| Control                                     | Effect                                         |
| ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| CAPTCHA on every card-validating request    | Slows automated traffic                        |
| [Velocity checks](node:Velocity%20check)    | Limits attempts per card, device, IP, account  |
| Required CVV and [address verification](node:Address%20verification) | Adds checks on entry     |
| Protect add-card and save-card flows        | Closes commonly overlooked endpoints           |
| Rotate API keys if abused                   | Cuts off stolen credentials                    |

During an active attack, block the traffic quickly and tell your provider or acquirer. Reverse approved test payments with an [authorization reversal](node:Authorization%20reversal), or [refund](node:Refund) them if already captured, because those [cardholders](node:Cardholder) did not make them.

Keep customer-facing error messages generic, so the checkout does not reveal which card field failed.
quotes: We just had 4,000 one-dollar auths in twenty minutes, nearly all declined.
That's card testing. Turn on the CAPTCHA, rate-limit the endpoint and tell the acquirer.

nodes.name: Account takeover
nodes.description: Fraud in which a criminal gains access to a real customer's account and uses its saved payment methods or balance.
nodes.markdown:
Account takeover (ATO) is fraud in which a criminal gains access to a genuine customer's account and acts as that customer. In a payments context, the attacker uses saved cards, spends a stored balance, redirects a [payout](node:Payout), or changes contact details to lock out the owner. Access commonly comes from reused passwords leaked elsewhere, phishing or malware on the customer's device.

ATO differs from stolen-card fraud. With a stolen card, the fraudster brings a card to a new account. With ATO, the account, the card on file and the purchase history all look legitimate, so payment signals such as a passing [CVV](node:CVV) or a known card reveal little. Detection has to focus on the session and the account's behaviour.

| Warning sign                                       | Why it matters                            |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Login from a new device or unusual location        | Possible credential use                   |
| Many failed logins across accounts from one source | Automated password testing against the site |
| Password reset followed quickly by a purchase      | Attacker securing access                  |
| Email, phone or payout details changed             | Locks out the owner or redirects funds    |

The real [cardholder](node:Cardholder) then disputes the charges, so the [merchant](node:Merchant) receives a fraud [chargeback](node:Chargeback) on what looked like a loyal customer's order.

| Control                                            | Purpose                                 |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Multi-factor authentication                        | Stolen password alone is not enough     |
| Breached-password checks                           | Blocks known leaked credentials         |
| Login rate limits and [velocity checks](node:Velocity%20check) | Slows automated attempts    |
| Step-up on sensitive changes                       | Reconfirms before payout or email edits |
| Notify the old email or phone of changes           | Lets the real owner react               |
| Delay payouts after bank detail changes            | Gives time to catch a redirect          |

When ATO is confirmed, revoke all sessions and API tokens, reset credentials, reverse attacker changes, and review recent orders and payouts.
quotes: This customer's been with us five years, and suddenly three orders shipped to a new address.
Password reset an hour earlier from a new device. Looks like account takeover, so lock it and hold the orders.

nodes.name: Friendly fraud
nodes.description: A chargeback on a genuine purchase, raised by mistake or dishonestly by the cardholder or someone they know.
nodes.markdown:
Friendly fraud is a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) raised on a genuine purchase, where the [cardholder](node:Cardholder) or someone connected to them received the goods or service. The name is misleading because many cases are not deliberate. Visa uses the more neutral term first-party misuse for cardholders reporting fraud on transactions they actually made.

| Cause                   | Example                                                  | Deliberate? |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Unrecognised charge     | Unclear [statement descriptor](node:Statement%20descriptor) | No       |
| Family use              | A child buys in-game currency on a parent's card         | Usually no  |
| Forgotten subscription  | Renewal the customer forgot about                        | Usually no  |
| [Refund](node:Refund) shortcut | Customer calls the bank instead of the [merchant](node:Merchant) | Mixed |
| Buyer's remorse         | Customer keeps the item and claims fraud                 | Yes         |

It differs from true third-party fraud, where a stranger used stolen card details. The two look identical to the merchant at first because both typically arrive under a fraud [dispute reason code](node:Dispute%20reason%20code). Do not assume dishonesty.

Use a descriptor customers recognise, send clear receipts, remind customers before a renewal, make cancelling easy, and offer a visible refund route so that contacting support is easier than calling the bank.

When a dispute arrives, the merchant can contest it through [representment](node:Representment) with evidence that the cardholder took part. Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0, under Dispute Condition 10.4, lets a merchant use matching data from earlier undisputed transactions on the same card, such as IP address or device ID, when specific conditions are met. Those conditions change, so check the current Visa rules. Mastercard has its own evidence requirements for its fraud-related chargebacks.

To be usable, the evidence must be collected at purchase time. Log device, IP, account and delivery data against each order, within applicable privacy law. Each dispute also adds to the merchant's [chargeback ratio](node:Chargeback%20ratio).
quotes: He says he never bought it, but he's played the game on that account for two years.
Looks like friendly fraud. Pull the device and IP history and see whether it qualifies for CE 3.0.

nodes.name: Velocity check
nodes.description: A fraud control that counts events per card, device, IP or account in a time window and reacts when a limit is exceeded.
nodes.markdown:
A velocity check is a fraud control that counts how many times something happens within a time window and acts when the count exceeds a limit. In payments, it might count attempts per card in ten minutes, or the number of different cards used by one device in an hour. It is used against automated attacks such as [card testing](node:Card%20testing) and [account takeover](node:Account%20takeover).

A rule has four parts.

| Part   | Options                                                    |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Key    | Card fingerprint, device, IP, account, email, [BIN](node:BIN) |
| Event  | Attempt, decline, approval, new card added, login, [refund](node:Refund)  |
| Window | Minutes, hours or days                                     |
| Action | Allow, add friction, send to review, block                 |

Different keys catch different patterns.

| Pattern                       | Useful count                               |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| One card tried repeatedly     | Attempts per card                          |
| Many cards from one source    | Distinct cards per device, IP or session   |
| Stolen list spread across IPs | Declines per [merchant](node:Merchant), overall or by BIN   |
| Reused accounts               | Failed logins per account or per source    |

Limits should be based on your own traffic, because a normal pattern for a ticketing site at launch time would look like an attack for a furniture store. Test rules in log-only mode first.

The common failure is blocking legitimate customers. Offices, universities and mobile carriers put many users behind one IP address, so a strict per-IP limit can stop everyone at that location. Combine keys, prefer a step-up such as [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) over an outright block where possible.

Implementation has its own traps. A counter that reads and then writes separately can undercount under concurrency, so use an atomic increment in a store such as Redis. Avoid using a raw [PAN](node:PAN) as a key, since that places the counter store in [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) scope. Use the provider's card fingerprint or a token.
quotes: The whole university campus is getting blocked at checkout.
Our IP velocity rule is too tight. Key it on device plus distinct cards instead.

nodes.name: Risk scoring
nodes.description: Assigning a payment a score estimating its fraud risk, used to approve it, add authentication, review or block it.
nodes.markdown:
Risk scoring assigns a transaction, account or event a value that estimates how likely it is to be fraudulent. A system then uses the score to choose an action. Scores may come from rules, machine-learning models or both, and several parties can compute them independently.

| Party                                 | What it scores from                                 |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| [Merchant](node:Merchant)             | Account history, device, basket, delivery details   |
| [Payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) | Patterns across its merchants |
| [Card network](node:Card%20network)   | Activity across its members          |
| [Issuer](node:Issuer)                 | [Cardholder](node:Cardholder)'s spending and account behaviour         |

The score is an input to a decision, and the action is set by thresholds.

| Score band | Typical action                                       |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Low        | Approve, possibly request an [SCA exemption](node:SCA%20exemption) |
| Medium     | Add [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure)                  |
| High       | Send to manual review                                |
