| Very high  | Block                                                |

Scales are vendor-specific, so a score of 80 from one provider is not comparable with 80 from another.

The cost of false positives is easy to miss. A blocked legitimate customer rarely complains and may leave, so a dashboard can show falling fraud while revenue drops. Measure false declines by sampling blocked orders or holding back a small control group, where that is lawful and acceptable.

Training data has a built-in delay. Fraud labels often arrive weeks later through [chargebacks](node:Chargeback), and [friendly fraud](node:Friendly%20fraud) can label genuine customers as criminals. Blocked orders also have no outcome, so a model learns only from what it allowed. Monitor for drift, and keep the score, model version and input features for each decision so it can be explained later.

Regulation can make risk analysis mandatory for some uses. Under EU Delegated Regulation 2018/389, a provider using the transaction risk analysis exemption must perform real-time analysis covering factors such as abnormal spending, unusual device information, known fraud scenarios and abnormal payer location.
quotes: Fraud is down since we tightened the model, but so are sales.
The threshold's too aggressive. Send the middle band to 3DS rather than blocking it.

nodes.name: Chargeback
nodes.description: A forced reversal of a card payment, started by the issuer through the card network after a cardholder dispute.
nodes.markdown:
A chargeback is a forced reversal of a card payment, initiated by the [issuer](node:Issuer) through the [card network](node:Card%20network), usually after a [cardholder](node:Cardholder) disputes a charge. The money is taken back from the [acquirer](node:Acquirer), which recovers it from the [merchant](node:Merchant). Visa's rules call this a Dispute, defined as a transaction an issuer returns to an acquirer, and Mastercard's call it a chargeback.

A chargeback differs from a [refund](node:Refund). A merchant chooses to issue a refund. A chargeback happens regardless of what the merchant wants, generally adds a fee, and counts toward the merchant's [chargeback ratio](node:Chargeback%20ratio).

| Stage                  | Visa term       | Mastercard term        | Who acts                 |
| ---------------------- | --------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Claim                  | Dispute         | First chargeback       | Issuer                   |
| Merchant's challenge   | Dispute Response, or [pre-Arbitration](node:Pre-arbitration) | Second presentment | Acquirer, for merchant |
| Further challenge      | Pre-Arbitration, or its response | Pre-arbitration (optional) | Depends on the flow |
| Final decision         | Arbitration     | Arbitration            | The network decides      |

Visa's flow depends on the category. For fraud and authorization disputes, the acquirer's first challenge is a pre-Arbitration. For processing errors and consumer disputes, it is a Dispute Response. The general term for the merchant's challenge is [representment](node:Representment).

Each case has a [dispute reason code](node:Dispute%20reason%20code) that determines what evidence can win it. Time limits are strict and differ by network, reason and region, so use the dates your provider gives you and do not hard-code them.

Merchants usually discover a chargeback when a [payout](node:Payout) arrives short, with the disputed amount and a fee deducted. The merchant can lose both the product and the money even when the sale was genuine, as with [friendly fraud](node:Friendly%20fraud).

Do not issue a refund after a chargeback has already been raised, because the customer may be paid twice. Handle disputes as a separate state in your [ledger](node:Ledger), because funds can leave and return weeks apart.
quotes: This payout is 240 short and I can't see why.
There's a chargeback on an order from May. The issuer pulled the funds, so check the response deadline.

nodes.name: Retrieval request
nodes.description: An issuer's request for a copy of a card transaction's details, used before or instead of raising a chargeback.
nodes.markdown:
A retrieval request is a request from an [issuer](node:Issuer), sent through the [acquirer](node:Acquirer), for a copy of the records behind a card transaction. It is usually triggered when a [cardholder](node:Cardholder) does not recognise a charge and the issuer wants more information. The request does not take money back from the [merchant](node:Merchant).

| Step | Who      | What happens                                                |
| ---- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Cardholder | Queries a charge with the issuer                          |
| 2    | Issuer   | Requests transaction information                            |
| 3    | Acquirer or provider | Passes the request to the merchant              |
| 4    | Merchant | Supplies a receipt, order details or other records          |
| 5    | Issuer   | Resolves the query, or may proceed to a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) |

A retrieval request leaves funds in place, while a chargeback pulls them from the merchant.

Availability differs by network, and this is where older guides are often wrong. Visa announced in August 2020 that it would sunset its retrieval request process after 16 October 2020, when signature capture became optional. Mastercard's Mastercom dispute system continues to document retrieval request and fulfilment functions for its members. Because many merchants reach these systems through a [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider), whether you ever see one depends on the provider and network.

Where the process exists, a merchant may see a dashboard notice with a short response time. Ignoring it can remove the chance to resolve an innocent misunderstanding, and the issuer may go on to raise a dispute. Answer with clear records: the order date, amount, customer details, delivery confirmation and the exact [statement descriptor](node:Statement%20descriptor).

Do not include a full [PAN](node:PAN) or [CVV](node:CVV) in the documents you upload. Mask card numbers and follow [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) when storing or transmitting receipts.

Repeated requests from customers who do not recognise a charge usually point to a descriptor problem.
quotes: The provider sent a retrieval request on a Mastercard sale. Is that a chargeback?
Not yet. No money has moved. Send the receipt and delivery proof so it doesn't become one.

nodes.name: Representment
nodes.description: The merchant's challenge to a chargeback, submitted through the acquirer with evidence that the charge was valid.
nodes.markdown:
Representment is the process of contesting a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) by resubmitting the transaction with evidence that the charge was valid. The [merchant](node:Merchant) prepares the case, and the [acquirer](node:Acquirer) presents it to the [issuer](node:Issuer) through the [card network](node:Card%20network). The word is industry shorthand, and each network uses its own terms.

| Network    | Dispute type                              | Merchant's first challenge is called |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Visa       | Fraud and authorization (categories 10, 11) | [Pre-Arbitration](node:Pre-arbitration) |
| Visa       | Processing errors and consumer (12, 13)   | Dispute Response                     |
| Mastercard | Chargebacks generally                     | Second presentment                   |

The evidence must answer the specific [dispute reason code](node:Dispute%20reason%20code). A merchant facing a fraud claim submits a delivery receipt, but delivery alone does not show who placed the order. A merchant facing "not as described" sends proof of payment, which does not address the quality complaint.

| Claim                          | Useful evidence                                                |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Fraud, card-not-present        | [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) result, Visa Compelling Evidence if eligible |
| Goods not received             | Carrier tracking to the [cardholder](node:Cardholder)'s address                   |
| Not as described               | Product description, correspondence, return policy             |
| Credit not processed           | [Refund](node:Refund) details and [acquirer reference number](node:Acquirer%20reference%20number) |
| Cancelled recurring            | Terms shown, consent, cancellation records                     |
| Authorization-related          | Valid approval and timely [capture](node:Capture)              |

Some disputes cannot be won with evidence of delivery. Visa's merchant guidance says that for authorization disputes, proof that the customer received the goods generally does not override a missing, expired or incorrectly used authorization.

Representment takes staff time and can add fees if it escalates, so accept disputes the merchant would lose. Winning returns the funds, though the original dispute may still count toward the [chargeback ratio](node:Chargeback%20ratio) depending on the network's method.

Deadlines are strict and set by network rules. A late response usually loses automatically, so route dispute notifications to a monitored queue, and rely on the due date your provider supplies.
quotes: We sent the tracking number, and we still lost the fraud dispute.
Tracking shows delivery, not who bought it. For representment we needed the 3DS result or device history.

nodes.name: Pre-arbitration
nodes.description: The dispute stage after a challenged chargeback, giving both sides a last chance to settle before network arbitration.
nodes.markdown:
Pre-arbitration is the stage of a card dispute that follows an initial challenge, giving the [issuer](node:Issuer) and [acquirer](node:Acquirer) a final chance to resolve the case before the [card network](node:Card%20network) is asked to decide it. Who acts at this stage depends on the network and the type of dispute.

Visa's rules use two flows.

| Stage                    | Fraud and authorization (categories 10, 11) | Processing and consumer (12, 13) |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| [Chargeback](node:Chargeback) | Issuer raises a Dispute                | Issuer raises a Dispute          |
| Dispute Response         | Not a stage in this flow                    | Acquirer responds                |
| Pre-Arbitration          | Acquirer challenges                         | Issuer challenges                |
| Pre-Arbitration Response | Issuer accepts or rejects                   | Acquirer accepts or rejects      |
| Arbitration              | Acquirer may file                           | Issuer may file                  |

So in a Visa fraud dispute, pre-arbitration is the [merchant's](node:Merchant) first challenge. In a consumer dispute, it is the issuer's reply to the merchant's evidence.

Mastercard works differently. After a chargeback and second presentment, the issuer may file an optional pre-arbitration case, and its Chargeback Guide says Mastercard strongly recommends skipping that step and going directly to an arbitration case.

In pre-arbitration, the two sides can still settle. In arbitration, the network reviews the case and issues a decision, and the losing side generally bears additional fees. Those fees can exceed the value of a small transaction.

For a merchant, this stage usually appears as a notice from the provider that a dispute it thought was finished has come back. Check whether new evidence addresses the objection, compare the transaction amount with the possible fees, and accept liability if the case is weak.

Time limits at this stage are short and differ by flow, so take them from your [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider). Model each stage as a separate state, because a [representment](node:Representment) win can be reopened.
quotes: We won that dispute last month. Why is it back?
The issuer went to pre-arbitration. It's a 30-euro order, so accept it unless we have new evidence.

nodes.name: Dispute reason code
nodes.description: A network code stating why a card payment was disputed, which determines the evidence needed to respond.
nodes.markdown:
A dispute reason code is the value a [card network](node:Card%20network) attaches to a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) to state why the payment is being disputed. It tells the [merchant](node:Merchant) which rules apply and what evidence can answer the claim. Code sets are network-specific, so the same complaint can carry different labels.

Visa organises its codes as dispute conditions within four categories. Mastercard uses message reason codes.

| Type of claim   | Visa                                                  | Mastercard example                     |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Fraud           | Category 10, such as 10.4 Other Fraud, Card-Absent    | 4837 No Cardholder Authorization       |
| Chip liability  | 10.1 and 10.2, [EMV](node:EMV) [liability shift](node:Liability%20shift)                 | 4870 Chip Liability Shift              |
| Authorization   | Category 11, such as 11.3 No Authorization/Late Presentment | 4808 Authorization-related       |
| Processing error | Category 12, such as 12.6 Duplicate Processing       | 4834 Point-of-Interaction Error        |
| Consumer        | Category 13, such as 13.1 Not Received                | 4853 Cardholder Dispute                |

Examples are from Visa's October 2026 rules and Mastercard's May 2025 guide, and can change.

A reason code is different from a [decline code](node:Decline%20code). A decline code explains why an authorization was refused at the time of payment. A reason code explains why a completed payment is being challenged afterward.

The code decides the strategy for [representment](node:Representment). A 13.1 "not received" claim can often be answered with carrier tracking. The same tracking does little against a 10.4 fraud claim, where the question is who made the purchase.

A customer who forgot a subscription may still be recorded under a fraud code, a common sign of [friendly fraud](node:Friendly%20fraud).

[Payment service providers](node:Payment%20service%20provider) often map raw codes to simplified categories such as "fraudulent" or "product not received". Store the raw code and network too. Reporting by code also shows where to fix the source: rising 13.1 points to fulfilment, and rising 12.6 points to a [double charge](node:Double%20charge) bug.
quotes: Should I send the delivery proof for this dispute?
Check the reason code first. It's a 10.4, so we need evidence of who bought it, not just where it went.

nodes.name: Chargeback ratio
nodes.description: A merchant's disputes relative to its transactions, calculated differently by each card network for risk monitoring.
nodes.markdown:
A chargeback ratio measures a [merchant's](node:Merchant) disputes relative to its transactions. [Card networks](node:Card%20network) and [acquirers](node:Acquirer) use it to identify businesses with unusually high fraud or customer problems. There is no universal formula, so a dashboard percentage may not match a network's figure.

| Network    | Program                              | Measure                                                              |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Visa       | Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program (VAMP) | Count of fraud reports plus disputes, divided by settled transactions, card-not-present only |
| Mastercard | Excessive Chargeback Program         | Chargebacks in a calendar month, divided by Mastercard transactions in the preceding month |

The differences change the result. Visa's VAMP ratio includes reported fraud, so a transaction can count even when no chargeback follows. It can also exclude some disputes resolved through pre-dispute tools and fraud that qualifies for Compelling Evidence 3.0. Mastercard divides by the previous month's transactions, so a seasonal drop in sales can raise the ratio even if the number of chargebacks stays flat.

Both programs apply thresholds and minimum counts, which differ by region and have changed recently. Visa's published fact sheet, for example, records a lower merchant threshold for several regions from April 2026. Take current figures from the network or your acquirer.

Exceeding a program's level can lead to remediation plans, fees passed on by the acquirer, a [rolling reserve](node:Rolling%20reserve), or closure of the [merchant account](node:Merchant%20account). Because disputes arrive weeks after a sale, the ratio lags the cause.

To manage it, compute each network's metric separately, by merchant ID, and alert on the trend rather than waiting for a notice. Address the sources: unclear [statement descriptors](node:Statement%20descriptor), hard-to-cancel subscriptions, slow delivery, and fraud controls such as [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure). A prompt [refund](node:Refund) before a dispute avoids a chargeback entirely.

Splitting payments or moving volume between merchant accounts to dilute the ratio can breach network rules.
quotes: Our dashboard says disputes are under one percent, so we're fine, right?
That's blended. Visa counts fraud reports too, so check the VAMP ratio by merchant ID.

nodes.name: Interchange fee
nodes.description: A fee the acquirer pays the issuer on most card payments, set by network schedules and capped by regulators in some regions.
nodes.markdown:
An interchange fee is a fee the [acquirer](node:Acquirer), the [merchant](node:Merchant)'s bank, pays to the [issuer](node:Issuer), the [cardholder](node:Cardholder)'s bank, on most card purchases in a [four-party model](node:Four-party%20model). The [card network](node:Card%20network) publishes the rates. They vary by card type, region, merchant category, sales channel and the data sent with the transaction. The merchant does not pay the issuer directly. The acquirer recovers the cost through the merchant's pricing.

Interchange is often confused with the total cost of accepting a card. It is one component. A [scheme fee](node:Scheme%20fee) goes to the network, the acquirer adds its own margin, and the [merchant discount rate](node:Merchant%20discount%20rate) expresses the combined charge.

Regulators cap interchange in some markets, and the rules differ:

| Region    | Rule                                                               | Current point to check                                                     |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| EU        | Regulation (EU) 2015/751 caps most consumer debit and credit cards | Commercial cards and three-party schemes generally fall outside the caps   |
| UK        | Onshored version of the EU caps                                    | The Payment Systems Regulator is working on a UK-EEA cross-border cap      |
| US        | Regulation II caps debit interchange for large issuers             | An October 2026 Eighth Circuit ruling upheld vacating the cap, effective only once the court's mandate issues |
| Australia | Reserve Bank of Australia standards                                | Lower domestic caps began on 1 October 2026                                |

A merchant usually notices interchange when monthly card costs rise while prices and sales stay flat. A larger share of premium, commercial or foreign cards can cause this. Missing transaction data can also push a payment into a more expensive category, which acquirers call a downgrade. Whether interchange comes back on a [refund](node:Refund) depends on the network and the acquirer contract, so check it instead of assuming.
quotes: Card costs went up this month, but revenue is flat.
More volume came from commercial and foreign cards, and interchange is higher on both. Pull the fee report by card type.

nodes.name: Scheme fee
nodes.description: A fee the card network charges acquirers and issuers for using its network, separate from interchange.
nodes.markdown:
A scheme fee is a charge that a [card network](node:Card%20network) such as Visa or Mastercard applies for use of its network. [Acquirers](node:Acquirer) and [issuers](node:Issuer) both pay scheme fees, and in the US they are often called assessments or network fees. An acquirer normally passes its share on to the [merchant](node:Merchant), either as itemised lines or inside a single rate.

Scheme fees differ from an [interchange fee](node:Interchange%20fee) in who receives the money. Interchange moves from the acquirer to the issuer. A scheme fee goes to the network. Interchange is capped in some jurisdictions, while scheme fees are set by each network and are generally not covered by those same caps.

A single payment can trigger several scheme fees:

| Fee type            | Triggered by                                                  |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Volume assessment   | The value of transactions processed                           |
| Authorization fee   | Each authorization request, including declined ones in some programmes |
| [Clearing](node:Clearing) fee        | Each transaction submitted for clearing                       |
| [Cross-border fee](node:Cross-border%20fee)    | The issuer and merchant being in different countries or regions |
| Compliance or misuse fee | Breaching a network rule, which can include repeated reattempts |

The names, amounts and triggers change, and each network publishes updates to its acquirers rather than a single public price list. For that reason, a merchant's statement can gain an unfamiliar line with no change to its contract.

The usual symptom is a set of small, oddly named charges that finance cannot explain. A retry loop can make this worse, because each repeated [authorization](node:Card%20authorization) attempt may incur a fee even when the issuer declines it. To investigate, ask the acquirer for a per-transaction fee report, group charges by fee code, and compare the count of authorization attempts with the count of successful orders. A large gap often points to retries or [card testing](node:Card%20testing).
quotes: What is this new network access line on the acquirer statement?
It's a scheme fee charged per authorization. Our retry job doubled the attempts last month, so the line doubled too.

nodes.name: Merchant discount rate
nodes.description: The total percentage an acquirer or provider deducts from a card sale, covering interchange, scheme fees and margin.
nodes.markdown:
The [merchant](node:Merchant) discount rate, or MDR, is the total percentage an [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) deducts from a merchant's card sales. It normally covers the [interchange fee](node:Interchange%20fee), the [scheme fee](node:Scheme%20fee) and the acquirer's margin. Some contracts add a fixed amount per transaction, so the quoted percentage may not be the full cost.

The MDR is often mistaken for interchange. Interchange is one input, paid to the [issuer](node:Issuer). The MDR is what the merchant sees deducted. Under [blended pricing](node:Blended%20pricing) the MDR is one published rate. Under [interchange-plus pricing](node:Interchange-plus%20pricing) there is no single rate in advance, but an effective MDR can be calculated after the fact.

This worked example uses invented figures to show how a sale of 100.00 divides:

| Component          | Receiver | Amount |
| ------------------ | -------- | -----: |
| Interchange        | Issuer   |   1.20 |
| Scheme fee         | Network  |   0.15 |
| Acquirer margin    | Acquirer |   0.65 |
| **Total deducted** |          |   2.00 |
| **Net to merchant** |         |  98.00 |

The effective rate is total fees divided by processed volume. Calculate it over a full statement, including fixed fees, monthly charges and [chargeback](node:Chargeback) fees. A fixed per-transaction fee matters more on small orders: the same fixed amount is a much larger share of a 3.00 sale than of a 300.00 sale.

The failure finance teams see is a [payout](node:Payout) lower than recorded sales, with the difference booked as an unexplained variance. Record gross, fees and net separately for each transaction so that [payment reconciliation](node:Payment%20reconciliation) can explain the gap. When comparing provider quotes, compare effective rates on your own card mix, because a lower headline rate can cost more if other fees apply.
quotes: The provider quoted us 1.9%, but we're paying nearer 2.6%.
That quote left out the per-transaction fee. On our small baskets, the effective merchant discount rate is much higher.

nodes.name: Interchange-plus pricing
nodes.description: A pricing model passing actual interchange and often scheme fees to the merchant, plus a disclosed acquirer markup.
nodes.markdown:
Interchange-plus pricing is a card pricing model in which the [acquirer](node:Acquirer) charges the [merchant](node:Merchant) the actual [interchange fee](node:Interchange%20fee) for each transaction plus a fixed, disclosed markup. A common variant, interchange-plus-plus or IC++, itemises the [scheme fee](node:Scheme%20fee) as well. Providers use these labels inconsistently, so check the contract to see whether scheme fees are passed through or included in the markup.

The alternative is [blended pricing](node:Blended%20pricing), where the merchant pays one rate and the provider absorbs the variation. With interchange-plus, the merchant carries that variation and can see what each card cost.

This example uses invented figures for two sales of 100.00 with a markup of 0.30:

| Line             | Domestic debit | Foreign commercial credit |
| ---------------- | -------------: | ------------------------: |
| Interchange      |           0.20 |                      1.80 |
| Scheme fees      |           0.05 |                      0.40 |
| Acquirer markup  |           0.30 |                      0.30 |
| **Total cost**   |       **0.55** |                  **2.50** |
| **Net received** |      **99.45** |                 **97.50** |

The markup is the same in both columns, and the total differs because of the underlying card. This transparency makes it easier to compare acquirers, since the markup is the part they control.

The drawback is unpredictability. A merchant's monthly cost can rise with no change in contract because customers used more premium or foreign cards. Statements are also longer, and fees may be reported a day or more after the sale, or billed monthly rather than netted from each [payout](node:Payout). Engineering teams feel this during [payment reconciliation](node:Payment%20reconciliation), because the final fee is unknown when the order is recorded. Store an estimated fee if needed, then post an adjusting [ledger](node:Ledger) entry when the actual fee arrives, keeping both visible.
quotes: Why did our fees move when the acquirer's rate didn't change?
We're on interchange-plus pricing. Our markup stayed fixed, but more customers paid with foreign commercial cards.

nodes.name: Blended pricing
nodes.description: A card pricing model charging one rate across card types, with the provider absorbing variation in underlying costs.
nodes.markdown:
Blended pricing is a card pricing model in which a [merchant](node:Merchant) pays one published rate, or a small set of rates, regardless of the underlying card. A provider might quote one percentage plus a fixed fee for every online card payment. The provider pays the actual [interchange fee](node:Interchange%20fee) and [scheme fee](node:Scheme%20fee) from that amount and keeps the difference.

The provider's margin therefore changes from one transaction to the next. It earns more on a low-cost domestic debit card and less, or even loses money, on an expensive foreign commercial card. Providers set the rate using an expected card mix, and may reprice or add surcharges for categories such as international cards.

| Model              | Merchant pays                     | Predictability | Cost visibility |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------- | -------------- | --------------- |
| Blended            | One rate                          | High           | Low             |
| Tiered             | A rate per provider-defined bucket | Medium        | Low             |
| [Interchange-plus pricing](node:Interchange-plus%20pricing) | Actual cost plus a markup   | Lower          | High            |

Tiered pricing, sometimes described as qualified, mid-qualified and non-qualified rates, is a related model. The provider decides which transactions fall into each tier, so the rate paid can be hard to predict or audit.

Blended pricing suits merchants that value a simple bill and have modest volume. The usual problem appears as a business grows. A merchant whose customers mostly use domestic debit cards may pay well above the underlying cost, and nothing on the statement reveals it because the components are hidden. To check, ask for a sample of transaction-level costs or request an interchange-plus quote, then compare both against the last few months of your real card mix. Include fixed fees, since they can outweigh a small percentage difference on low-value orders.
quotes: Our provider charges one flat rate. Is that good for us?
It's blended pricing, and most of our volume is domestic debit. We're probably overpaying, so let's get an interchange-plus quote.

nodes.name: Surcharging
nodes.description: Adding a fee at checkout for paying with a particular method, which is allowed, limited or banned depending on place and network.
nodes.markdown:
Surcharging is when a [merchant](node:Merchant) adds a fee to the price because the customer chose a particular payment method, usually a credit card. Whether a merchant may do it depends on the jurisdiction, the [card network](node:Card%20network)'s rules, the card type and sometimes the sector. There is no universal rule.

| Jurisdiction | Position at the time of writing                                                                                     |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| EU           | [PSD2](node:PSD2) bars surcharges on consumer cards under the interchange caps and on SEPA transfers and debits. Other instruments vary by member state |
| UK           | The Consumer Rights (Payment Surcharges) Regulations 2012 ban surcharges on consumer cards and some other methods. Commercial cards may be surcharged up to cost |
| US           | State laws and network rules apply, and network rules generally exclude debit and [prepaid cards](node:Prepaid%20card)                     |
| Australia    | From 1 October 2026, Reserve Bank of Australia changes ended surcharging on designated eftpos, Mastercard and Visa cards |

Surcharging is often confused with two nearby practices. A convenience fee is charged for using a particular channel and has its own network rules. A cash discount lowers the price for non-card payment instead of raising it for card payment. Relabelling a surcharge does not necessarily change how it is classified.

A merchant may apply a blanket checkout fee and then receive a network compliance notice, a regulator complaint or a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) for the added amount. An engineering team detects card type from the [BIN](node:BIN) and applies a credit surcharge to a debit card, because the lookup data was stale.

Before launching, confirm the current rules for every country and network you sell in, and ask your [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or a lawyer. Keep the fee as its own line item, so it can be refunded and reported correctly.
quotes: Can we add a 2% card fee to all checkouts?
Not across all markets. The EU and UK ban it on consumer cards, and US rules vary by state and network. Ask legal first.

nodes.name: Rolling reserve
nodes.description: A share of each payout that a provider holds for a set period to cover future refunds and chargebacks.
nodes.markdown:
A rolling reserve is an arrangement in which a [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) withholds a percentage of each [settlement](node:Settlement) and releases it after a fixed period. It protects the provider against losses that arrive after a sale, mainly a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) or [refund](node:Refund) the [merchant](node:Merchant) can no longer fund. If the merchant fails, the [acquirer](node:Acquirer) can still be liable to the [card network](node:Card%20network), so it holds this money as cover.

The contract sets the percentage and the holding period. Providers commonly apply a reserve to higher-risk categories, new businesses, merchants with long delivery times, or accounts with rising disputes. Other forms exist: a fixed reserve holds one lump sum, and delayed [payout](node:Payout) lengthens the time before any funds are paid.

This example uses invented figures and a 10% reserve, with amounts in [minor units](node:Minor%20unit):

| Event                   | Available | Reserve | Total |
| ----------------------- | --------: | ------: | ----: |
| Sale of 100000 settles  |     90000 |   10000 | 100000 |
| Chargeback of 5000      |     85000 |   10000 |  95000 |
| Reserve period ends     |     95000 |       0 |  95000 |

A reserve is not a fee. The money still belongs to the merchant, subject to the contract, and is normally recorded as a receivable. Booking the withheld amount as an expense overstates costs and hides money the business expects to receive.

Merchants usually discover a reserve when a payout is lower than expected, or when cash runs short during fast growth because a growing portion of revenue is held at any one time. Model a separate reserve balance in the [ledger](node:Ledger), using the release date from the settlement data, and forecast cash on that basis. To negotiate a lower reserve, show the provider a clean dispute history and shorter delivery times.
quotes: Payouts are 10% lower than sales since we moved to the new provider.
They put us on a rolling reserve. It's released after the holding period, so book it as a receivable, not a fee.

nodes.name: Cross-border fee
nodes.description: A charge applied when a card's issuing country differs from the merchant's or acquirer's country, even in one currency.
nodes.markdown:
A cross-border fee is a charge applied when a card payment crosses a country or region boundary, usually because the [issuer](node:Issuer) and the [merchant](node:Merchant)'s [acquirer](node:Acquirer) are in different places. The [card network](node:Card%20network) defines what counts as cross-border, and those definitions can treat a region such as the European Economic Area differently from a single country.

The term covers several charges that people often merge:

| Charge                    | Who pays                 | Who sets it          | Trigger                                 |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------ | -------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Network cross-border fee  | Acquirer and issuer      | Card network         | Issuer and acquirer in different regions |
| Cross-border interchange  | Acquirer, paid to issuer | Network or regulator | Inter-regional transaction              |
| Foreign transaction fee   | [Cardholder](node:Cardholder)               | Issuer               | Foreign purchase, under the card terms  |
| Currency conversion margin | Payer or merchant       | Whoever converts     | Currencies differ                       |

A cross-border fee does not require a currency conversion. A US cardholder paying a merchant in US dollars can still be charged a foreign transaction fee if the merchant's acquirer is abroad. The customer then complains about a fee on a payment that appeared to be domestic, and the merchant's support team cannot see the charge because the issuer applied it.

Merchants see the cost as a higher fee on foreign cards. Interchange can rise sharply when a payment becomes inter-regional. Payments between the UK and EEA are a current example: the UK's Payment Systems Regulator has been working on a cap for fees on EEA-issued cards used online at UK businesses.

Businesses with significant foreign volume can reduce the cost by acquiring locally, using a domestic acquirer in each main market. That requires a local legal entity or an eligible provider setup in many countries, so check the requirements. [Payment routing](node:Payment%20routing) can then send each card to the local acquirer.
quotes: A US customer was charged a foreign fee, but we billed in dollars.
Our acquirer is in Ireland, so the issuer treated it as cross-border. Currency wasn't the trigger.

nodes.name: Dynamic currency conversion
nodes.description: An option at checkout or an ATM to pay in the card's home currency, using a rate set by the merchant's provider.
nodes.markdown:
Dynamic currency conversion, or DCC, is a service that offers a [cardholder](node:Cardholder) the choice to pay in their card's home currency at a terminal, ATM or online checkout. The [merchant](node:Merchant)'s provider performs the conversion and sets the rate, usually including a markup. If the customer declines, the payment proceeds in the local currency and the [card network](node:Card%20network) or [issuer](node:Issuer) handles the conversion.

The choice is commonly shown as a prompt such as "Pay 54.20 USD or 50.00 EUR". Choosing the home currency gives certainty about the amount, but the rate can be less favourable than the one the card would otherwise receive.

| Option                 | Who converts          | Who sets the price shown        |
| ---------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Pay in local currency  | Network or issuer     | Merchant, in local currency     |
| DCC                    | Merchant's provider   | Provider, at the point of sale  |
| [Multi-currency pricing](node:Multi-currency%20pricing) | Usually the [acquirer](node:Acquirer)  | Merchant, in the buyer's currency |

DCC is often confused with multi-currency pricing. With multi-currency pricing the merchant sets a price in the buyer's currency in advance. With DCC the item is priced in local currency and converted at the moment of payment.

Card network rules require the cardholder to make an active choice. In the EU, Regulation (EU) 2021/1230 requires parties offering conversion at an ATM or point of sale to disclose the charges before payment as a percentage markup over the latest European Central Bank reference rate.

The typical failure is a traveller who sees a higher amount than expected on their statement and says they never agreed to the conversion. A terminal that preselects home currency, or staff who choose for the customer, can lead to complaints and [chargebacks](node:Chargeback). Keep evidence of the customer's choice, the rate and the markup on the receipt.
quotes: A customer disputes the amount, saying we charged them in pounds without asking.
The terminal had dynamic currency conversion on by default. Turn off preselection and check the receipt shows the markup.

nodes.name: Multi-currency pricing
nodes.description: Showing and charging customers in their own currency at merchant-set prices, while settling in another or the same currency.
nodes.markdown:
Multi-currency pricing is a setup in which a [merchant](node:Merchant) displays and charges prices in the buyer's currency, then receives [settlement](node:Settlement) in that currency or a different one. The currency shown to the customer is the presentment currency. The currency paid out to the merchant is the settlement currency. When they differ, the [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) usually performs the conversion and charges a margin.

The merchant controls the customer-facing price, using a price list per currency or a base price with a chosen rate and rounding rule. This differs from [dynamic currency conversion](node:Dynamic%20currency%20conversion), where the item is priced in local currency and converted at the moment of payment, with the provider setting the rate.

A multi-currency payment needs more fields than a single amount:

| Field               | Example | Why it is stored                     |
| ------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Presentment amount  | 5000 JPY | What the customer agreed to pay     |
| Settlement amount   | 3120 USD [minor units](node:Minor%20unit) | What the merchant received |
| Exchange rate       | As reported by the provider | Audit and reconciliation |
| Conversion fee      | 62 USD minor units | Margin cost              |

Each amount is stored in the minor unit of its own currency. In this example, 5000 JPY means 5,000 yen because the yen has no decimal places, while 3120 USD means 31.20 dollars.

The common failure happens on a [refund](node:Refund). A customer paid 100.00 EUR, the merchant settled in USD, and the rate moved before the refund. The customer gets 100.00 EUR back, but the USD debited from the merchant differs from what it originally received. Finance sees a small unexplained gain or loss. Record the rate for each leg and post the difference to a foreign exchange gain or loss account in the [ledger](node:Ledger).
quotes: Our refund cost more in dollars than the original sale brought in.
That's the exchange rate moving under multi-currency pricing. Record it as an FX loss rather than adjusting the original payment.

nodes.name: Minor unit
nodes.description: The smallest unit of a currency under ISO 4217, such as cents for USD, used to store money as an integer.
nodes.markdown:
A minor unit is the smallest denomination of a currency, as defined by the ISO 4217 currency standard. One US dollar is 100 cents, so USD has an exponent of 2. Payment systems commonly store and transmit money as an integer count of minor units, because binary floating-point numbers cannot represent many decimal values exactly and accumulate rounding errors.

```json
{ "amount": 1050, "currency": "USD" }
```

That value means 10.50 dollars. The same integer means something else in another currency, so an amount must always be stored with its currency code.

| Currency | ISO 4217 exponent | 1050 means  |
| -------- | ----------------: | ----------- |
| USD      |                 2 | 10.50       |
| EUR      |                 2 | 10.50       |
| JPY      |                 0 | 1,050       |
| KRW      |                 0 | 1,050       |
| KWD      |                 3 | 1.050       |
| BHD      |                 3 | 1.050       |
| CLF      |                 4 | 0.1050      |

A common bug is multiplying every price by 100. A 1,000 yen order is sent as 100000 and the customer is charged 100,000 yen. Dividing by 100 for display makes the reverse error, and a Kuwaiti dinar amount is off by a factor of ten.

Read the exponent from a maintained ISO 4217 table instead of hardcoding it. SIX, the standard's maintenance agency, publishes the current list, and exponents can change when a currency is reformed. Providers sometimes diverge from ISO for particular currencies, such as requiring a two-decimal format for a zero-decimal currency or restricting fractional amounts, so check each provider's documentation and convert at that boundary.

Some message formats use decimal strings instead. [ISO 20022](node:ISO%2020022), for example, carries amounts such as `10.50` with a currency attribute. Convert these to integers at the system edge using exact decimal parsing, and define a rounding rule for tax, fee and foreign exchange calculations.
quotes: A Japanese customer was charged 100 times the price.
We multiplied by 100 for every currency. JPY has no minor unit, so read the exponent from the ISO 4217 table.

nodes.name: ACH
nodes.description: The US batch bank-to-bank network for credits and debits, governed by Nacha rules and operated by FedACH and EPN.
nodes.markdown:
ACH, the Automated Clearing House network, is the US system for moving batched electronic credits and debits between bank accounts. Nacha writes the operating rules. Two operators process the entries: the Federal Reserve's FedACH and The Clearing House's Electronic Payments Network. Payroll and bill payments commonly use it.

| Step | Who                              | What happens                                      |
| ---- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Originator (business)            | Gets authorization and creates an entry           |
| 2    | ODFI (originating bank)          | Submits batched entries to an operator            |
| 3    | ACH operator                     | Sorts entries and delivers them to receiving banks |
| 4    | RDFI (receiving bank)            | Posts the credit or debit to the receiver's account |
| 5    | RDFI                             | Sends a return if the entry cannot be honoured    |

An ACH credit pushes money to a receiver. An ACH debit pulls money from a payer under an authorization, which is why debits carry more risk for the business collecting them. Same Day ACH offers faster processing within windows and per-payment limits set by Nacha, but it remains batched. It is not the same as an instant rail such as [FedNow](node:FedNow) or the [RTP network](node:RTP%20network).

ACH is often confused with a wire. A [Fedwire](node:Fedwire) payment settles individually and is final. An ACH debit can settle and still come back later as a [payment return](node:Payment%20return), for reasons such as insufficient funds or a claim that it was unauthorised.

The failure this causes is familiar to anyone shipping goods on ACH. The dashboard shows "paid", the order ships, and days later a return such as `R01` reverses the money. Treat a debit as provisional until your risk window has passed, and record the return as a new [ledger](node:Ledger) entry. Nacha also added fraud-monitoring duties that took effect in phases during 2026, so confirm current obligations with your bank.
quotes: The customer's payment cleared Monday, so why did we lose the money today?
It was an ACH debit and came back `R01`. Settled doesn't mean final, so hold high-value orders longer.

nodes.name: SEPA Credit Transfer
nodes.description: The euro bank transfer scheme across SEPA countries, where the payer's bank pushes funds under European Payments Council rules.
nodes.markdown:
A SEPA Credit Transfer, or SCT, is a euro payment that a payer instructs their bank to push to a payee's account within the Single Euro Payments Area. The European Payments Council publishes the rulebook for participating [payment service providers](node:Payment%20service%20provider) (PSPs). SEPA is wider than the EU and includes non-EU countries such as Norway, Switzerland and the United Kingdom.

| Step | Who         | What happens                                         |
| ---- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Payer       | Enters the payee's [IBAN](node:IBAN), name, amount and reference  |
| 2    | Payer's PSP | Validates and debits the account                     |
| 3    | Clearing system | Exchanges the [ISO 20022](node:ISO%2020022) message and settles between PSPs |
| 4    | Payee's PSP | Credits the payee                                    |

EU payment services law generally requires a euro transfer to reach the payee's provider by the end of the next business day. A standard SCT is therefore not instant. [SEPA Instant](node:SEPA%20Instant) is a separate scheme that runs continuously, while [SEPA Direct Debit](node:SEPA%20Direct%20Debit) is a pull payment started by the creditor.

Since 9 October 2025, the Instant Payments Regulation has required euro-area banks to offer verification of payee on euro credit transfers. The check compares the payee name with the IBAN before the payer confirms. Providers in non-euro EU member states have a later date of 9 July 2027, and payment and e-money institutions follow their own timetable.

Two failures are common for businesses collecting by transfer. A customer omits or mistypes the reference, so the money arrives but nothing links it to an invoice, and it waits in a suspense account. Or a payer sends funds to the wrong IBAN and asks for them back. The payer's bank can send a recall, which the receiving side may refuse. Issue a unique reference per invoice and match on it automatically.
quotes: The customer sent proof of transfer, but the invoice is still unpaid.
The SEPA Credit Transfer arrived without a reference. Match it from the suspense account and make the reference field clearer on the invoice.

nodes.name: SEPA Instant
nodes.description: The European Payments Council's euro instant credit transfer scheme, running around the clock under the Instant Payments Regulation.
nodes.markdown:
SEPA Instant, formally the SEPA Instant Credit Transfer or SCT Inst, is a euro credit transfer scheme that runs 24 hours a day on every day of the year. The European Payments Council publishes the rulebook. Regulation (EU) 2024/886, the Instant Payments Regulation, requires funds to reach the payee within 10 seconds of the order being received, and it requires EU providers that offer euro credit transfers to support instant ones.

The regulation phases in by location and firm type, according to the European Central Bank's published timetable:

| Obligation           | Euro area        | Non-euro EU     |
| -------------------- | ---------------- | --------------- |
| Receive instant      | 9 January 2025   | 9 January 2027  |
| Send instant         | 9 October 2025   | 9 July 2027     |
| Verification of payee | 9 October 2025  | 9 July 2027     |

Payment and e-money institutions have separate dates, starting 9 April 2027. Instant transfers may not cost more than the same provider's comparable standard transfers. Providers must also check their customers against EU targeted financial sanctions at least daily, in place of screening each instant transfer against those EU measures.

SEPA Instant differs from a [SEPA Credit Transfer](node:SEPA%20Credit%20Transfer) in speed and availability, but both are credit pushes that the payer starts. Completed transfers cannot be reversed by the payer, so a misdirected payment relies on a recall the receiver can refuse.

For engineers, the short deadline changes failure handling. A client timeout does not prove that a transfer failed, because the provider may have completed it just as the connection dropped. Treat it as an [unknown payment outcome](node:Unknown%20payment%20outcome) and query the status using your end-to-end reference before sending again. Also, release goods only on a confirmed credit, not on the customer's "sent" screen. Speed also helps fraudsters, since stolen money can be moved onward within seconds.
quotes: The transfer API timed out. Should I resend the SEPA Instant payment?
Not yet. Query the status with the end-to-end ID, since it may already have landed.

nodes.name: SEPA Direct Debit
nodes.description: The euro pull-payment scheme in which a creditor collects from a debtor's account under a signed mandate.
nodes.markdown:
SEPA Direct Debit, or SDD, is a European Payments Council scheme that lets a creditor collect euro payments from a debtor's account under a [direct debit mandate](node:Direct%20debit%20mandate). There are two schemes. SDD Core is available to consumers and businesses. SDD B2B is for business debtors only and needs the debtor bank to confirm the mandate.

| Step | Who           | What happens                                              |
| ---- | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Creditor      | Obtains the mandate with its creditor identifier and a unique reference |
| 2    | Creditor      | Gives the debtor advance notice of the amount and date    |
| 3    | Creditor's PSP | Submits the collection                                   |
| 4    | Debtor's PSP  | Debits the account, or rejects or returns the collection  |
| 5    | Debtor        | May request a refund under the scheme rules               |

The refund right is where SDD differs most from a card payment. Under the current SDD Core rulebook, a debtor can get a no-questions-asked refund within eight weeks of the debit, and can claim for an unauthorised collection for up to 13 months. SDD B2B has no equivalent refund right for an authorised collection. These periods come from the rulebook and can change.

An SDD refund is also different from a [chargeback](node:Chargeback). Card disputes have a [representment](node:Representment) stage where the [merchant](node:Merchant) can contest with evidence. In the eight-week window, the creditor cannot block the refund through the scheme and must pursue any valid debt separately.

The symptom is revenue reversing weeks after delivery, with a reason code such as `MD06`, while a failed collection may show `AM04` for insufficient funds. Treat each collection as provisional in your [ledger](node:Ledger), post reversals as new entries, and keep the mandate available, because the debtor's bank can request a copy for an unauthorised claim.
quotes: A customer got their money back seven weeks after we delivered.
That's an SDD Core refund, `MD06`. We can't contest it in the scheme, so finance has to invoice them again.

nodes.name: SWIFT
nodes.description: The member-owned network that sends payment messages between banks without itself holding or moving their funds.
nodes.markdown:
SWIFT, the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, now styled Swift, is a member-owned cooperative based in Belgium that runs a secure messaging network for financial institutions. It carries payment instructions between banks. It does not hold customer accounts or settle funds. The money moves through accounts that banks hold with each other, known as [correspondent banking](node:Correspondent%20banking), or through a [settlement](node:Settlement) system such as an [RTGS](node:RTGS).

A "Swift code" is a Business Identifier Code, or BIC, defined by ISO 9362. It identifies a bank or branch. It is different from an [IBAN](node:IBAN), which identifies a customer account.

| Layer       | Example                         | Job                               |
| ----------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Identifier  | BIC                             | Names the institution             |
| Message     | `pacs.008`, formerly MT103      | Describes the payment             |
| Network     | Swift                           | Delivers the message              |
| Funds       | [Nostro account](node:Nostro%20account) or RTGS          | Moves the value                   |

The message format has changed. For cross-border payment instructions between financial institutions, the coexistence period for legacy MT messages and [ISO 20022](node:ISO%2020022) ended on 22 November 2025. Swift had also planned to remove fully unstructured postal addresses in November 2026. In 2026 it agreed to extend that timeline for payment messages after community requests, so check its current roadmap before relying on a date.

The usual confusion appears when a business receives a "Swift copy" as proof of payment. That document shows an instruction was sent. It does not prove the beneficiary was credited. A payment can still be held by an intermediary for compliance review, rejected for bad details, or arrive short because a bank in the chain deducted a fee. To trace one, ask the sending bank for its Unique End-to-end Transaction Reference (UETR), which banks use to track the payment across the chain.
quotes: The supplier says they never got the money, but we have the Swift confirmation.
That only proves our bank sent the message. Give them the UETR and ask the bank to trace it.

nodes.name: Fedwire
nodes.description: The Federal Reserve's real-time gross settlement service for final, typically high-value US dollar payments.
nodes.markdown:
Fedwire, formally the Fedwire Funds Service, is a real-time gross [settlement](node:Settlement) system operated by the Federal Reserve Banks. A participating institution sends a payment order, and the Reserve Banks settle it individually by debiting the sender's Federal Reserve account and crediting the receiver's. Once settled, the payment is final and irrevocable. Businesses know it as a "wire", and it is typically used for large or time-critical payments such as property closings and interbank transfers.

| Rail    | Operator                       | Processing            | Can the money come back automatically? |
| ------- | ------------------------------ | --------------------- | ------------------- |
| Fedwire | Federal Reserve Banks          | Individual, business hours | No, it is final |
| [ACH](node:ACH)     | FedACH and EPN                 | Batched               | Yes, through returns |
| [FedNow](node:FedNow)  | Federal Reserve Banks          | Individual, 24x7x365  | No, it is final     |

Fedwire adopted [ISO 20022](node:ISO%2020022) on 14 July 2025, replacing its proprietary format. Its operating day runs on business days, so a payment instructed late may wait until the next one. In October 2025, the Federal Reserve Board announced that the service will expand to 22 hours a day, six days a week, with implementation planned for 2028 or 2029. Check the published schedule for current hours and cut-offs, because banks often set earlier internal deadlines for their customers.

Finality makes wire fraud hard to recover from. In a common scam, a criminal impersonates a supplier by email and sends new bank details. The finance team pays, the funds settle, and the sending bank can only ask the receiving bank to return them. The receiving bank does not have to agree, and the account may already be empty.

Confirm any change of payment details through a known phone number, require a second approver on high-value wires, and report suspected fraud to your bank immediately.
quotes: Can we pull back the wire we sent to the new supplier account?
Fedwire payments are final. Call the bank now and ask for a recall, but the receiving bank has to agree.

nodes.name: RTGS
nodes.description: Real-time gross settlement, where a central bank settles each interbank payment individually and with finality.
nodes.markdown:
Real-time gross [settlement](node:Settlement), or RTGS, is a type of settlement system in which interbank payments settle one at a time, as soon as they are processed, usually across accounts at a central bank. "Gross" means each payment settles for its full amount and is not netted against others. Settlement in central bank money removes the risk that the paying bank fails before settling.

Major examples are [Fedwire](node:Fedwire) in the US, T2 in the euro area and the Bank of England's RTGS service, which settles CHAPS payments in the UK.

The main alternative is deferred net settlement, where a system adds up what participants owe each other and settles only the difference at set times:

| Property          | RTGS                                | Deferred net settlement             |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Settlement        | Each payment, in full               | Net positions, in cycles            |
| Liquidity needed  | Higher                              | Lower                               |
| Settlement risk   | Low, because settlement is immediate | Exists between cycles unless covered |
| Example           | Fedwire, T2, CHAPS                  | [Faster Payments](node:Faster%20Payments)                     |

RTGS is often confused with instant payments. RTGS describes how banks settle. Instant payments describe what the customer experiences. Faster Payments credits customers quickly but settles between banks on a net basis three times per business day, according to the Bank of England, with participants prefunding their exposure. A traditional RTGS can also close overnight and on weekends, while a customer-facing instant service runs all the time.

Because every payment needs its full value, a bank must hold enough liquidity during the day. If it does not, the system may queue the payment until incoming funds arrive. A treasury team sees this as a high-value payment stuck in "queued" near a cut-off. Banks manage it with intraday credit, payment scheduling and liquidity-saving features in the system.
quotes: Why is this CHAPS payment still queued?
Our settlement account is short on intraday liquidity. RTGS needs the full amount, so treasury has to fund it first.

nodes.name: FedNow
nodes.description: The Federal Reserve's around-the-clock US instant payment service for final, individually settled credit transfers.
nodes.markdown:
FedNow is an instant payment service operated by the Federal Reserve Banks, launched in July 2023. It runs 24 hours a day, every day of the year. A participating bank or credit union sends a credit transfer, and the service settles it individually across Federal Reserve master accounts, or through a correspondent acting for the institution. The receiver can have the funds within seconds, and the payment is final.

| Step | Who            | What happens                                 |
| ---- | -------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Payer's bank   | Validates the payment and sends an [ISO 20022](node:ISO%2020022) message |
| 2    | FedNow         | Checks it and forwards it to the receiving bank |
| 3    | Receiver's bank | Accepts or rejects                          |
| 4    | FedNow         | Settles and notifies both banks              |
| 5    | Receiver's bank | Makes the funds available                   |

FedNow is often confused with [Fedwire](node:Fedwire) because both belong to the Federal Reserve. Fedwire is the established high-value wire service with a limited operating day. FedNow is designed for continuous, everyday instant payments. It is also separate from the [RTP network](node:RTP%20network), a private-sector instant system run by The Clearing House. A bank can join either, both or neither, and the two do not automatically exchange payments.

FedNow is a credit push. The payer's institution sends the money, so the service cannot be used as a card-style pull. Request-for-payment messages exist, but the payer still has to approve the payment. The Federal Reserve sets a network transaction limit, and participants may set lower ones, so check current values with your bank.

The failure teams usually meet is reachability. A checkout or [payout](node:Payout) offers "instant", but the recipient's bank is not enabled to receive FedNow, or it only receives and cannot send. Check reachability by routing number first, and fall back to another rail with the customer told about the slower timing.
quotes: Why did this instant payout fail for only some customers?
Their banks aren't enabled for FedNow. Check reachability by routing number and fall back to [ACH](node:ACH).

nodes.name: RTP network
nodes.description: The Clearing House's private US instant payment network, settling final credit transfers around the clock from a prefunded account.
nodes.markdown:
The RTP network is a US instant payment system operated by The Clearing House, a company owned by large banks. It launched in 2017 and runs around the clock. Participating institutions send credit transfers using [ISO 20022](node:ISO%2020022) messages, and receivers can have the funds within seconds. Payments on the network are final.

[Settlement](node:Settlement) relies on a prefunded joint account held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Participants fund their positions in that account, and each payment adjusts their balances on The Clearing House's records as it is processed. This model lets the network settle while traditional wire systems are closed.

| Property     | RTP network       | [FedNow](node:FedNow)                | [ACH](node:ACH)                 | [Fedwire](node:Fedwire)             |
| ------------ | ----------------- | --------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------- |
| Operator     | The Clearing House | Federal Reserve Banks | Nacha rules, two operators | Federal Reserve Banks |
| Availability | Continuous        | Continuous            | Processing windows  | Business days       |
| Direction    | Credit push       | Credit push           | Credit and debit    | Credit push         |
| Finality     | Final             | Final                 | Returns possible    | Final               |

The RTP network and FedNow are separate. A bank on one is not automatically reachable through the other, which is the main point of confusion for teams adding instant [payouts](node:Payout) in the US. The network also carries Request for Payment messages, which ask a payer to approve a push. A request is not a debit, so nothing moves until the payer agrees.

The failure engineers meet is a payout that works in testing and then fails for a portion of real customers because their bank does not receive RTP payments. Check eligibility for each routing number before promising instant delivery, and keep a fallback rail. Because payments are final, a payout to a wrong account depends on the recipient's bank and the recipient agreeing to send it back. Limits are set by the network and by each bank, and they change, so confirm them with your provider.
quotes: Can we promise instant payouts to every US account?
No. The RTP network doesn't reach every bank, so check the routing number and fall back to ACH.

nodes.name: Faster Payments
nodes.description: The UK's always-on retail bank transfer system, operated by Pay.UK and settled net at the Bank of England.
nodes.markdown:
Faster Payments is the UK's system for near-real-time bank transfers in sterling, operated by Pay.UK. It runs 24 hours a day and carries everyday transfers, bill payments and many [payouts](node:Payout). A customer usually sees the money arrive within seconds, although banks can hold a payment for fraud checks.

| Step | Who                  | What happens                                 |
| ---- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Payer                | Enters the sort code, account number and reference |
| 2    | Sending bank         | Checks the payment and submits it            |
| 3    | Faster Payments      | Routes it to the receiving bank              |
| 4    | Receiving bank       | Accepts it and credits the payee             |
| 5    | Bank of England      | Settles net positions in cycles              |

The customer experience is immediate, but interbank [settlement](node:Settlement) is not. According to the Bank of England, Faster Payments settles on a deferred net basis three times each business day in its [RTGS](node:RTGS) service, with direct participants prefunding their maximum exposure. It should not be confused with CHAPS, the UK's high-value system, which settles each payment gross. Bacs is a third, batch-based UK system and is the one used for UK direct debits.

Pay.UK's New Payments Architecture is intended to replace Faster Payments and use [ISO 20022](node:ISO%2020022). Its timing has moved before, so check Pay.UK's current plans.

A common failure is authorised push payment fraud, where a criminal persuades a customer to send money. The customer approved it, so the transfer completes. Since 7 October 2024, Payment Systems Regulator rules have required in-scope payment firms to reimburse victims, subject to conditions and a maximum amount that can be revised. A missing reference is a separate problem, because it leaves a received payment unmatched. Give each customer a unique reference, and use Confirmation of Payee, the UK name-checking service, before paying new accounts.
quotes: The customer says they paid by bank transfer, but the order is still open.
The Faster Payment landed without our reference. Match it manually and show the reference more clearly at checkout.

nodes.name: Correspondent banking
nodes.description: An arrangement where one bank holds an account at another to make payments in a currency or country it cannot reach directly.
nodes.markdown:
Correspondent banking is an arrangement in which one bank, the correspondent, holds an account for another bank, the respondent, and makes or receives payments on its behalf. A bank needs this when it has no direct access to the payment system of a currency. A small bank in France, for example, usually cannot settle US dollars in [Fedwire](node:Fedwire), so it holds dollars at a US bank that can.

A cross-border payment may pass through several banks:

| Step | Who                    | What happens                                       |
| ---- | ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Payer's bank           | Debits the payer and sends the instruction         |
| 2    | Its correspondent      | Debits the payer's bank's account and screens the payment |
| 3    | Intermediary, if any   | Passes value toward the beneficiary's bank         |
| 4    | Beneficiary's bank     | Receives value and credits the beneficiary         |

Correspondent banking is often confused with [SWIFT](node:SWIFT). Swift carries the messages between these banks. The correspondent accounts, or a [settlement](node:Settlement) system such as an [RTGS](node:RTGS), carry the value. The account is called a [nostro account](node:Nostro%20account) by the bank that owns it and a vostro account by the bank that holds it.

Each bank in the chain performs its own compliance checks, including [sanctions screening](node:Sanctions%20screening) and [AML](node:AML) review, and may charge a fee. This produces two common complaints. The first is a short payment: an invoice for 10,000 arrives as 9,965 because an intermediary deducted its charge. The sender can reduce this by choosing a charge option, where `OUR` means the sender pays, `SHA` means costs are shared and `BEN` means the beneficiary pays, though not every bank honours it fully. The second is a payment that stops for days while a bank asks about its purpose or parties.

Correspondents may also withdraw from relationships they consider high-risk, known as de-risking.
quotes: The supplier received 35 dollars less than we sent.
An intermediary in the correspondent banking chain took its fee. Send it as `OUR` next time, and gross up if needed.

nodes.name: Nostro account
nodes.description: A bank's account held at another bank, usually in foreign currency, which the other bank calls a vostro account.
nodes.markdown:
A nostro account is an account that a bank holds at another bank, usually in a foreign currency, in order to make and receive payments in that currency. The word comes from the Italian for "ours". The bank holding the account calls the same account a vostro account, meaning "yours". Both names describe one account seen from two sides.

A nostro is an asset on the owning bank's books, because it is money owed to that bank. The matching vostro is a liability on the correspondent's books. This example shows Bank A paying 1,000 USD on behalf of a customer through its nostro at Bank B, with the beneficiary also banking at B:

| Bank | Account                   | Type      | Debit | Credit |
| ---- | ------------------------- | --------- | ----: | -----: |
| A    | Customer's USD account    | Liability | 1,000 |        |
| A    | Nostro at Bank B          | Asset     |       |  1,000 |
| B    | Vostro for Bank A         | Liability | 1,000 |        |
| B    | Beneficiary's account     | Liability |       |  1,000 |

Each bank's entries balance. Bank A's nostro asset and its liability to the customer both fall by 1,000. Bank B's total liabilities stay the same, because its obligation moves from Bank A to the beneficiary.

Banks use nostros as part of [correspondent banking](node:Correspondent%20banking), and their treasury teams must keep enough in each currency to cover outgoing payments. Too little causes failed or delayed payments or overdraft charges. Too much ties up cash in idle balances.

The operational task is nostro reconciliation: comparing the bank's internal record of the account with the statements sent by the correspondent. An item on one side but not the other is called a break. Common causes are a fee the correspondent deducted, a payment in transit across a cut-off, or a duplicate. Unresolved breaks can hide errors or fraud, so teams track their age.
quotes: Why is the USD position 25 dollars off this morning?
There's a nostro break. The correspondent deducted a fee that we haven't booked, so post it and clear the item.

nodes.name: IBAN
nodes.description: An international bank account number under ISO 13616, with a country code, check digits and a domestic account identifier.
quotes: The form rejected a customer's IBAN, but it's correct on their statement.
They pasted it with non-breaking spaces. Strip all whitespace before validating.

nodes.name: ISO 20022
nodes.description: An international standard for financial messages, used by major payment systems for richer, structured payment data.
nodes.markdown:
ISO 20022 is an international standard for building financial messages from a shared data model. It defines business concepts such as debtor, creditor and remittance information, and message definitions built from them, most commonly expressed in XML. It is a language for payment data. It is not a network or a payment rail.

Message names show their purpose:

| Family | Example    | Use                                   |
| ------ | ---------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `pain` | `pain.001` | Customer instructs its bank to pay    |
| `pacs` | `pacs.008` | Bank-to-bank customer credit transfer |
| `pacs` | `pacs.004` | [Payment return](node:Payment%20return)                        |
| `camt` | `camt.053` | Account statement                     |

ISO 20022 is sometimes confused with [ISO 8583](node:ISO%208583), the older standard for card messages. [Card networks](node:Card%20network) still rely mainly on ISO 8583, while ISO 20022 has spread across bank payment systems:

| System              | ISO 20022 status                                       |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| SEPA schemes        | Used by the schemes                                    |
| T2 (euro area)      | Migrated March 2023                                    |
| CHAPS (UK)          | Migrated June 2023                                     |
| CHIPS (US)          | Migrated April 2024                                    |
| [Fedwire](node:Fedwire)             | Migrated 14 July 2025                                  |
| [Swift](node:SWIFT) cross-border  | MT coexistence for payment instructions ended 22 November 2025 |
| [FedNow](node:FedNow), [RTP network](node:RTP%20network) | Built on ISO 20022                                     |
| [Faster Payments](node:Faster%20Payments)     | Planned through Pay.UK's New Payments Architecture     |

Structured addresses are the main unfinished item. Swift planned to reject fully unstructured postal addresses from November 2026, then agreed in 2026 to extend the timeline for payment messages. Check its current roadmap.

The failures usually come from translation between formats. A system that converts rich ISO 20022 fields into an older format can truncate a long name or lose invoice references, and reconciliation then fails downstream. A payment can also be rejected because a required structured field is empty. Keep the original message, map fields explicitly, and test with real long names, non-Latin transliterations and full remittance data.
quotes: Invoice references started disappearing from incoming payments.
Our adapter still flattens ISO 20022 into the old format and truncates the remittance field. Map it directly.

nodes.name: Direct debit mandate
nodes.description: A payer's authorization allowing a named creditor to collect payments from their bank account under scheme rules.
nodes.markdown:
A direct debit mandate is the authorization a payer gives a creditor to collect money from their bank account. It identifies the parties and the account, and it sets the terms of the collection. Without a valid mandate, a debit can be returned as unauthorised. Each scheme has its own name and rules for it:

| Region | Scheme or service         | Mandate details                                                   |
| ------ | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| SEPA   | [SEPA Direct Debit](node:SEPA%20Direct%20Debit)         | Creditor identifier plus a unique mandate reference               |
| UK     | Bacs Direct Debit         | Direct Debit Instruction, backed by the Direct Debit Guarantee    |
| US     | [ACH](node:ACH)                       | Authorization under Nacha rules, with requirements by entry type  |
| India  | [UPI](node:UPI) AutoPay and NACH      | Registered e-mandate, under Reserve Bank of India and NPCI rules  |
| Brazil | [Pix](node:Pix) Automático            | Payer's prior authorization, under Banco Central do Brasil rules  |

A mandate differs from a [stored credential](node:Stored%20credential). A stored credential is a saved card used under [card network](node:Card%20network) rules. A mandate authorises debits from a bank account under a bank scheme. It also differs from [recurring billing](node:Recurring%20billing), which is the business process that decides when to collect. A mandate is only the permission.

Under the UK guarantee, if an error is made, the payer's bank must give a full and immediate refund, then reclaim it from the collecting organisation through an indemnity claim.

The failures are mostly about evidence and lifecycle. A customer disputes a debit and the business cannot produce the mandate, so it loses the money. A migration between providers drops mandate references, and the next collection is rejected. A price rise goes out without the required advance notice, and customers claim refunds.

Store the reference, scheme, signature date, wording version and proof of consent. Mark a mandate as cancelled as soon as the bank or customer revokes it, and stop collecting against it.
quotes: The bank returned the debit saying there's no valid mandate.
We lost the mandate references in the provider migration. Pause collections and re-collect them from affected customers.

nodes.name: Payment return
nodes.description: A bank-rail reversal in which a debit or credit is sent back, with a reason code, after being submitted or settled.
nodes.markdown:
A payment return is a bank-rail message that sends a debit or credit back to the originating bank because it could not be applied or is being contested. The money moves back, and the message carries a reason code. Returns occur on [ACH](node:ACH), SEPA and other bank rails, often after the payment appeared successful.
