A return is different from a [refund](node:Refund), which the [merchant](node:Merchant) chooses to issue, and from a [chargeback](node:Chargeback), which is the card dispute process. It also differs from a rejection, where a payment is refused before [settlement](node:Settlement). SEPA groups these exceptions as R-transactions, including rejects, returns, refunds and recalls.

| Rail | Code   | Meaning                              |
| ---- | ------ | ------------------------------------ |
| ACH  | `R01`  | Insufficient funds                   |
| ACH  | `R02`  | Account closed                       |
| ACH  | `R03`  | No account, or unable to locate it   |
| ACH  | `R10`  | Consumer says the debit was unauthorised |
| ACH  | `R29`  | Business says the debit was unauthorised |
| SEPA | `AC04` | Account closed                       |
| SEPA | `AM04` | Insufficient funds                   |
| SEPA | `MD01` | No valid mandate                     |

Return windows depend on the rail, the code and the payer type. Nacha and the European Payments Council set them in their rules, and they can change. An unauthorised claim can arrive much later than an insufficient-funds return.

A loss occurs when a platform credits a user's balance on submission, the user withdraws the money, and the debit then returns. The platform carries the loss. Hold funds according to risk, and treat bank debits as provisional until the relevant window has passed.

Record a return as a new [ledger](node:Ledger) entry that reverses the original, and never edit or delete the original row. Handle codes differently: `R01` may justify a later retry within scheme limits, while `R10` means stop collecting and investigate. Nacha limits how a returned debit may be reinitiated.
quotes: This user's balance went negative overnight. What happened?
Their funding debit came back as a payment return, `R01`, after they'd withdrawn. Post a reversal and restrict the account.

nodes.name: Open banking
nodes.description: Regulated or standardised access for authorised third parties to bank account data and payment initiation, with customer consent.
nodes.markdown:
Open banking is a framework that lets authorised third parties, with a customer's consent, read bank account data or initiate payments from that account through the bank's interfaces. An account information provider reads balances and transactions. A payment initiation provider starts a payment from the customer's account.

The legal basis differs by country:

| Jurisdiction | Basis                                  | Status to check                                         |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| EU           | [PSD2](node:PSD2)                                   | PSD3 and a Payment Services Regulation were provisionally agreed in November 2025; check publication and application dates |
| UK           | 2017 Competition and Markets Authority order for the largest banks | Long-term framework under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 is still being put in place |
| US           | Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Section 1033 rule | The 2024 rule is under agency reconsideration, and compliance dates have been in flux |
| Brazil       | Open Finance under Banco Central do Brasil rules | Operating, with rules that continue to develop |

Open banking differs from [pay by bank](node:Pay%20by%20bank), which is one product built on top of it. It also differs from screen scraping, where a service logs in with the customer's credentials and reads web pages. Regulated interfaces use consent and scoped access, so the third party never receives the banking password.

Consent is the most common operational problem. Access can expire or need renewed customer authentication, depending on the regime and the bank. A lending or accounting product then stops receiving transactions, and users see stale balances with no obvious error. Bank interfaces also vary in quality, so one bank's outage can break a segment of customers.

Track consent expiry and prompt users before it lapses. Monitor success rates per bank, and show the last successful sync time so a stale balance is visible. Check whether your activity requires authorisation or can run through a licensed provider.
quotes: Half our users' bank feeds stopped updating last night.
Their open banking consents expired. Prompt them to reauthenticate, and warn them before expiry from now on.

nodes.name: Pay by bank
nodes.description: A checkout method where the customer pays directly from their bank account, often through open banking payment initiation.
nodes.markdown:
Pay by bank is a checkout method in which a customer pays a [merchant](node:Merchant) directly from a bank account instead of with a card. In many markets it uses [open banking](node:Open%20banking): a licensed payment initiation provider sends the customer to their bank to approve a pre-filled transfer. The underlying rail depends on the country, for example [Faster Payments](node:Faster%20Payments) in the UK or a [SEPA Credit Transfer](node:SEPA%20Credit%20Transfer) or [SEPA Instant](node:SEPA%20Instant) in Europe. In the US, products under this name often use linked accounts and an [ACH](node:ACH) debit, and some use instant rails.

| Step | Who                   | What happens                                 |
| ---- | --------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Customer              | Chooses pay by bank and selects a bank       |
| 2    | Payment provider      | Creates a payment with amount and reference  |
| 3    | Customer's bank       | Authenticates the customer, who approves     |
| 4    | Customer's bank       | Sends the payment on the rail                |
| 5    | Merchant              | Confirms receipt, then fulfils               |

Compared with cards, there is no [interchange fee](node:Interchange%20fee) and usually no card-style [chargeback](node:Chargeback). That shifts the risk. Consumer protection comes from the rail and local law, not [card network](node:Card%20network) rules, and it differs by market. A push payment is generally hard to reverse, while a US ACH debit can come back later as a [payment return](node:Payment%20return).

The common engineering mistake is treating the customer's approval as payment received. "Authorised" at the bank can still become rejected, pending or delayed by a fraud check. A customer can also close the browser after approving, so the redirect never reaches your site and the order looks abandoned. Rely on server-side status from the provider and query it if no update arrives.

[Refunds](node:Refund) also work differently. There is no card to credit, so the merchant needs the payer's account details or a provider feature that returns funds.
quotes: The customer's bank says they paid, but our order is still pending.
With pay by bank the redirect can fail after approval. Query the provider's status instead of relying on the return URL.

nodes.name: Digital wallet
nodes.description: An app or account that stores payment credentials or a balance, so a customer can pay without entering card details.
nodes.markdown:
A digital wallet is an app or online account that stores a customer's payment credentials, a balance, or both, and uses them to make payments. The type determines who holds the money and which rail carries the payment.

| Type          | Example               | How it pays                                             | Holds funds? |
| ------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| Pass-through  | Apple Pay, Google Pay | Passes a card credential, often a [network token](node:Network%20token), to the [merchant](node:Merchant) | No |
| Staged        | PayPal paying with a linked card | Wallet charges the funding source, then pays the merchant | Sometimes |
| Stored value  | Balance in a wallet account | Spends a balance held by the provider              | Yes          |

In a pass-through wallet, the payment is still a card payment. The [issuer](node:Issuer) approves it, the merchant's [acquirer](node:Acquirer) processes it, and the usual card fees and [chargeback](node:Chargeback) rules apply. A wallet is therefore not a rail in its own right. A staged or stored-value wallet is different, because the wallet provider is a party to the payment, and holding customer balances generally requires a licence such as e-money authorisation, with duties such as [safeguarding](node:Safeguarding).

Device wallets replace the card number with a device-specific token and authenticate the customer with a biometric or passcode. Because of this, the last four digits shown in the wallet may differ from those printed on the physical card. A common support ticket follows: a customer gives the digits from their plastic card, and the agent cannot find the order. Search by the token's last four digits, the amount and the date, or use the provider's transaction reference.

Expect a saved wallet token to stop working when a customer changes device or removes the card. Store the wallet type separately for reporting, since [authorization rates](node:Authorization%20rate) and fraud patterns can differ from manually entered cards.
quotes: Support can't find this order using the customer's card number.
They paid with a digital wallet, so the last four belong to the device token. Search by amount and date.

nodes.name: Buy now pay later
nodes.description: Short-term credit at checkout that splits a purchase into instalments, with rules that depend on the jurisdiction.
nodes.markdown:
Buy now pay later, or BNPL, is a form of short-term credit offered at checkout that lets a customer split a purchase into instalments or defer payment. A BNPL provider typically pays the [merchant](node:Merchant) up front, less a fee, and then collects repayments from the customer. Some plans charge no interest and may charge late fees, while longer plans can charge interest. Terms vary by provider and country.

| Party    | Role                                                   |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Customer | Agrees a credit plan and repays on schedule            |
| Provider | Assesses the customer, pays the merchant, collects     |
| Merchant | Receives funds, pays a fee, handles returns and [refunds](node:Refund) |

BNPL differs from a credit card in that each purchase is usually a separate loan with a fixed schedule, not a revolving limit.

The product depends heavily on regulation, which has been changing:

| Jurisdiction | Position                                                                                      |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| UK           | The Financial Conduct Authority began regulating deferred payment credit on 15 July 2026      |
| EU           | Consumer Credit Directive (EU) 2023/2225 applies from 20 November 2026 and covers BNPL, with limited exclusions |
| US           | The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau withdrew its 2024 BNPL interpretive rule in May 2025. Federal and state lending laws may still apply |

Merchants offering BNPL should confirm the required disclosures and marketing rules with the provider and legal counsel. This entry describes the product and is not financial advice.

The operational failure usually involves returns. A customer returns one item from a split order, but the instalments do not update until the merchant sends the refund to the provider. The customer sees a payment still due on goods they sent back and contacts support. Send partial refunds through the provider's API against the original order, and keep the provider's plan ID in your payment record.
quotes: A customer returned the shoes but is still being asked for instalments.
We never sent the refund to the buy now pay later provider. Post it against the original order so the plan recalculates.

nodes.name: UPI
nodes.description: India's real-time account-to-account payment system, operated by NPCI under Reserve Bank of India oversight.
nodes.markdown:
UPI, the Unified Payments Interface, is India's real-time payment system for moving money between bank accounts through mobile apps. The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) operates it, under the oversight of the Reserve Bank of India. Banks and licensed third-party apps connect to it, so customers of different banks can pay each other.

| Element           | What it is                                                |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| UPI ID            | A virtual address such as `name@bank`, hiding account details |
| UPI PIN           | A secret the customer enters to authorise a debit         |
| PSP app           | The app the customer uses to send or approve a payment    |
| [QR code payment](node:QR%20code%20payment)   | A [merchant](node:Merchant) code the customer scans to pay                 |
| AutoPay           | A registered mandate for recurring debits                 |
| UPI Lite          | An on-device balance for small payments without a PIN     |

UPI is the rail, and consumer apps are built on it. It differs from a card payment because funds normally come straight from a bank account, although NPCI also supports RuPay credit cards and pre-sanctioned credit lines on UPI.

NPCI's rules change regularly. Its consolidated circular of September 2026 says the collect function must not be available for person-to-person payments. For recurring payments, the Reserve Bank's E-mandate Framework, 2026 covers registration, additional authentication and pre-debit notification. Limits and fees are set by NPCI, the Reserve Bank and banks, so confirm them at the source.

The typical failure is a payment stuck as pending. The customer's bank has debited the account, but the merchant has received no confirmation, and the customer pays again. Treat pending as an unknown outcome. Query the transaction status with your reference before offering a retry.
quotes: The customer was debited, but the order shows unpaid.
The UPI transaction is still pending. Run a status check on our reference before letting them pay again.

nodes.name: Pix
nodes.description: Brazil's instant payment system, created and run by the Banco Central do Brasil, available around the clock.
nodes.markdown:
Pix is Brazil's instant payment system, created and operated by the Banco Central do Brasil. It runs 24 hours a day and moves money between accounts at participating institutions within seconds. Transfers settle through the central bank's Instant Payment System, known as SPI.

| Element         | What it is                                                   |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Pix key         | An alias such as a tax ID, phone, email or random key        |
| DICT            | The central bank's directory mapping keys to accounts        |
| Static QR       | A reusable code, often with an open amount                   |
| Dynamic QR      | A code generated per charge, with an amount and identifier   |
| Pix Automático  | Recurring collection under one prior payer authorization, live since 16 June 2025 |
| MED             | Special Return Mechanism for suspected fraud and certain failures |

Pix is a credit push: the payer's institution sends the funds. That distinguishes it from a card payment, which involves an authorization and later [settlement](node:Settlement), and from boleto, a payment slip that clears on a slower cycle.

Pix has a dedicated fraud-return process. Under MED, the receiving institution can block funds and return them when fraud is reasonably suspected. The central bank made MED 2.0, which extends tracing of funds across accounts, mandatory from 2 February 2026. A [merchant](node:Merchant) can therefore lose funds it believed were final. Rules continue to change, so check the current Pix regulation.

For merchants, the most common operational failure is matching. A static QR code without a usable identifier produces a credit that cannot be tied to an order. Use a dynamic QR with a unique transaction ID per order, confirm from the provider's server-side event, and never accept a customer's screenshot as proof, because it can be faked. Record any later MED return as a new [ledger](node:Ledger) entry.
quotes: Finance has a Pix credit with no matching order.
That came through our old static QR. Move checkout to dynamic codes so every payment carries an order ID.

nodes.name: Virtual card
nodes.description: A card number issued digitally for a specific use, often with limits on merchant, amount or time.
nodes.markdown:
A virtual card is a payment card that exists only as digital details: a card number, expiry date and security code. An [issuer](node:Issuer) creates it, often through a card programme run by a fintech with a [sponsor bank](node:Sponsor%20bank). It can be restricted to one [merchant](node:Merchant), one use, a maximum amount or a period of time. Businesses use them to pay suppliers, control employee spending and book travel.

| Control          | Effect                                               |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Single use       | Closes after the first successful payment            |
| Merchant lock    | Works only at a chosen merchant or [merchant category code](node:Merchant%20category%20code) |
| Amount limit     | Declines anything above the set value                |
| Expiry           | Stops working after a chosen date                    |

A virtual card is often confused with a [network token](node:Network%20token). A virtual card has a real [PAN](node:PAN) and can be used anywhere its controls allow, on the [card network](node:Card%20network) like any other card. A network token replaces an existing card number for a specific merchant or device, and it cannot be typed into another checkout.

The controls that make these cards useful also cause most of their failures. A merchant lock fails because the supplier's payment went through a parent company or a different merchant category. A hotel adds an [incremental authorization](node:Incremental%20authorization) above the amount limit and the charge is declined. A single-use card is closed, and a later top-up or subscription renewal fails. A [refund](node:Refund) to a closed virtual card may need manual handling by the issuer.

A hotel or rental desk may also ask for the physical card used at booking, which does not exist. Set the limit to cover expected holds and final charges, keep the card open until the transaction has fully completed, and tell the traveller in advance how payment will work.
quotes: The supplier says our payment was declined again.
The virtual card is locked to their old merchant category. Reissue it with the new one and raise the limit.

nodes.name: Prepaid card
nodes.description: A payment card that spends a preloaded balance held by the programme, not a linked current account or a credit line.
nodes.markdown:
A prepaid card is a payment card that draws on money loaded in advance rather than on a linked bank account or a credit line. An [issuer](node:Issuer), or a programme manager working with one, holds the balance. Common forms are gift, payroll, travel and reloadable general-purpose cards. Most run on a [card network](node:Card%20network), so a [merchant](node:Merchant) accepts them like other cards.

| Card type | Spends from                        | Issuer's exposure       |
| --------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Credit    | A credit line, repaid later        | Credit risk             |
| Debit     | The holder's bank account          | Mostly the account balance |
| Prepaid   | A balance loaded in advance        | Limited to the balance, plus programme risk |

Regulation depends on the product and the jurisdiction. In the US, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Prepaid Rule applies disclosure and error-resolution protections to many prepaid accounts. In the EU and UK, many prepaid products are e-money, so issuers need authorisation and must meet [safeguarding](node:Safeguarding) requirements. Gift cards and closed-loop cards usable at one merchant may fall under different rules or exemptions.

A merchant usually meets prepaid cards through declines. An [authorization hold](node:Authorization%20hold) for an estimated amount can exceed the remaining balance, which is common at fuel pumps and hotels, even if the final charge would have fit. The [BIN](node:BIN) can also show that a card is prepaid, and some merchants block these cards for subscriptions because they run out of funds on renewal.

Some card programmes support partial approval, where the issuer approves only the available balance and the customer pays the rest another way. Enable it if your checkout can collect a second payment. [Refunds](node:Refund) can also be awkward when a card has expired or been discarded, so keep an alternative refund route, such as store credit where the law allows.
quotes: This customer's card keeps declining at pre-auth, but they say there's money on it.
It's a prepaid card and our hold is bigger than the balance. Lower the hold or support partial approval.

nodes.name: QR code payment
nodes.description: A payment started by scanning a QR code, which carries payment data while a separate rail moves the money.
nodes.markdown:
A QR code payment is a payment started by scanning a two-dimensional code that carries payment information. The QR code is only a way to pass data between devices. The money moves on a separate rail, such as [UPI](node:UPI), [Pix](node:Pix), a [card network](node:Card%20network) or a [digital wallet](node:Digital%20wallet)'s own system. Two transactions that look identical at the till can therefore have different fees, finality and dispute rights.

EMVCo, the card industry's technical standards body, publishes QR specifications for two modes:

| Mode                | Who shows the code | Who scans | Typical use                |
| ------------------- | ------------------ | --------- | -------------------------- |
| Merchant-presented  | Merchant           | Customer  | Stickers, screens, invoices |
| Consumer-presented  | Customer's app     | Merchant  | Retail tills with scanners |

Merchant-presented codes can be static or dynamic. A static code is printed once and normally identifies only the payee, so the customer types in the amount. A dynamic code is generated for one payment and includes the amount and a reference, which makes automatic matching possible. National systems define their own formats, many of them based on the EMVCo specification.

QR payment is often confused with contactless card payment. A tap uses NFC, a short-range radio link, and [EMV](node:EMV) card technology. A QR payment uses a camera and usually an app, and needs no card terminal in merchant-presented mode.

Static codes create two recognisable failures. A fraudster places a sticker with their own code over the merchant's, and customers pay the wrong account while believing the payment succeeded. A shop assistant accepts a customer's success screen, which can be faked or may show a payment that later failed.

Use dynamic codes where possible, and check displayed codes regularly if you use static ones. Release goods only when your own terminal, app or provider confirms the credit.
quotes: Three customers say they paid, but nothing reached our account.
Someone put a fake sticker over the QR code at the till. Replace it and switch to dynamic codes.

nodes.name: Cash voucher
nodes.description: A payment reference that a customer takes to a shop or bank to pay in cash, with the merchant confirmed afterwards.
nodes.markdown:
A cash voucher is a payment method in which a [merchant](node:Merchant)'s checkout generates a reference or barcode, and the customer pays it in cash at a participating location such as a convenience store, bank agent or lottery kiosk. The collection network then reports the payment. Examples include boleto in Brazil, OXXO in Mexico and konbini payments in Japan. Vouchers let people without cards or bank accounts buy online. Boleto can also be paid through banking apps.

| Step | Who                | What happens                               |
| ---- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| 1    | Customer           | Chooses the voucher method at checkout     |
| 2    | Provider           | Issues a reference with an amount and expiry |
| 3    | Customer           | Pays at a store, agent or banking app      |
| 4    | Collection network | Records the payment and notifies the provider |
| 5    | Merchant           | Receives confirmation and fulfils          |

A voucher is asynchronous. The order sits unpaid between steps 2 and 4, for hours or days, and some customers never pay. It is different from a [prepaid card](node:Prepaid%20card), where value is loaded before the purchase and spent through a [card network](node:Card%20network). It also has no authorization step, so a merchant cannot know at checkout whether payment will happen.

Stock is the usual problem. Reserving items for every voucher lets unpaid orders hold stock, while reserving nothing lets a customer pay for an item that has sold out. Set an expiry that fits your stock, and define what happens when a payment is reported after expiry. Provider notifications may also arrive late or more than once, so make the handler safe to run repeatedly.

Vouchers generally have no card-style [chargebacks](node:Chargeback), but a [refund](node:Refund) can need the customer's bank details because there is no card to credit. Forged vouchers also exist, so generate them only through your provider.
quotes: A customer paid their boleto, but the order had already been cancelled.
The cash voucher expired before the payment was reported. Refund it or reinstate the order, and handle late payments in the state machine.

nodes.name: Stablecoin payment
nodes.description: A payment using a blockchain token designed to track a reference asset, subject to crypto and payments regulation.
nodes.markdown:
A stablecoin payment is a transfer of value using a blockchain token designed to hold a stable price against a reference asset, usually a currency. An issuer creates the tokens and, for fiat-backed designs, holds reserves intended to support redemption. A sender signs a transaction from a wallet, the blockchain records it, and the recipient's wallet receives the token. Businesses often use a provider to convert between bank money and tokens, known as on-ramping and off-ramping.

A stablecoin is not a bank deposit, and stability is not guaranteed. A token can trade below its reference value if confidence in its reserves or redemption falls. Whether holders can redeem directly, and on what terms, depends on the issuer and the applicable law. This entry is not investment or financial advice.

The legal position differs by jurisdiction:

| Jurisdiction | Position                                                                                 |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| EU           | MiCA regulates e-money and asset-referenced tokens. The European Banking Authority advised that some e-money token services also need [PSD2](node:PSD2) authorisation from 2 March 2026 |
| US           | The GENIUS Act and the OCC's final rule for its issuers take effect on 18 January 2027   |
| UK           | Financial Conduct Authority stablecoin rules are final, with the regime starting 25 October 2027 |

Unlike a card payment, a stablecoin transfer has no [chargeback](node:Chargeback), and a confirmed transfer to a wrong address is generally unrecoverable. The same token can exist on several blockchains, so sending on a network the recipient does not support can strand funds. [Sanctions screening](node:Sanctions%20screening) and [AML](node:AML) duties can still apply.

Wait for the confirmation depth your risk policy requires before crediting a user. Store the chain, token contract, transaction hash and amount as an integer in the token's base units, because tokens define their own decimals.
quotes: The customer sent the stablecoin payment, but our wallet shows nothing.
They used a chain we don't support. Check the transaction hash, and show the network at checkout.

nodes.name: Payment intent
nodes.description: A record of what a customer intends to pay, which tracks one or more attempts until the payment reaches a final state.
nodes.markdown:
A payment intent is a record that represents one thing a customer intends to pay for, including the amount, currency and current status. It stays the same while the attempts to fulfil it change. Stripe uses the name PaymentIntent. Other providers call a similar object an order, session or payment, and many teams build their own.

The important split is between the intent and its attempts. A customer may try one card, get a decline, and succeed with another. That is one intent with two attempts.

```json
{
  "id": "pi_123",
  "order_id": "ord_987",
  "amount": 4999,
  "currency": "EUR",
  "status": "requires_payment_method",
  "attempts": [{ "id": "att_1", "outcome": "declined" }]
}
```

| Concept  | Question it answers             | Cardinality            |
| -------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Order    | What is being bought?           | One order              |
| Intent   | What needs to be paid?          | Usually one per order  |
| Attempt  | What happened this time?        | Many per intent        |

The amount is stored as an integer in the currency's [minor unit](node:Minor%20unit), so 4999 in EUR means 49.99.

Without this object, a system often models each click as a new payment. The failure is familiar: a customer's card is declined, they reload the page and try again, the earlier request also completes, and they suffer a [double charge](node:Double%20charge) because two independent payments exist. With an intent, every attempt attaches to one record, and the system can refuse a new attempt once one has succeeded.

Enforce one active intent per order with a unique database constraint. Reuse the existing intent when the checkout page reloads, and send a provider idempotency key (a unique value that lets a server recognise a repeated request) for each attempt. Drive its status through a [payment state machine](node:Payment%20state%20machine) rather than free updates. If the amount changes, update the intent only while no attempt is in progress.
quotes: Refreshing checkout creates a new payment each time.
Look up the existing payment intent by order ID and reuse it. Only attempts should multiply.

nodes.name: Payment state machine
nodes.description: A model defining a payment's allowed states and transitions, so that late or duplicate events cannot corrupt its status.
nodes.markdown:
A payment state machine is a model that lists every status a payment can have and the transitions allowed between them. Payment events arrive from customers, providers and scheduled jobs, often late, duplicated or out of order. The state machine decides whether each event may change the record.

| From       | Event                | To         |
| ---------- | -------------------- | ---------- |
| `created`  | Authorization approved | `authorized` |
| `created`  | Declined             | `failed`   |
| `created`  | Timeout              | `unknown`  |
| `unknown`  | Status query: approved | `authorized` |
| `unknown`  | Status query: not processed | `failed` |
| `authorized` | [Capture](node:Capture) confirmed  | `captured` |
| `authorized` | [Void](node:Void) confirmed     | `voided`   |
| `captured` | Funds settled        | `settled`  |
| `settled`  | [Refund](node:Refund) confirmed     | `refunded` |

Real systems add partial states, such as partially captured or partially refunded, and a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) path. The separate `unknown` state matters because a timeout is not a failure. It holds the payment until a status query resolves an [unknown payment outcome](node:Unknown%20payment%20outcome).

A status column without these rules is the usual starting point, and it fails under concurrency. A `failed` event from an earlier attempt arrives after `captured` and overwrites it, so support sees a failed payment that the customer has paid for. Or a provider resends an event, and the fulfilment code ships twice.

Apply transitions atomically with a conditional update, so that only one writer can win:

```sql
UPDATE payments
SET status = 'captured', version = version + 1
WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'authorized';
```

If zero rows change, read the current state. A repeat of the same event is a harmless no-op, so acknowledge it. An impossible transition should be logged and alerted, not forced. Keep an append-only history of every event, because the current status alone cannot explain how the payment got there. Side effects such as shipping should run once per transition.
quotes: A late failure event flipped a captured payment back to failed.
The handler writes whatever status it receives. Put it behind the payment state machine and reject that transition.

nodes.name: Double charge
nodes.description: A customer being billed twice for one purchase, usually from an unsafe retry or duplicate processing.
nodes.markdown:
A double charge is when a customer is billed more than once for a single purchase. The usual causes are a retry after a timeout, a repeated click, two workers processing the same job, or a duplicated [capture](node:Capture). The customer sees two entries on their statement and contacts support, or disputes one with their bank.

Not every pair of entries is a true duplicate. An [authorization hold](node:Authorization%20hold) can appear next to the final charge for a few days, particularly when the amounts differ, such as a hotel or fuel purchase. The bank later drops the hold. Before refunding, check whether both items were captured.

| Cause                          | How it happens                                           | Prevention                                  |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Retry after timeout            | First request succeeded, client sent a new one           | Query status, reuse the same idempotency key |
| Double click                   | Two submissions from one form                            | Disable button, enforce one intent per order |
| Concurrent workers             | Two jobs pick up the same invoice                        | Unique constraint or row lock               |
| Replayed provider event        | Handler repeats its side effect                          | Deduplicate on event ID                     |
| Failover to another provider   | Second provider charges after an unknown first outcome   | Resolve the first attempt before routing    |

An idempotency key (a unique value that lets a server recognise a repeated request) protects one provider boundary only, so a failover to a second provider needs a status check first.

To repair a real duplicate, [void](node:Void) the second payment if it has not been captured, or [refund](node:Refund) it if it has. Record that correction as a new [ledger](node:Ledger) entry, leaving the original entries in place. Then find every affected customer by searching for multiple successful payments with the same order, or the same card, amount and short time window. Contact them before they raise a [chargeback](node:Chargeback).
quotes: Support has ten tickets about a double charge since this morning.
The new retry job generates a fresh key per attempt. Stop it, find the duplicates by order ID, and refund them.

nodes.name: Unknown payment outcome
nodes.description: A payment whose result is not known after a timeout or lost response, and which must be resolved before any retry.
nodes.markdown:
An unknown payment outcome is the state a payment is in when the sender cannot tell whether it succeeded. It usually follows a timeout, a dropped connection, a crash after sending, or a 5xx error from a provider. The request may never have arrived, or it may have been approved with only the response lost.

This is different from a decline. A decline is a definite answer from the [issuer](node:Issuer) that no payment was approved. A timeout is no answer at all. Treating it as a failure can cause a [double charge](node:Double%20charge): the app shows "Payment failed", the customer pays again, and both payments succeed.

| Step | Action                                                         |
| ---- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Move the payment to `unknown` and do not fulfil or fail it     |
| 2    | Query the provider's status API with your own reference        |
| 3    | If approved, continue the normal flow                          |
| 4    | If declined or never processed, mark it failed                 |
| 5    | If not found, wait and query again, as records can lag         |
| 6    | If still unresolved, follow the provider's reversal or support route |

```text
on timeout:
  payment.status = "unknown"
  result = provider.get_by_reference(payment.reference)
  if result is pending or not_found: schedule another status check
  else: apply result through the state machine
```

Generate your reference and persist it before sending the request, or you will have nothing to query after a crash. If the provider supports idempotency keys (unique values that make a repeat return the first result), a retry with the same key is safe within the provider's documented window. Do not switch to another provider until the first attempt is resolved.

Card systems also use an [authorization reversal](node:Authorization%20reversal) to release a possibly approved authorization when the response is lost. Show the customer a neutral message such as "We're confirming your payment", and alert when items stay unknown beyond an agreed time. [Payment reconciliation](node:Payment%20reconciliation) is the final safety net.
quotes: The gateway timed out. Should I show an error so they can try again?
No, it's an unknown payment outcome. Query status by our reference first, because the charge may have gone through.

nodes.name: Payment retry
nodes.description: Attempting a failed or uncertain payment again, with rules based on why it failed and network limits on reattempts.
nodes.markdown:
A payment retry is another attempt at a payment that did not succeed or whose result is uncertain. Whether a retry is safe depends on the previous outcome. Retrying the wrong case produces a [double charge](node:Double%20charge), a pointless decline or a network rule breach.

| Previous outcome              | Action                                                                  |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Hard decline](node:Hard%20decline)                  | Do not retry the same credential. Ask for another payment method        |
| [Soft decline](node:Soft%20decline)                  | Retry later, or after the customer completes the requested step         |
| [Issuer](node:Issuer) unavailable            | Retry with backoff, possibly through another route                      |
| Connection failed before sending | Safe to retry with the same idempotency key                          |
| Timeout or unknown            | Query status first. Retry only if the attempt did not succeed           |

An idempotency key is a unique value that lets a server recognise a repeated request. Reuse it when repeating an attempt after a lost response. A new attempt after a definite decline needs a new key, because the old key would return the old decline.

[Card networks](node:Card%20network) restrict repeated attempts. Visa groups [decline codes](node:Decline%20code) into categories with reattempt rules, and some codes must never be retried. Mastercard returns [merchant](node:Merchant) advice codes, such as one telling the merchant not to try again. Limits and fees change, so get the current rules from your [acquirer](node:Acquirer). Hammering an issuer can also lower your [authorization rate](node:Authorization%20rate) and resemble [card testing](node:Card%20testing).

[Dunning](node:Dunning) is the wider recovery process for failed subscription payments, which schedules retries and contacts the customer.

The common failure comes from generic HTTP retry middleware wrapped around a payment client. It treats a 504 as retryable, sends a fresh request, and charges the customer twice. Remove automatic retries from payment-creating calls and put the decision in code that understands the provider's result. Add exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum attempt count, and a log of every attempt.
quotes: Should the job retry every declined card overnight?
Only the soft declines. A payment retry on a hard decline breaks network rules and won't succeed anyway.

nodes.name: Ledger
nodes.description: An append-only record of money movements between accounts, from which balances are derived and audited.
nodes.markdown:
A ledger is an append-only record of every movement of money between accounts. Each posting records the account, amount, currency, direction and a reference to the event that caused it. Balances are computed from those entries, or kept as a cached figure that can be rebuilt from them.

A ledger differs from a `payments` table. The payments table describes the state of a payment attempt and changes over time. The ledger records the financial effect of each step and never changes. A `balance` column on a user row shows a total but cannot explain it, so when a customer asks why their balance is wrong, there is no answer.

Most payment ledgers use [double-entry bookkeeping](node:Double-entry%20bookkeeping), so each transaction's debits and credits are equal. Amounts are integers in each currency's [minor unit](node:Minor%20unit).

Entries are never edited or deleted. To correct a mistake, post a reversal and then the correct entry. In this example, a 5000 top-up was recorded instead of 500:

| Txn | Reason         | Account          | Debit | Credit |
| --- | -------------- | ---------------- | ----: | -----: |
| 1   | Original       | Cash at provider |  5000 |        |
| 1   | Original       | Customer balance |       |   5000 |
| 2   | Reversal of 1  | Customer balance |  5000 |        |
| 2   | Reversal of 1  | Cash at provider |       |   5000 |
| 3   | Correct amount | Cash at provider |   500 |        |
| 3   | Correct amount | Customer balance |       |    500 |

After all three, cash has a net debit of 500 and the customer balance a net credit of 500. The error and its fix both remain visible to auditors.

Enforce the invariants in the database. Reject a transaction whose debits and credits differ per currency, write all of its entries atomically, and use a unique key on the source event so a replayed event cannot post twice. Reconcile it against provider and bank records, because a balanced ledger can still be wrong.
quotes: Can I just update this customer's balance to fix the mistake?
No. Post a reversal and a correcting entry in the ledger, so the history still adds up.

nodes.name: Double-entry bookkeeping
nodes.description: Recording every transaction as equal debits and credits across accounts, so that errors show up as an imbalance.
nodes.markdown:
Double-entry bookkeeping is an accounting method in which every transaction is recorded in at least two accounts, with total debits equal to total credits. Money is always shown as coming from somewhere and going somewhere. If the two sides differ, the record is wrong, and the system can detect it.

Debit and credit do not mean minus and plus. Their effect depends on the account type:

| Account type | Example                 | Debit    | Credit   |
| ------------ | ----------------------- | -------- | -------- |
| Asset        | Cash, provider receivable | Increases | Decreases |
| Liability    | Customer balances owed  | Decreases | Increases |
| Revenue      | Sales                   | Decreases | Increases |
| Expense      | Processing fees         | Increases | Decreases |

This explains a common confusion. When your bank "credits" your account, the bank's liability to you is rising. On your own books, the same cash is an asset and increases with a debit.

Here is a 100.00 sale with a 2.90 processing fee, in [minor units](node:Minor%20unit):

| Account             | Type    | Debit | Credit |
| ------------------- | ------- | ----: | -----: |
| Provider receivable | Asset   |  9710 |        |
| Processing fees     | Expense |   290 |        |
| Sales revenue       | Revenue |       | 10000 |
| **Total**           |         | **10000** | **10000** |

When the provider pays out, debit bank cash by 9710 and credit the provider receivable by 9710. The receivable returns to zero, showing that nothing is still owed.

A single-column approach would record only +100.00 of sales, and finance would then find the bank deposit 2.90 short on every order. Double entry puts the fee in its own account, so the gap is explained.

Balance each currency separately. A conversion between currencies needs a foreign exchange account in each currency, because 100 EUR and 108 USD cannot be summed. Balanced entries do not prove correctness, since a wrong amount posted to both sides still balances, so the [ledger](node:Ledger) must also be reconciled against external records.
quotes: The [payout](node:Payout) is lower than sales. Where did the rest go?
Look at the fees account. With double-entry bookkeeping, each sale splits into the receivable and the fee, so the gap is itemised.

nodes.name: Payment reconciliation
nodes.description: Comparing internal payment records with provider and bank records to find and resolve differences.
nodes.markdown:
Payment reconciliation is the process of comparing your own payment records with external records, such as provider reports, a [settlement file](node:Settlement%20file) and bank statements, and resolving every difference. Internal systems can show that a payment succeeded when it did not, or miss one that did. Reconciliation is how a business finds out.

A full reconciliation usually has three layers:

| Layer | Compares                           | Finds                                 |
| ----- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| 1     | Internal [ledger](node:Ledger) and provider report | Missing or mismatched transactions   |
| 2     | Provider report and [payout](node:Payout) total   | Fees, [refunds](node:Refund) and [chargebacks](node:Chargeback) netted out |
| 3     | Payout total and bank statement    | Payouts that did not arrive          |

An item that does not match is called a break:

| Break                 | Likely cause                         | Action                                  |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Provider has it, you don't | Lost response or event          | Create the record from provider data    |
| You have it, provider doesn't | Failed call marked successful | Correct status, check fulfilment        |
| Amount differs        | Fee, [partial capture](node:Partial%20capture), currency       | Post an adjustment                      |
| Timing difference     | Cut-off or time zone                 | Expect it to clear in the next run      |

The familiar symptom is a payout that does not equal the day's orders. The payout is net of fees, refunds and disputes, and it may span several days under the provider's cut-off. Comparing it directly with a daily sales total will always produce noise.

Match on a stable identifier that you send to the provider and receive back in its reports, and store the provider's own ID too. Run reconciliation automatically every day and track each break's age, because a timing difference clears within days while a real error does not. Fix breaks by posting a new correcting ledger entry, never by editing history. An [unknown payment outcome](node:Unknown%20payment%20outcome) that was never resolved will often first show up here.
quotes: The provider's report shows 14 payments that aren't in our database.
Those are payment reconciliation breaks from the event outage. Backfill them from provider data and check they were fulfilled.

nodes.name: Settlement file
nodes.description: A report from an acquirer or provider listing transactions, fees and adjustments that make up a payout.
nodes.markdown:
A [settlement](node:Settlement) file is a report from an [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) that lists each transaction, fee and adjustment included in a [payout](node:Payout). The bank statement usually shows one net deposit. The settlement file explains how that number was reached, so teams use it as the main input to [payment reconciliation](node:Payment%20reconciliation).

Formats vary by provider and include CSV, fixed-width files, XML and API reports. Typical fields are:

| Field            | Purpose                                     |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Batch or payout ID | Ties rows to one bank deposit             |
| [Merchant](node:Merchant) reference | Links a row to your order or payment      |
| Provider reference | Provider's own transaction ID             |
| Type             | Sale, [refund](node:Refund), [chargeback](node:Chargeback), fee or adjustment |
| Gross, fee, net  | The amounts for that row                    |
| Currency         | Settlement currency, sometimes also presentment |
| Dates            | Transaction date and settlement date        |

Rows must add up to the payout. This example uses [minor units](node:Minor%20unit):

| Row type   | Net amount |
| ---------- | ---------: |
| Sales      |      10000 |
| Fees       |       -300 |
| Refunds    |      -2000 |
| Chargeback |      -1500 |
| **Payout** |   **6200** |

A settlement file is not a transaction export from a dashboard. An export shows activity by the time it occurred, while the settlement file groups items by the payout they were paid in. A sale on Friday night may fall into Monday's file because of a cut-off, so comparing it with Friday's orders produces false mismatches.

A provider can resend a corrected file, and if its rows import twice, revenue doubles. A column changes and the parser silently reads the fee as zero. A file arrives late and the reconciliation run reports hundreds of false breaks.

Keep the raw file unchanged, and make the import idempotent using the file identifier and a stable row key. Validate that rows sum to the stated total before accepting the file, and alert when a file is missing or its schema changes.
quotes: Revenue doubled on Tuesday, but the bank balance didn't.
The provider resent the settlement file and we imported it twice. Dedupe on the row key and rerun.

nodes.name: Payment routing
nodes.description: Choosing which acquirer, network or rail handles a payment, based on cost, approval odds, availability and rules.
nodes.markdown:
Payment routing is the decision about which path a payment takes: which [acquirer](node:Acquirer), which debit network, or which bank rail. A [merchant](node:Merchant) with several providers can route each payment based on the card, country, amount and current performance.

| Strategy           | Decides by                                | Trade-off                                  |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Local acquiring    | Matching acquirer to the [issuer](node:Issuer)'s country | Better approvals and lower [cross-border fee](node:Cross-border%20fee) costs, more contracts |
| Least-cost         | Expected fees                             | May lower approval rates                   |
| Performance-based  | Recent [authorization rate](node:Authorization%20rate)                 | Needs volume and monitoring                |
| Failover           | Provider or route health                  | Must handle uncertain outcomes             |
| Rule-based         | Regulation, currency or product           | Rules drift without maintenance            |

Routing is the decision. [Payment orchestration](node:Payment%20orchestration) is the wider layer that carries it out and also covers integrations, tokens and reporting.

Some routing is shaped by law. In the US, the Durbin Amendment requires debit cards to be enabled on at least two unaffiliated networks, which gives merchants a routing choice. In the EU, the [Interchange Fee](node:Interchange%20fee) Regulation addresses the choice of brand on co-badged cards.

Failover after a timeout can charge a customer twice. Provider A does not answer, the router sends the same payment to provider B, B approves it, and A's approval then appears. The customer has a [double charge](node:Double%20charge), and an idempotency key cannot prevent it because each provider has its own key space. Fail over only after a definite failure, such as a connection refused before sending or a retryable decline. For a timeout, resolve the first attempt by querying its status.

Stored cards add a constraint. A token issued by one provider usually cannot be charged through another unless you hold portable credentials or [network tokens](node:Network%20token). Log the chosen route and reason on every attempt.
quotes: Provider A timed out, so the router sent it to B. Now the customer has two charges.
Payment routing can't fail over on a timeout. Check A's status first and only reroute if it didn't go through.

nodes.name: Payment orchestration
nodes.description: A software layer connecting a business to several payment providers and methods through one integration.
nodes.markdown:
Payment orchestration is a software layer that connects a business to multiple payment providers, [acquirers](node:Acquirer) and payment methods through one integration. The [merchant](node:Merchant)'s checkout calls the orchestration layer, and that layer decides where each payment goes and normalises the responses.

| Function            | What it does                                                |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Connectors          | Translates one internal API to each provider's API          |
| [Payment routing](node:Payment%20routing)     | Picks a provider per transaction                            |
| Token management    | Stores credentials so they can be used across providers     |
| Retry and failover  | Applies rules after a failed attempt                        |
| Normalisation       | Maps [decline codes](node:Decline%20code) and statuses to one model                |
| Reporting           | Combines data across providers                              |

An orchestrator is often confused with a [payment service provider](node:Payment%20service%20provider) or [payment gateway](node:Payment%20gateway). A PSP has acquiring relationships and processes payments. A gateway transmits payments to a processor. An orchestrator usually sits above them and depends on their contracts, so the merchant typically still needs its own agreement with each provider.

The benefits are redundancy, access to local methods and bargaining power. The layer also adds a network hop and another dependency that can fail, so an orchestrator outage can stop all payments. If it handles raw card data, it also affects [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) scope. Normalising responses can hide the detail needed to debug a decline, so keep the raw provider response.

Token ownership often causes problems at migration time. A business adopts multiple providers and finds that its saved cards are tokens owned by the original provider, which cannot be charged elsewhere. Negotiate token portability in advance, or use a neutral [card vault](node:Card%20vault) or [network tokens](node:Network%20token).

Pass a stable reference from the merchant through the orchestrator to the provider, so that a retry at any level can be recognised. Treat a timeout at any hop as an [unknown payment outcome](node:Unknown%20payment%20outcome).
quotes: Can we just add a second provider if the first goes down?
Only with payment orchestration and portable tokens. Otherwise our saved cards won't work on the second provider.

nodes.name: Authorization rate
nodes.description: The share of card authorization attempts that issuers approve, which depends heavily on how attempts are counted.
nodes.markdown:
An authorization rate, also called an approval rate, is the share of [card authorization](node:Card%20authorization) requests that [issuers](node:Issuer) approve. Teams use it to judge payment performance. The figure is meaningful only if everyone agrees on what is being counted.

The same traffic can yield different results. This example uses invented figures:

| Measure                | Approved | Total | Rate  |
| ---------------------- | -------: | ----: | ----: |
| All attempts           |      850 |  1000 | 85.0% |
| Unique payments, final outcome | 830 | 900 | 92.2% |

The first line counts every retry as a separate attempt. The second counts each payment once, using its final result. Neither is wrong, but comparing one provider's attempt-level figure with another's payment-level figure is misleading. Also decide how to treat zero-amount card checks, fraud blocks made before the issuer is asked, and [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) failures.

Authorization rate differs from conversion rate, which measures how many visitors complete checkout and includes people who abandon before paying. It also differs from [capture](node:Capture) rate, which is how many authorized payments are later captured.

A sudden fall is a common alert, and the cause is not always a provider fault. [Card testing](node:Card%20testing) floods checkout with stolen numbers that mostly fail, pulling the rate down while real customers are unaffected. An aggressive retry job has the same effect. A real problem usually concentrates in one place, such as a single issuer, [BIN](node:BIN) range, country or [acquirer](node:Acquirer).

Segment the metric by network, issuer, country, card type, channel, acquirer and [decline code](node:Decline%20code). Exclude known bot traffic into a separate view. Common improvements include sending complete data, using [network tokens](node:Network%20token), keeping stored cards fresh with an [account updater](node:Account%20updater), flagging stored-credential payments correctly, and using local acquiring. Benchmarks vary widely by industry and region, so compare against your own history first.
quotes: Authorization rate dropped eight points overnight. Is the acquirer down?
Segment it first. Declines are all from one BIN range with new cards, so it looks like card testing.

nodes.name: Stored credential
nodes.description: Card details saved with the cardholder's consent for later payments, flagged under card network rules.
nodes.markdown:
A stored credential is a card number or token that a [merchant](node:Merchant) or its provider saves, with the [cardholder](node:Cardholder)'s consent, to use for future payments. Visa and Mastercard define frameworks for these transactions. Under them, the first payment establishes the agreement, and later payments are flagged to show that the credential was stored and how it is being used.

| Stage                     | Who starts it | What must happen                                     |
| ------------------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Consent                   | Cardholder    | Agrees to storage and the terms of future use        |
| Initial transaction       | Cardholder    | Authenticated where required, flagged as first storage |
| Later customer payment    | Cardholder    | Sent as a [customer-initiated transaction](node:Customer-initiated%20transaction)             |
| Later merchant payment    | Merchant      | Sent as a [merchant-initiated transaction](node:Merchant-initiated%20transaction) with the original reference |

The original reference is usually the [network transaction ID](node:Network%20transaction%20ID) returned by the first authorization. Keep it with the saved credential, because later merchant-initiated payments must reference it.

Stored credentials are often confused with [tokenization](node:Tokenization). Tokenization is how the card number is protected, by replacing it with a substitute value. A stored credential describes the business arrangement and its transaction flags. Saving a token does not by itself create the consent or the correct flags.

The failure is often silent. A team saves cards and charges them later as if each were a normal online payment, with no stored-credential flag and no original ID. [Issuers](node:Issuer) see an unexpected transaction with no [CVV](node:CVV) and decline more of them, and European issuers may demand [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication) that the absent customer cannot complete. Renewals fail while first payments look healthy.

Record the consent text and time, the agreed purpose, the initial transaction ID and the credential's status. Do not store the CVV after authorization, which [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) prohibits. If a customer removes a saved card, stop using it.
quotes: First payments work, but renewals decline far more often.
We're not sending the stored credential flags or the original transaction ID. Issuers can't tell these are agreed renewals.

nodes.name: Customer-initiated transaction
nodes.description: A card payment the cardholder actively starts and takes part in, even when using a saved card.
nodes.markdown:
A customer-initiated transaction, or CIT, is a card payment in which the [cardholder](node:Cardholder) is present in the flow and actively takes part, for example by pressing Pay on a website or in an app. Visa calls these cardholder-initiated transactions. The card can be newly entered or saved. What makes it a CIT is the customer's involvement at that moment.

| Question                       | CIT                         | [Merchant-initiated transaction](node:Merchant-initiated%20transaction)       |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Who starts it?                 | Cardholder                  | [Merchant](node:Merchant), under a prior agreement    |
| Is the customer in session?    | Yes                         | No                                   |
| Can they complete a challenge? | Yes                         | No                                   |
| EEA and UK authentication      | [Strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication) unless exempt | Generally outside it when set up correctly |

The most common confusion is treating any saved-card payment as merchant-initiated. A returning customer who clicks Buy using a saved card is still making a CIT. In the EEA and UK, that payment falls under strong customer authentication unless an [SCA exemption](node:SCA%20exemption) applies, and the European Banking Authority has said that card payments initiated by the payer through the payee are in scope.

A CIT also normally sets up a [stored credential](node:Stored%20credential). The first payment carries the authentication and consent, and its [network transaction ID](node:Network%20transaction%20ID) anchors later merchant-initiated payments.

The failure appears when an engineer marks one-click checkout as merchant-initiated to avoid the extra authentication step. [Issuers](node:Issuer) can decline these payments, networks can treat the flag as misuse, and the merchant may lose [3-D Secure](node:3-D%20Secure) liability protection. The reverse error also occurs, when an off-session renewal is sent as a CIT and fails because nobody is there to complete a challenge.

Set the initiator from what the user is doing in that request, rather than from whether a card is saved.
quotes: Can we flag one-click purchases as MIT to skip 3-D Secure?
No. The customer clicked Buy, so it's a customer-initiated transaction and needs SCA unless an exemption applies.

nodes.name: Merchant-initiated transaction
nodes.description: A payment the merchant starts without the cardholder present, under an agreement made in an earlier transaction.
nodes.markdown:
A merchant-initiated transaction, or MIT, is a card payment that a merchant starts without the [cardholder](node:Cardholder) taking part, relying on an agreement made earlier. The merchant must have a [stored credential](node:Stored%20credential) and consent to use it, and each MIT is flagged so the [issuer](node:Issuer) can see it belongs to an existing agreement.

| Type         | Example                              | Schedule                |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| Recurring    | Monthly software subscription        | Fixed interval          |
| Instalment   | A purchase split into set payments   | Fixed number of payments |
| Unscheduled  | Account top-up when balance runs low | Triggered by an event   |
| Industry-specific | Hotel no-show or delayed charge | Set by network rules    |

Each MIT normally carries the [network transaction ID](node:Network%20transaction%20ID) of the original or a previous transaction. This links it to the [customer-initiated transaction](node:Customer-initiated%20transaction) in which the cardholder agreed. Without that link, an issuer may treat the payment as unexpected and decline it.

In the EEA and UK, an MIT is treated as outside [strong customer authentication](node:Strong%20customer%20authentication) because the payer is not involved at the time of payment. That position depends on a valid setup. European Banking Authority Q&As say SCA applies when the mandate is given, usually during the first payment. An MIT is not an [SCA exemption](node:SCA%20exemption), and labelling a payment MIT when the customer is present is misuse.

The failure teams see is a batch of renewals declined with an authentication-required code. Cards saved before SCA, or saved without authentication, have no valid agreement behind them. The customer is offline and cannot complete a challenge, so the fix is to bring them back for an authenticated payment that creates a new agreement.

A customer who forgot about a subscription may dispute it as fraud, so keep the consent record and stop billing as soon as they cancel.
quotes: Half the renewal batch failed with authentication required.
Those cards were saved without SCA, so the merchant-initiated transactions have no valid mandate. Email customers to reauthenticate.

nodes.name: Recurring billing
nodes.description: Charging a customer automatically on a schedule, using a saved card, bank mandate or local recurring rail.
nodes.markdown:
Recurring billing is the process of charging a customer automatically at regular intervals, such as monthly for a subscription. A billing system determines what is due and creates a payment on an underlying method, which sets the rules for authentication, notice and failure.

| Method                  | Permission                 | Typical failure signal        |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Card                    | [Stored credential](node:Stored%20credential), charged as a [merchant-initiated transaction](node:Merchant-initiated%20transaction) | Immediate decline |
| [SEPA Direct Debit](node:SEPA%20Direct%20Debit)       | [Direct debit mandate](node:Direct%20debit%20mandate)       | Later return or refund        |
| US [ACH](node:ACH) debit            | Authorization under Nacha rules | Later [payment return](node:Payment%20return)     |
| [UPI](node:UPI) AutoPay (India)     | Registered e-mandate       | Mandate or debit failure      |
| [Pix](node:Pix) Automático (Brazil) | Prior payer authorization  | Scheduled payment failure     |

Rules differ by market. India's E-mandate Framework, 2026, from the Reserve Bank of India, generally requires a notification before each recurring debit on cards, prepaid instruments and UPI, and additional authentication above set amounts. Consumer rules on renewal notices and cancellation also vary by market.

Recurring billing differs from a saved card used for one-click checkout, where the customer starts each payment. It also differs from [dunning](node:Dunning), which handles what happens after a recurring payment fails.

A scheduler rerun after a crash can bill the same period twice. To prevent this, use an idempotency key (a unique value marking one logical charge) built from the subscription ID and billing period, and enforce it with a unique constraint. Date arithmetic also causes errors: adding one month to 31 January has no obvious answer, so store a fixed billing anchor day and clamp it to the month's length. Mid-cycle plan changes need explicit proration rules, using integer [minor units](node:Minor%20unit) and a defined rounding direction.

Expired cards are the main cause of unintended cancellation. An [account updater](node:Account%20updater) reduces these, and dunning recovers some of the remainder.
quotes: Some customers were billed twice on the first of the month.
The recurring billing job restarted mid-run. Key each charge on subscription and period so a rerun can't duplicate it.

nodes.name: Dunning
nodes.description: The process of recovering failed recurring payments through scheduled retries and customer reminders.
nodes.markdown:
Dunning is the process of recovering a failed recurring payment through scheduled retries and messages to the customer. In subscription businesses, it mainly addresses involuntary churn, where a customer who intended to stay loses service because a payment failed.

A dunning policy combines payment actions and communication:

| Stage | Action                                                       |
| ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1     | Payment fails. Classify the decline and record the reason    |
| 2     | Run an [account updater](node:Account%20updater) check if the card may have changed    |
| 3     | Notify the customer with a link to update payment details    |
| 4     | Retry [soft declines](node:Soft%20decline) on a spaced schedule                     |
| 5     | Send further reminders and warn of service loss              |
| 6     | Restrict or cancel the subscription, and stop retrying       |

Dunning differs from a [payment retry](node:Payment%20retry). A retry is one technical attempt, and dunning is the business process that decides when to retry, what to tell the customer, and when to give up. The retry schedule must respect the rail: a [hard decline](node:Hard%20decline) should not be repeated, [card networks](node:Card%20network) limit reattempts, and Nacha restricts how a returned [ACH](node:ACH) debit can be reinitiated. Reminder content and timing may also be subject to local consumer and debt-collection rules, particularly once an amount is treated as overdue.

Dunning systems fail through missing state. A customer updates their card, but the job keeps retrying the old one and sends another warning. A customer cancels, and a scheduled retry charges them anyway, producing a complaint or a [chargeback](node:Chargeback).

Before each step, re-read the subscription, invoice and payment method, and exit if the invoice is paid or the subscription is cancelled. When a customer adds a new card, attempt the outstanding invoice once, then end the sequence on success. Track recovered revenue and recovery rate per stage to tune the schedule.
quotes: A customer cancelled last week and we charged them again today.
The dunning job didn't recheck the subscription before retrying. Exit the sequence on cancel and [refund](node:Refund) that charge.

nodes.name: Account updater
nodes.description: A card network service that gives merchants updated card numbers and expiry dates for stored cards.
nodes.markdown:
An account updater is a [card network](node:Card%20network) service that gives [merchants](node:Merchant) new details for cards they have on file when a card is reissued, expires or is closed. Visa Account Updater and Mastercard Automatic Billing Updater are the main examples. [Issuers](node:Issuer) report changes to the network, and the merchant's [acquirer](node:Acquirer) or provider requests updates, either in batches before billing or in real time during authorization.

| Response             | Meaning                         | Merchant action                         |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| New card number      | Card was replaced               | Update the [stored credential](node:Stored%20credential)            |
| New expiry           | Same number, new date           | Update the expiry                       |
| Account closed       | Card is no longer valid         | Stop billing and ask for a new method   |
| Contact [cardholder](node:Cardholder)   | Issuer gives no replacement     | Ask the customer                        |
| No match             | Issuer has no change or doesn't participate | Continue, and handle any decline |

Coverage depends on issuer participation, and some cardholders can opt out, so a stored card may still fail.

An account updater differs from a [network token](node:Network%20token). A token is a substitute credential whose lifecycle is managed by the network, so the merchant can keep charging the same token after the underlying card is replaced. Account updater returns new card data to whoever holds the original [PAN](node:PAN). [Dunning](node:Dunning), by contrast, reacts after a payment fails.

The symptom it addresses is a burst of renewal declines around month end from expired cards, with customers who never meant to leave. A related bug happens when the provider updates its vault but the merchant's own record keeps the old last four digits and expiry, so the billing page shows an expired card.

Consume the provider's update events and sync display fields. Also stop charging on a closed-account response. Updated card numbers are cardholder data, so handle them within your [PCI DSS](node:PCI%20DSS) scope, or leave them with the provider.
quotes: Renewals are failing because so many cards expired this month.
Turn on the account updater with our acquirer, and sync the new expiry dates to our billing records.

nodes.name: Split payment
nodes.description: One customer payment divided among several parties, such as a marketplace, its sellers and fee recipients.
nodes.markdown:
A split payment is a single customer payment whose funds are divided among several recipients, such as a marketplace, one or more sellers and a delivery partner. The customer sees one charge.

This example uses [minor units](node:Minor%20unit) for a 10000 order:

| Account             | Debit | Credit |
| ------------------- | ----: | -----: |
| Provider receivable |  9700 |        |
| Processing fees     |   300 |        |
| Seller payable      |       |   8500 |
| Platform commission |       |   1500 |
| **Total**           | **10000** | **10000** |

The platform absorbs the processing fee here, so its net income from this order is 1200.

A split payment differs from split tender, where one customer pays a single bill using two cards or methods.

Regulation is a central design issue. Receiving money and passing it to third parties can count as a regulated payment service or money transmission, depending on the country. Platforms commonly use a licensed provider's marketplace product, or act as a [payment facilitator](node:Payment%20facilitator) or a [merchant of record](node:Merchant%20of%20record). Get legal advice on the chosen structure, and expect [KYC](node:KYC) or [KYB](node:KYB) checks on sellers.

The hard failures occur after the split. A customer gets a [refund](node:Refund) or wins a [chargeback](node:Chargeback) after the seller has already received a [payout](node:Payout). The platform must recover the money from that seller, and if the seller has no balance or has left, the platform carries the loss. Delay seller payouts according to risk, and let seller balances go negative in the [ledger](node:Ledger) so future earnings can offset them.

Rounding is the other common bug. Splitting 10000 three ways gives 3333 each and leaves 1 unit unallocated. Use integer minor units, assign any remainder by a fixed rule, and assert that the parts sum to the total. Record the split at payment time so that later commission changes do not alter past orders.
quotes: The seller was paid out, then the buyer got a chargeback. Who covers it?
Under our split payment terms, the seller. Post it against their balance, and we carry it if they can't repay.

nodes.name: Safeguarding
nodes.description: Rules requiring non-bank payment and e-money firms to protect customer funds so they can be returned if the firm fails.
nodes.markdown:
Safeguarding is the legal requirement for non-bank payment firms and e-money issuers to protect customer money so that it can be returned if the firm becomes insolvent. In the EU, the requirement comes from [PSD2](node:PSD2) and the Electronic Money Directive. In the UK, it comes from the Payment Services Regulations 2017 and Electronic Money Regulations 2011, supplemented by Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) rules.

Firms typically safeguard in one of two ways:

| Method      | How it works                                                       |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Segregation | Keep relevant funds apart from the firm's own money, in a designated account or approved secure assets |
| Insurance or guarantee | A policy or guarantee pays out an equivalent amount if the firm fails |

Safeguarding is often confused with deposit insurance. A bank deposit may be covered by a national scheme, such as the UK's Financial Services Compensation Scheme. Money held with a payment or e-money firm generally is not. If the firm fails, customers rely on the safeguarded pool, and the insolvency process can cause delay or shortfall. A [rolling reserve](node:Rolling%20reserve) is also different, because it protects a provider from a [merchant](node:Merchant)'s losses.

The FCA's Policy Statement PS25/12 introduced a supplementary safeguarding regime that took effect on 7 May 2026, adding requirements such as monthly regulatory returns and, for many firms, annual safeguarding audits. US money transmitters are instead generally subject to state rules on permissible investments. Confirm the rules that apply to your licence with a qualified adviser.

The firm must know how much it owes customers at any time and prove that the safeguarded balance covers it, which requires an accurate [ledger](node:Ledger) and regular [payment reconciliation](node:Payment%20reconciliation) against the safeguarding account. Failures include customer funds sitting in an operating account during a [payout](node:Payout) delay and shortfalls discovered days late. Alert on any difference.
quotes: Can we pay this supplier from the customer funds account until Friday?
No, that account is for safeguarding. Customer money can't fund operations, even temporarily.
